title: ‘Jackson is rolling’: Mayor John Horhn touts promises delivered in ‘State of the City’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
About a year after Jackson Mayor John Horhn began touting that “Jackson is rising,” he unveiled a new catchphrase Tuesday at his State of the City address.
“Comebacks don’t get announced,” he told a jubilant audience at the Jackson Convention Center. “They get built. They get repaired. They get paved. And ‘Jackson is rolling.’” 
Jackson Mayor John Horhn and his family stand for the Pledge of Allegiance during his State of the City address at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Horhn, a Democrat who took office July 1, 2025, returned to the catchphrase repeatedly throughout his speech to remind Jacksonians that his administration is following through on at least some of its promises. 
New business permits are being approved faster than before, Horhn said, citing data from the Planning and Development Department. A much-anticipated bid to redevelop the dilapidated Jackson Zoo has been posted. And Thalia Mara Hall was reopened. 
“Broadway is back in Jackson,” Horhn said to whoops and cheers. 
While Jackson still lacks up-to-date annual financial reports, the city has made progress, Horhn said, in completing the 2023 audit last year. Working with the Jackson City Council, he asserted his administration erased a $25 million deficit in the city budget – a claim contested by some council members who sat behind Horhn during the speech. 
Audience members pray before Jackson Mayor John Horhn’s State of the City address at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“You deserve to know where your money goes,” Horhn said. “And anyone thinking about investing in Jackson deserves confidence that our financial house is in order.” 
The development-minded mayor praised the private investment underway in Jackson, shouting out affordable housing developments planned for Robinson and Raymond roads, as well as apartment complexes that developer Gabriel Prado is constructing in north Fondren.
Horhn also repeatedly applauded recent steps to nab what many view as Jackson’s economic white whale: A developed riverfront on the flood-controlled banks of the Pearl River. 
Some influential Jacksonians backing these efforts joined the mayor on stage, including key supporters Bishop Ronnie Crudup Sr. of New Horizon Church International, lawyer-developer Robert Graham and local restaurateur Jeff Good.
Horhn made new pledges for the city. He said his administration will repave Woodrow Wilson Road and Medgar Evers Boulevard. He pledged to publish quarterly data on permitting timelines, code enforcement and housing investments. He plans to ask the council to pass a new zoning code. And, finally, Horhn promised to redevelop Farish Street. 
“Yeah, I said that, too,” Horhn said. “We’re gonna get it done this time.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Parent advocates seek stronger AI chatbot protections in next Colorado legislative session
text:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Wesier speaks about social media safety policy on Oct. 13, 2026 in Denver. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Parents of children harmed by social media and artificial intelligence chatbots called for Colorado to pass stronger protections into law next year, while standing beside the Democrat likely to become the state’s next governor.
“When I hear from people that they know young people who have easier access to guns or fentanyl than a job, we’ve got to do something about it,” Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic candidate for governor in November, said Tuesday afternoon ahead of a symposium about online safety for young people. “When we hear young people are struggling because they’re feeling disconnected and lonely, we’ve got to do something about it.”
Parent advocates from the organization Blue Rising want state lawmakers to strengthen a law regulating artificial intelligence chatbots that passed this year. That law requires companies that operate chatbots to take steps to determine a user’s age and implement anti-self-harm protocols. It also seeks to prohibit chatbots from having sexual conversations with children.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As the new law wound its way through the legislative process, parents pushed back on what they saw as weak provisions in the policy. The law, for example, requires chatbot operators to institute “technically feasible measures” to prevent the technology from showing sexual content to minors and take “reasonable measures” to prevent harm. Parents say that language leaves it up to the technology companies themselves to self-regulate and decide what is feasible.
“It was basically two words that gave Big Tech a get-out-of-jail card. No more,” said Lori Schott, whose daughter Annalee died by suicide in 2020 after becoming addicted to social media. “With the legislation we have coming up, we are going to do anything and everything we can to change the language of that bill and possibly add others that will protect children from harmful content.”
“Those words save them from any legal ramifications and any harms that families experience, because if it’s not technically feasible to implement safety, they’re not going to do it,” she added.
Bill sponsors said during the legislative session that the language mirrored statutory requirements for landlords and companies who possess private consumer data, and they also said at the time they would be willing to work on it in future legislative sessions.
Schott and other parents who spoke on Tuesday said they were left “standing in the hallway” at the Capitol while tech companies influenced bills about social media. Google played a role in shaping the chatbot bill, according to reporting from NPR.
“Let this be the year that parents have a seat at the table, because we know these harms better than anyone,” Schott said.
She, and others, are excited about the likelihood of Weiser’s governorship next year and his proven commitment to social media protections for youth, including his work on the recent $17 billion settlement with Meta. Democrats are favored by 12 percentage points according to recent polling, and Colorado voters last elected a Republican governor in 2002.
“This upcoming legislative session brings new leadership in the governor’s office and a big opportunity to truly protect kids like Juliana,” said Cynthia Montoya, referring to her 13 year-old daughter who died by suicide after interacting with an AI chatbot. “This session, I hope that legislators will work with people who have lived in this unbelievable pain.”
She wants to see a “robust, common-sense framework” that will evolve alongside the technology.
“I am certain that many more lives, like my Juliana’s life, will be lost if we wait to improve our chatbot laws here in Colorado,” she said.
In a statement, Mary Kate Morr, the director of communications for Healthier Colorado, which led the chatbot bill, wrote that the bill was developed through an “extensive and diverse stakeholder process” with groups including mental health providers, technology companies and teen advocates.
“We used the best available data and lessons learned from other states to make Colorado’s law the strongest in the country. We had pushed for even more than was ultimately signed and consider this law a strong foundation on which we intend to continue building,” she wrote.
Blue Rising also wants to see the reintroduction of a bill that would require social media companies to take down accounts if they are sexually exploiting minors or selling guns or drugs. Gov. Jared Polis vetoed the bill in 2025 over privacy and innovation concerns.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor, corrections board appeal ruling over who can fire top prison officials
text:
Attorney General Tim Griffin (center) at a Sept. 5, 2025 press conference with Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (far left), Department of Corrections Secretary Lindsay Wallace (right) and U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton (center right). (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas is appealing a circuit court ruling that kept in place an injunction blocking two laws that gave Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders the authority to fire top corrections officials.
The attorney general’s office filed a notice that it would appeal Pulaski County Circuit Judge Patricia James’ ruling which invalidated a settlement between Sanders and the Board of Corrections. 
Arkansas judge keeps block on laws giving governor firing power over prison officials

The filing said the governor and the board would also appeal several other rulings made by James that allowed Abtin Mehdizadegan to serve as the board’s attorney and to intervene in the lawsuit along with a current and former member of the board.
The case has already been to the Arkansas Supreme Court twice. The Republican governor  asked justices to lift the permanent injunction or order James to do so earlier this year. Justices did not, instead ruling that James should consider lifting her 2025 injunction following the settlement.
Sanders and the board said a settlement agreement the board voted to accept in March, and the Supreme Court ruling, meant James had little say in whether or not to lift her earlier ruling. But the Pulaski County circuit judge disagreed.
James ruled that the settlement was “in direct conflict with the Arkansas Constitution” and the Supreme Court’s decision gave her discretion on whether to lift her injunction. 
James also ruled this month that her September ruling also applies to provisions of the settlement that prohibited Mehdizadegan and his law firm from being paid for their work by declaring they were hired illegally. The Supreme Court has previously turned away efforts by Sanders and Attorney General Tim Griffin to have Mehdizadegan disqualified as the board’s attorney.
The long-running legal battle over who has ultimate control over the state prison system’s top leaders began nearly three years ago after the board voted to suspend Joe Profiri, Sanders’ chosen corrections secretary.
Profiri said he answered to Sanders and pointed to the two laws passed by the Legislature earlier that year. The board, then led by Benny Magness, sued, arguing the laws violated Amendment 33 of the Arkansas Constitution, which safeguards the independence of the corrections board. James agreed, placing a permanent injunction on the laws last October.
After Sanders appointed several members of the board last year, giving her appointments a majority on the seven-member body, it agreed to a settlement in March. The settlement effectively saw the board reverse the position it had taken under Magness’ chairmanship, endorsing the laws it had been challenging in court.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC elections board to notify 1,392 voters flagged as potential noncitizens
text:
A pile of voter registration forms is seen at the booth of Fairfax County Republican Committee during the annual KORUS festival, a Korean cultural festival, in Tysons Corner, Virginia, in October 2016. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)The North Carolina State Board of Elections will begin sending letters this week to 1,392 registered voters flagged by the federal SAVE database as potential noncitizens. 
The letters will explain how recipients can verify their U.S. citizenship or request removal from the voter rolls if they registered to vote by mistake. 
The list is down from 1,599 registrations initially flagged in July. State election officials said they narrowed the count after cross-referencing federal data with the state Division of Motor Vehicles and other records.  
“Receiving this letter does NOT mean your voter registration has been cancelled,” the letter reads in bold type.
The letter asks people who are not U.S. citizens to complete an enclosed form to cancel their voter registration. Those who are citizens are asked to contact the board by phone or email and provide proof of citizenship so officials can update their records. 
The letter also stresses that only U.S. citizens are eligible to vote, and lists documents, such as a birth certificate, U.S. passport or naturalization certificate, that voters can provide to verify their citizenship. Those who cannot provide a copy of an official record can submit the document’s identification number and type for review, it says. 
NC has a list of nearly 1600 people flagged as noncitizens on its voter rolls. How will it be used?

“Maintaining accurate voter rolls and ensuring that only U.S. citizens participate in our elections are fundamental duties of the State Board,” said Sam Hayes, executive director of the State Board of Elections. “While these registrations represent a small percentage of our voter rolls, one ineligible registrant is still one too many.”
The move comes after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled late last month that states could continue using the SAVE database to check voter registration records for potential noncitizens while litigation continues. 
North Carolina signed up for that program last year. 
The database, run by the Department of Homeland Security, has come under criticism for flagging people who are citizens and eligible to vote. Because SAVE tracks immigration status records, its data can be outdated for naturalized citizens who obtained citizenship after their initial federal filings or license applications. 
The 1,392 registrations represent about 0.02% of North Carolina’s 7.9 million registered voters, according to the board.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: No, this is NOT the place, for a pipeline
text:
A cyclist road biking in Emigration Canyon outside of Salt Lake City, Utah. (Mike Tittel/Getty Images)Emigration Canyon residents recently found surveyors for the oil company HF Sinclair poking around their yards. Sinclair wants to lay a new 12-inch gasoline pipeline through the canyon and foothills of Salt Lake City carrying up to 4 million gallons a day of gasoline and diesel.

Since 2010 the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) has counted 9,329 fossil fuel pipeline leaking incidents, an average of at least 1.7 events per day. Even that official statistic is a vast underestimation, as Texas alone reports an average of nearly 30 pipeline leaks per day.
These statistics are not an abstraction or theoretical risk to long-time residents of Salt Lake City. In 2010, two oil spills six months apart from a Chevron pipeline rocked the city. In the first spill, 33,600 gallons of crude oil escaped from a half-inch hole in a 10-inch pipe and poured down Red Butte Creek, smothered Liberty Park Pond and continued into the Jordan River. Chevron did not respond to the leak for over 10 hours, and it took another 10 hours before they could get the pipeline shut down. The encore released 21,000 gallons of Chevron oil — same pipeline, same area.
People with homes on the creek were sickened by the toxic vapors and had multiple symptoms for years afterwards. In perhaps the most affected household, with the windows open that night, a teenager was taken to the ER with sudden blindness which lasted for several hours. In that same family, the father, previously healthy in his late 50s, died five years later of pulmonary fibrosis, almost certainly caused by the exposure. A healthy 40-year-old church groundskeeper who frequently worked near and in the creek for several years after the spill, came down with leukemia. Water sampling over a year later still found carcinogenic chemicals in some spots 400 times higher than the EPA’s “acceptable limits.”
People exposed to VOCs (volatile organic compounds) from oil spills show decreased lung function, more lung scarring, impaired heart and liver function, abnormal blood counts, and are plagued by chronic symptoms like headache, shortness of breath, skin rash, cough, fatigue, painful joints, and chest pain that can persist for years.
The most vulnerable targets are the brain, bone marrow, and chromosomes, damage that can be permanent. I’ve been an expert witness in litigation on behalf of several patients with severe neurologic impairment appearing after these exposures. The most heartbreaking are those involving children.
At least 150 toxic chemicals like benzene, ethyl benzene, toluene, and xylene (BTEX) are found in both crude oil and its refined products. Generally the chemicals in gasoline have smaller molecular weight, and therefore may be slightly less toxic to adults, but more toxic to a developing fetus. Benzene, the most well studied, is prominent in gasoline, diesel, and crude oil, and, as with other potent toxins like lead, there may be no safe level of exposure.
However, in the proposed pipeline location spilled gasoline is likely a greater hazard than crude oil. It penetrates soil and subsurface geologic formations more easily, increasing the risk of contaminating the well water that 300 Emigration homes depend on and the entire Parley’s Mountain Dell watershed serving nearly 400,000 people. Gasoline is far more flammable than oil and its vapor is explosive, adding greatly to fire risk in a canyon with only one exit road and an “extreme” fire risk rating.
Chevron dodged paying for a long-term health study of exposed Red Butte residents. Sinclair may enjoy even more immunity thanks to the Utah Legislature recently passing HB591 which prohibits common-law civil claims for public and private “nuisance,” a critical tool for plaintiffs suing companies for damage they cause.
Sinclair’s pipeline is intended to increase sales in Nevada and California. It is not to deliver more product to Utah, nor is that needed. Twenty-three percent of Utah’s refined products are shipped out of state and instate demand is projected to fall by at least 19% by 2054.
Much like Granite Construction relentlessly pursuing a new mine in Parley’s Canyon and dozens of tech companies forcing their AI data centers on communities all over the state, this is yet another example of a billion-dollar corporation force feeding Utahns from a trough of environmental gruel to fatten their own bottom line — socializing the risks and privatizing the profits.
Rather than fight for a paltry crumb of justice after the inevitable spill, Salt Lake City residents should demand that local and state officials protect their interests, not Sinclair’s. The eminent domain that Sinclair would like to invoke on property owners requires the pipeline be a “common good.” City officials need to understand it is the opposite. No, Emigration Canyon is not “the place” for a pipeline.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Press groups condemn Moore’s treatment of Sinclair journalists
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) speaks to reporters after his debate with Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maryland Public Television. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Several national press freedom groups are condemning a practice used by Democratic Gov. Wes Moore’s administration in response to inquiries from news outlets affiliated with Sinclair and The Baltimore Sun.
In a letter to Moore’s administration, the organizations — including the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Committee to Protect Journalists — took issue with Moore’s office sending “routine” inquiries from those outlets for legal review, as Moore faces a defamation lawsuit filed by David Smith, the executive chairman of Sinclair and principal owner of The Baltimore Sun.
“We urge you to instruct all Maryland agencies that Smith’s lawsuit against you is a personal matter and not an excuse to send media requests into a legal review black hole, and to cease any other unlawful retaliation against news outlets you personally dislike,” reads the letter, which is also signed by five other press and civil liberties advocacy groups.
In a statement, Ammar Moussa, a spokesperson for Moore, argued that the premise of the letter is “completely false.”
“There is no blanket refusal to engage. In the last week alone, state agencies and the Governor’s Office have answered dozens of questions from Sinclair outlets,” Moussa wrote.
Last week, state officials approved a contract that would send $50,000 in taxpayer funds to a powerhouse law firm to defend the governor against Smith’s suit.
In the lawsuit, filed this summer, Smith argues that Moore made defamatory statements about him on the MSNOW show “The Weeknight,” when he said that the media executive “had been invested in” by sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In the same appearance, Moore argued that Smith was using the Baltimore Sun “to do Donald Trump’s work and to spread his message.”
Lawyers for Moore have asked the court to dismiss the suit, arguing that Moore’s comments“are absolutely privileged” and that Moore has legal immunity.
“David Smith chose to sue the Governor. Having our legal team look over inquiries is basic due diligence, not a blackout,” Moussa wrote in his statement on Tuesday. “A litigant doesn’t get to dictate how the state protects itself, but that hasn’t stopped our agencies from doing their jobs for the people of Maryland.”
Seth Stern, the chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement on Tuesday that Moore’s actions have been “petty and ridiculous” — even if the foundation may take issue with the defamation lawsuit filed by Smith.
“While we’d certainly prefer that news executives not file defamation lawsuits that could set harmful precedents for journalists, Smith’s personal lawsuit against Moore is not the problem of Maryland taxpayers and news readers, and they’re the ones who suffer when the government evades transparency,” Stern wrote.
Moore’s decision to stonewall inquiries from Sinclair outlets is particularly concerning given the governor’s recent condemnation of President Donald Trump’s decision to ban journalists from certain news outlets from the White House.
“It’s particularly offensive that Moore seeks to boost his national profile by slamming the Trump administration’s unconstitutional attempts to ban disfavored media outlets from the White House when he’s engaged in such similar antics himself,” Stern wrote. “Moore should sit this one out and clean up his own house instead.”
The Baltimore Sun has reported that Moore’s agencies have been responding to Sun journalists’ inquiries with the following message.
“Because of the current lawsuit from Sinclair’s Executive Chairman, David D. Smith, against the Governor, we’re sending all media requests from Sinclair-affiliated outlets to our legal team for review. We’ll get back to you once that’s finished.”
The message has also been sent to journalists at Sinclair’s television stations in Baltimore and Washington, D.C. — FOX45 News and 7News — along with reporters at Spotlight on Maryland, a collaboration between the television stations and The Sun.
Moore’s “blanket refusal to answer inquiries from these news outlets” is “indicative of retaliatory motives on your part,” the press freedom groups wrote in their letter.
“Whatever concerns you have about Sinclair outlets’ coverage of you and Smith’s potential involvement in that coverage can be addressed by using your enormous platform to refute untrue or unfair reporting,” the letter reads.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: New program provides 5% down payment for qualifying South Dakota homebuyers
text:
The offices of the South Dakota Housing Development Authority in Pierre on June 15, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Housing Development Authority is starting a temporary program to give down-payment assistance to homebuyers.
The authority will launch its Give Me Five program on Nov. 2, lending qualifying homebuyers a down payment equal to 5% of their mortgage. Recipients are not required to make payments on the down-payment loan, and it’s forgiven after five years if recipients stay in the home and meet other program requirements. 
South Dakota’s housing affordability advantage has slipped

To qualify for the program, buyers must not have owned a home in the past three years, and must have a family income less than maximums ranging from $103,400 to $144,760 (depending on the county and family size). The maximum home purchase price is $410,000. 
The program will be available for a limited time through participating lenders. The authority has authorized up to 2,500 loans. 
The program is funded through surplus revenue generated by the authority’s existing First-Time Homebuyer Program. It uses tax-exempt bonds to finance mortgages at low interest rates. 
The authority is a self-supporting nonprofit created by state government. Executive Director Chas Olson said the authority has enough revenue to offer the additional incentive. In the past, the authority has offered other incentives, such as the Grants for Grads program that helped college graduates buy their first home.
“In today’s challenging housing market, first-time homebuyers need every advantage they can get,” Olson said in a statement. 
That challenging market includes mortgage interest rates above 7% and a median list price of $375,000 in South Dakota, up from about $240,000 five years ago.

name: VTDigger
title: An ‘arms embargo’ organization could cost Vermont dearly
text:
Dear Editor,
The Vermont People’s Arms Embargo (VPAE) has listed 35 Vermont companies that support thousands of jobs across our state in what effectively amounts to a blacklist. These employers provide skilled work across a range of industries, including positions advertised at six-figure salaries. Their employees own homes, raise families and send their children to Vermont schools. Losing these employers and the jobs they support could be catastrophic for communities already struggling with high taxes and the cost of living.
Vermonters deserve to know what the organizers expect this campaign to accomplish — and what they expect local families to sacrifice along the way. Under the banner of “Free Palestine,” VPAE is targeting these companies for alleged connections to a country thousands of miles away. As usual, that country is Israel. The demands, however, are being made on our communities right here at home.
The campaign advertised an Oct. 7 event in Burlington to promote its map targeting Vermont’s advanced manufacturing and technology employers. That date marks the solemn anniversary of Hamas’ savage attack on Israel and is a day of mourning and remembrance for Jewish communities around the world. The Vermont Coalition for Palestinian Liberation (VCPL) explicitly invited protesters to gather “on the 3rd anniversary of October 7th.” Its protest appeared alongside VPAE’s map presentation in the same Oct. 7 program. Choosing that anniversary for the demonstration shows a profound disregard for Jewish grief.
The words “Free Palestine” have also been invoked in horrific acts of violence. According to federal prosecutors, attackers shouted the slogan during the murders of two Israeli Embassy employees in Washington and the Boulder firebombing of people peacefully calling for the release of Israeli hostages. The ramming attack on Michigan’s Temple Israel and the massacre at a Hanukkah celebration on Bondi Beach underscore the broader threat to Jewish communities. 
Attacking Jews is not resistance.
Meanwhile, as Vermont’s student test scores remain well below proficiency goals, adult activists are helping shape how children engage politically. The Education Justice Coalition of Vermont (EJC) trains middle and high school organizers, publicly describes working with students who led pro-Palestinian school walkouts, and offers funding and help with “framing” Palestine-related events. They list VCPL among their partners and co-organizers — the same group that advertised the protest to mark the Hamas attack’s anniversary.

READ MORE

When a campaign targets Vermont employers, the stakes for students may include their families’ livelihoods and their own future job opportunities here at home. There is no social justice in encouraging our children to protest the very jobs their parents depend on to put food on the table.
Mark Treinkman, 
Athens, Vt.
and Rabbi Howard Cohen, Bennington, Vt.; Caryn Schwartz Olivetti, Burlington, Vt., a former educator; Dr. Richard Orlan, Westminster, Vt. and the Vermont Friends of Israel.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG concludes setting aside hunting tags for outfitters unconstitutional
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Oct. 13, 2026, released his analysis that a state law that reserves 10% of hunting tags for hunters who hire professional outfitters is unconstitutional. (Elk photo courtesy New Mexico Department of Wildlife)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Tuesday released a formal opinion that concludes an existing state policy reserving 10% of hunting tags for hunters who contract with private outfitters is unconstitutional and unfairly benefits wealthy, out-of-state sportsmen over local residents. 
The opinion follows a formal request from state lawmakers concerned about a 2011 law that requires the state Department of Wildlife to set aside 10% of hunting licenses in a given year to those who procure professional outfitters, who regularly charge hunters thousands of dollars for a guided hunting tour along with promises of better odds of bagging an elk, deer, bighorn sheep or other game. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Eighteen Democratic state lawmakers, many from rural areas, requested Torrez’s opinion in late April. The lawmakers wrote that they were concerned the “outfitter set-aside” left New Mexico residents “excluded from any opportunity to harvest healthy wild game as big game draw odds worsen year after year for residents.”
Separate from the 10% of tags designated for outfitters, state law requires that 84% of all tags go to in-state residents and the remaining 6% go to unguided nonresidents. Torrez’s office, in an opinion released Tuesday, notes that competition for tags is “intense,” particularly to hunt elk. 
In the hunting season that runs between late 2025 and early 2026, for example, more than 102,000 people applied. The Wildlife Department selected approximately one-fifth through a random draw to receive elk tags. 
Opponents of the “outfitter set-aside” argue that wealthy, out-of-state residents use the carveout to buy access to 10% of the tags, leaving most state residents, including those who hunt to feed their families or for Indigenous cultural practices, with lower odds to receive a tag. 
“For generations, hunting elk on our public lands hasn’t just been a sport in New Mexico. It’s been a way of life,” Torrez said in a statement Tuesday. “That tradition is being sold out from under working New Mexicans. Right now, a broken system lets wealthy out-of-state hunters buy their way to the front of the line while our own families wait year after year for a tag.”
According to a 2024 analysis from the New Mexico Wildlife Federation that Torrez’s office cited, nonresidents received more than 90% of the elk licenses the state issued to those who contracted with outfitters in the hunting season that ran between late 2022 and early 2023. 
Torrez concluded that carving out 10% of hunting licenses for outfitters violates the state’s Anti-Donation Clause, which prohibits state and local governments from giving public funds or anything else of value to private parties without a reasonable return on investment. 
“We’ve always believed the outfitter set-aside is illegal, and we’re pleased that Attorney General Torrez has concluded that in his legal opinion,” said Jesse Deubel, executive director of the New Mexico Wildlife Federation, in a statement Tuesday.
Torrez’s determination drew praise from a coalition of New Mexico hunters and tribal leaders, who said the carveout for outfitters has resulted in less food on the table for their families and called on the New Mexico Legislature to increase the share of hunting tags that go to New Mexico residents.
“Hunting has played an important role in Indigenous history and culture for generations,” said Keegan King, an Acoma Pueblo member and executive director of the Native Lands Institute. “It is woven into the fabric of our families and communities, and it remains a living tradition that carries knowledge, responsibility, and connection to place.”
The New Mexico Council of Outfitters and Guides has previously endorsed the carveout and said out-of-state hunters contribute millions of dollars to the state’s economy. Kerrie Cox Romero, the council’s executive director, did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Tuesday on Torrez’s opinion. 
Torrez’s opinion is not binding, but represents the official opinion of the state’s chief lawyer. Torrez also said he hopes the Legislature changes the law at the upcoming legislative session to repeal or reform set-aside.  
“My office is not going to let an unconstitutional program keep shortchanging New Mexico families indefinitely. If the Legislature doesn’t act, we will look at every tool available to this office, including going to court to stop it,” Torrez said in a statement Tuesday. 
Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces), who was one of the lawmakers who requested Torrez’s opinion, said in a statement Tuesday that Torrez’s determination “reaffirms what New Mexicans instinctively know: that we deserve fair access to hunting on our public lands.” 
He said the Legislature would take up the issue at the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Unknown white powder in letter shuts down Secretary of State’s office
text:
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry. A mysterious white powder was found in an envelope opened by an elections division employee at the Secretary of State's office on Tuesday afternoon. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)An unknown white powder was found Tuesday afternoon in a letter sent to the Louisiana Secretary of State’s office in Baton Rouge, according to a social media post from Secretary of State Nancy Landry. 
Deputy Secretary Trey Williams confirmed that an elections division employee at the office opened a letter around 12:20 p.m. that contained a powdery substance. Law enforcement were called in to test the substance as the elections department was evacuated and air conditioning in the office on Archives Avenue building was shut off to contain the powder. 
Williams said preliminary tests of the substance on site did not identify the powder as harmful, but a sample will undergo additional testing for confirmation. Police were no longer at the building, which plans to resume normal operating hours tomorrow, he said.
The state employee who opened the envelope was taken to the emergency room as a precautionary measure and was unharmed. 
There was no interruption in voter registration activity for the Nov. 3 election from the incident, Williams said. In-person registration ended earlier this month, and Tuesday — 20 days before Election Day — is the last day to register online to vote. 
Online registration remains available until 11:59 p.m. through the GeauxVote registration system and app.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson pledges support for border patrol, law enforcement if elected
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson (right), joined by Iowa law enforcement and members of the National Border Patrol Council, held a news conference in Urbandale Oct. 13, 2026 the organization endorsed her. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson said Tuesday she would support U.S. Border Patrol agents and law enforcement as the National Border Patrol Council endorsed her campaign for U.S. Senate.
Paul Perez, president of the National Border Patrol Council, joined Hinson at a news conference in Urbandale where he said Hinson, working with the Trump administration, helped border patrol agents get the resources needed “to finally secure the border once and for all.”
“There is no doubt in my mind; she is here to fight to make sure that Iowa is a secure state,” Perez said. “For the last four years of the Biden administration, we underwent the biggest transformation in border security history. We went from the highest of the highs to the lowest of the lows, and believe me when I tell you, that low was unbelievably low. … Now states like Iowa, every other state is a border state, and states like Iowa have to deal with the aftermath of having a completely unsecure border, in which millions of people were allowed through unvetted.”
Perez said there is “no stronger advocate for border security for your families” than Hinson, who has served in the U.S. House since 2021.
He contrasted Hinson’s border security stance with her Democratic opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek. In campaign ads, Turek has emphasized he supports border security efforts, including in an ad released Tuesday titled “Safety” that features Iowa law enforcement officers speaking about Turek’s vote in support of a 2024 law making illegal immigration a state crime in Iowa, which allows state officials to carry out certain immigration law enforcement actions.
Another ad released earlier in October features Turek meeting with Border Patrol agents in Laredo, Texas.
“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure,” Turek says in the ad. “What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it.”
But Hinson — as well as Perez — argued at the news conference that Turek supported defunding law enforcement, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol. Hinson referenced Turek’s statement during the primary campaign season that he he would not support funding for U.S. Department of Homeland Security unless there were “fundamental reforms to ICE.” This call came after two U.S. citizens were killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis earlier in 2026.
The Democratic candidate affirmed this was his position in an “Iowa Press” debate with Hinson.
“I think that we can have a couple of things be true at the same time. First, we need to have safe and secure borders. … But at the same time, I think we can recognize that we need to have a pathway to earned citizenship for those that have come here legally,” Turek said. “… I think we can all agree that we don’t want to see Americans shot in the street.”
Hinson said this statement showed Turek wants to “defund” ICE and border security.
“This election presents a very clear choice: I will fund law enforcement and border security. Josh Turek would defund it, as he said at our debate last week,” Hinson said. “So think about that. He would side with Chuck Schumer and Washington liberals over the men and women that are working hard to protect our border every single day, he’d put their liberal agenda ahead of the safety of Iowa families. Tell that to Iowa mom Michelle Root, whose daughter Sarah Root was killed by an illegal immigrant driving drunk. Tell that to the families of Laken Riley and Rachel Morin, who were murdered by criminal illegal aliens. I refuse to let that happen to another family.”
Hinson referenced the Laken Riley Act, an immigration law she voted for in the U.S. House which was signed shortly after President Donald Trump took office. The law expanded mass detention for immigrants charged or arrested for certain crimes.
A campaign spokesperson for Turek criticized Hinson for opposing “the bipartisan border deal that was endorsed by Border Patrol agents and called the “most restrictive,” “toughest,” “most stringent,” and “most conservative border bill in recent history,” a measure that failed in the U.S. Senate in 2024.
“Josh Turek is the only person in this race who has actually worked across the aisle to address immigration,” the spokesperson for Turek’s campaign said. “In the U.S. Senate, he’ll work with anyone – including President Trump – to secure the border and support law enforcement.”
Hinson also said Congress has taken action to address concerns about immigration agents’ use of force.
“By the end of August, every ICE agent should have been trained and have a body camera, and we’re working on making sure that our border patrol agents can as well,” Hinson said. “That helps protect law enforcement, and that helps protect our communities.”

name: VTDigger
title: Essex parking saga comes to a close
text:
Construction of the Essex County Courthouse in Guildhall abuts the Essex County Sheriff’s Deprtment on Wednesday, September 30, 2026. . Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Essex County sheriff lost his bid to block a parking lot redesign he says would jeopardize public safety.
Judge Joseph McLean recently dismissed Sheriff Trevor Colby’s appeal, finding that his concerns about department operations did not establish grounds to challenge the project under local zoning bylaws.
The revised plan would hinder the sheriff’s department’s ability to safely transport people from their vehicles into the station, Colby said in previous interviews with VTDigger.
The dispute centers on changes to a construction project at the Eben Judd Justice Center. The revised plan reduces parking spaces from 22 to nine and includes a retaining wall that Colby argues would limit direct access to the sheriff’s office.
But the ruling turns on who filed the challenge and whether his objections fall within zoning law, rather than whether the redesign would hamper the department.

READ MORE

Colby filed his appeal Sept. 4 in the Vermont Superior Court’s Environmental Division as an individual representing himself. He claimed standing as an “interested person”, a legal designation that allows certain people affected by a zoning decision to appeal it.
McLean wrote that Colby needed to establish that he qualified to appeal as an “interested person” under Vermont’s zoning law.
Colby argued that the sheriff’s office was his primary workplace and that he had participated by testifying and raising concerns at a July 15 public hearing.
Nicholas Low, an attorney representing the county’s assistant judges, challenged Colby’s claim to qualify as an occupant and questioned whether he was appealing personally or on behalf of his department.
After Colby hired attorney Brice Simon, Simon told the court at a Sept. 21 hearing that the sheriff was acting for the department. But neither revised the original notice of appeal, McLean wrote.
“In other words, neither the Essex County Sheriff’s Department nor Trevor Colby in his official capacity as sheriff of Essex County appealed the AMP’s decision,” McLean wrote.
Although Colby appealed as an individual, his arguments focused entirely on department operations, the judge found. McLean also found that Colby had not adequately demonstrated a violation of zoning bylaws.
“Thus, while the claimed impacts to operations may well be legitimate concerns, the court doubts that it has the authority to redress them under the bylaws,” McLean wrote.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: ADPH: International traveler in Huntsville tests positive for measles
text:
A woman scratches a measles rash. An international traveller tested positive for measles in early October, the Alabama Department of Public Health said Tuesday. (Getty Images)An international traveler who spent time in Huntsville in early October tested positive for measles, the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) said Tuesday afternoon.
The individual visited the Subway at 7900 Bailey Cove Road in Huntsville on Oct. 3, 4 and 5 between 11:30 a.m. and 3 p.m., and visited the Publix at 12796 Bailey Cove Road Southeast on Oct. 4 between 1 and 4 p.m., according to a press release. The statement did not list the individual’s vaccination status.
“In the United States, measles cases often originate from international travel,” a statement from ADPH said. “With many people traveling within the United States and to other parts of the world, ADPH emphasizes that the best way to protect yourself from measles is to get the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A private laboratory reported the positive test result to ADPH, and the department advises all who were in the vicinity of the infected person to check their vaccination status and monitor for symptoms.
As of Friday, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed 4,080 cases reported by 47 states of the highly contagious virus. In 2025, there were 2,289 cases reported by 45 states. There are currently outbreaks in Pennsylvania, Utah, Maryland, Delaware and Wisconsin. 
One Alabamian has tested positive for the disease this year, but they were out-of-state and posed no threat of an outbreak to Alabama.
There was one confirmed case of measles in Alabama in 2025: an unvaccinated child in the northern part of the state who was under five years old. The child later recovered. 
Symptoms of the disease can take seven to 14 days to present after infection, and can be particularly dangerous for infants and young children. Symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red, watery eyes and a rash.
According to CDC and ADPH guidance, children should get the first dose of the vaccine between 12 and 15 months, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years old before starting school. Adults should get one or two doses depending on individual risk factors, according to the department.
According to the CDC, 94.3% of Alabama kindergarteners were vaccinated against the disease for the 2025-26 school year. In the 2024-25 school year, 95.2% of kindergarteners were vaccinated. Herd immunity against the disease is reached at 95% vaccination.  
Measles vaccinations are common globally, but vaccination levels vary country-to-country, according to data from the World Health Organization. The individual’s country-of-origin was not provided by ADPH.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM Health watchdog turns its sights to Vermont’s broader healthcare system
text:
Mike Smith pictured at the Vermont Technical College campus in Williston in May 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The independent watchdog group tasked with assessing UVM Health’s finances since spring 2025 used the final months of its assignment to propose a broader look at how regulators, lawmakers and insurers can address healthcare affordability beyond the state’s largest health network. 
“We wanted to lay out some direction for everyone to pay attention to,” Mike Smith, who helmed the three-person liaison team, said in an interview. 
Smith, healthcare policy expert Nancy Kane and industry executive Stephen Gorman comprised the oversight group as part of the University of Vermont Medical Center’s 2025 settlement with the Green Mountain Care Board for earning more than the regulator had allowed. The team began analyzing the hospital group’s finances and operations in May of 2025 and concluded last month.
“In our minds, everything has to contribute to making healthcare affordable, and that includes the insurers, that includes the providers, that includes the regulator, that includes the unregulated,” Smith added.
The Green Mountain Care Board regulates 14 hospitals in Vermont, but those hospitals only make up 43% of Vermont insurers’ healthcare claim costs, the team’s memo noted. The remaining medical groups outside of hospitals, out-of-state hospitals and pharmacy costs are not subject to the same scrutiny. 
“This must change,” the authors wrote in their final memo. They outline a series of suggestions that could work to mediate this imbalance.
Over the course of 16 months, the group has produced six memos that have proven influential on the care board’s regulation of UVM Health and the hospital network’s own policy decisions. In May, the group found that the hospital network would need to dial up its physicians’ productivity and cut its expenses by $300 million in three years to remain solvent. The hospital group started to put those suggestions into practice soon after, with fast patient turn-around efforts, layoffs and an aggressive 2027 budget that prioritized expense cutting. A late July memo raised the alarm on how much Vermonters pay to support UVM’s medical education, and by September, the care board set a requirement on the hospital group to come up with a plan to address how much it spends on medical education by the end of the year.
Many of the team’s recommendations in their final memo call for a redesign of the Green Mountain Care Board’s process. The wide-reaching memo comes as the care board is already primed for a change. Its chair, Owen Foster, is set to step down, and the search for a replacement is underway. Smith, who leads the liaison team, is on the nominating committee for the new chair.
Currently, the care board approves rate increases for health insurance plans sold on Vermont’s Affordable Care Act marketplace, and to do so, board members consider how much an insurer needs to earn in order to pay out all of its claims and just how much ratepayers can afford to pay in premiums. 
Regulators should flip that, the liaison team wrote. Regulators should decide how much more in premiums payers can afford, which then would drive how much insurers should reimburse for services, such as hospital care and drugs. 
“I agree with that philosophically,” Foster, the board chair, said, but he doubts the feasibility of pulling down costs for the remaining 57% of claims that Vermont insurers pay out beyond regulated hospitals. For instance, he’s skeptical of how much power BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont, the main insurer on the state healthcare marketplace, really has to push pharmaceutical companies to lower prices. But hospitals are approaching their cost-cutting limits and can’t be the only source of savings, Foster said. 
The care board has the authority to set hospital budgets each fiscal year, and it has become Vermont’s primary approach to regulating healthcare costs.
“How can we achieve affordability in other ways? It’s gotten harder and harder,” Foster said. 
Smith agrees. His group’s recommendation that the hospital cut $300 million of expenses in three years, for instance, is a huge number, he said, and a one-time thing.
“Spreading the cost pressure beyond hospitals” is essential, he said.
For instance, the regulator and the state can address high pharmaceutical costs in Vermont, which are 13% higher than New England’s average, the team wrote. The authors suggest the care board commission a study to better understand why these pharmacy costs are so high and how the state can bring them into line with the region’s average. 
What about the other unregulated costs insurers pay for — out of state hospitals, private medical groups, drugs? And what about all the people who get healthcare coverage from their employers? The state and the care board should broaden their approach to include those considerations, too, the liaison team wrote.
The authors suggested new metrics the board could use in its budget orders to hospitals. Doing so would require a change in statute, but Foster is all for it, he said. 
That could include considerations such as patients’ payments relative to their household income, or how much an employer puts toward health insurance relative to employee wages. The care board and hospitals could regulate budgets with an eye to multi-year plans and longer-term sustainability, rather than on a year-to-year basis. The Vermont Association of Hospitals and Health Systems has been advocating for this type of longer-term budget review.
“Hospitals will continue to work on becoming more efficient and transforming care, but we’re not going to succeed with just cutting costs — we also need to grow,” Devon Green, a senior vice president of the hospital association, said. “Another side of the coin is growing our population and economy.” 
As the liaison’s engagement concludes, its members will keep watching the projects they have set in motion. Stephen Gorman, one of the team’s members, will check in with the hospital network on its progress every three months, for the next year.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Southern leader wants new higher ed formula to address historic underfunding
text:
The F. G. Clark Activity Center at Southern University in Baton Rouge is also known as the "Mini-Dome" and is a multi-purpose facility used for campus and community events. (Photo provided by Southern University)Interim Southern University President Orlando McMeans wants the task force studying how to revamp the state’s higher education funding formula to take underfunding of Louisiana’s largest historically Black college into consideration. 
McMeans asked the task force, which met Monday at the State Capitol, to take into account the $1.2 billion disparity in what LSU has received since the 1980s as it reconfigures the formula to ensure Southern, or any other university, is not financially harmed by the outcome. 
“There were some assumptions made, in my opinion, when (the current) formula was put together, it assumed that … all institutions begin from the same baseline,” McMeans said. “That’s definitely not factual.” 
“I would just ask that we do look at the 1.2 billion not as a whole, but as far as (increasing) our baseline (funding),” McMeans said. 
The gap was brought to the forefront of higher education funding discussions in 2023 when the Biden administration sent letters to 16 governors, including Gov. John Bel Edwards, whose states have historically shortchanged their Black land grant universities. 
Southern and LSU are among the more than 100 federal land grant universities in the United States. They were first established in the 19th century to create schools with a focus on teaching agriculture, science, engineering and military science. The colleges receive additional federal benefits, but states must match certain funds with their own dollars — a requirement Louisiana has not always met. 
The Biden administration found Louisiana had shortchanged Southern University to a tune of $1.2 billion less in comparison to LSU, the state’s other land grant institution with a predominantly white student body. LSU did not admit Black students until the 1960s. 
Similar disparities were found in other states, including Missouri, where alumni of of Lincoln University filed a lawsuit over a $549 million funding disparity earlier this month. 
Former Southern President Dennis Shields and former LSU President William Tate both called on the legislature to address the funding disparity. 
McMeans said he would like to see a $60 million to $100 million investment from the legislature to address infrastructure issues on campus, including an aging power grid that has led to repeated power outages and class cancellations. 
“This is decades and decades of deferred maintenance that contributed to these deficiencies in our utilities infrastructure,” McMeans said in an interview. 
McMeans said several years of disparate funding have impacted not only infrastructure but also student services and Southern’s ability to offer programs that meet the state’s workforce needs. 
McMeans’ request came at the second meeting of the Legislative Higher Education Funding and Formula Task. 
Questions about the formula were first raised earlier this year when some conservative lawmakers became aware of an old state metric that incentivized universities to graduate already-enrolled minority students. Though it had already been removed from the formula, this metric became the topic of an investigation by the Trump administration, which considers the standard discriminatory. 
The removal of the metric moved money away from Southern and primarily-white universities like LSU, one of the most racially diverse universities in the Southeast, with about 37% of all LSU students being non-white. 
Louisiana’s higher education funding problems are not new ones, although they have become more acute. 
During Gov. Bobby Jindal’s tenure from 2008-16, the state was in a self-inflicted fiscal crisis, with the governor choosing to use single-year budget surpluses to fund ongoing state government expenses. Higher education was on the chopping block annually to balance the budget, leading colleges and universities to switch from being primarily state-funded to student tuition-supported. 
Higher education leaders have said that Louisiana’s public colleges and universities are underfunded by more than $800 million compared with where they were at the beginning of the Jindal administration. This analysis doesn’t take into account the disparate funding between the state’s two land-grant universities, which stretches back to at least the 1970s. 
Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation has created additional constraints across state government. Gov. Jeff Landry has kept higher education spending at a standstill since he took office in January 2024.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana considers banning bail for those convicted of crimes against minors
text:
Rep. Debbie Billion speaks to the House and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday, May, 26, 2022. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana voters could remove the power of judges to grant bail to persons convicted of certain crimes involving minors. 
Constitutional Amendment 3, one of 10 proposed changes on the Nov. 3 ballot, was proposed by Rep. Debbie Villio, R-Kenner, who chairs the House Criminal Justice Committee. 
Post-conviction bail can be granted at a judge’s discretion before the convicted person reports to prison, such as when their case is on appeal or they haven’t been sentenced yet. Judges are currently allowed to grant bail except when someone is charged with an offense that’s punishable by death and there is a high degree of evidence of their guilt. 
An alleged perpetrator could also be ineligible for bail if a judge determines they are a high flight risk or pose a danger to the public, according to the Public Affairs Research Council. 
If the Amendment 3 passes, judges would no longer be allowed to grant bail for persons convicted of certain crimes in which the victim is under age 18. The offenses include rape and other sex crimes, kidnapping and human trafficking. 
In a written statement, Villio said she filed the bill following two recent incidents of child sexual abusers being granted bail, one who lived near his victim and another who is now on the run. 
“Judges should generally have discretion over post conviction bail,” Villio said. “But when a convicted child rapist could harm our most vulnerable population, our children, release should never be an option.” 
Villio’s bill easily passed the legislature with just one legislator, Sen. Sam Jenkins, D-Shreveport, in opposition. In an interview, Jenkins said his vote against the bill was accidental and that he supports the amendment. 
There was little to no discussion of the proposal at any stage of the legislative process. 
The Power Coalition, a group of progressive advocacy organizations, is in opposition to the amendment. 
“Judges should be able to look at each case. Our justice system makes mistakes, and appeals are an important part of due process,” the organization wrote in its voter guide. 
Leaders for a Better Louisiana, a civic organization that primarily advocates for education and fiscal issues, is neutral on the amendment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Farm, fuel groups celebrate EPA proposals to reallocate small refinery exemptions
text:
EPA is proposing to reallocate small refinery exemptions to keep renewable fuel standards consistent. Pictured is an ethanol plant in Atlantic. (Photo by Cecilia Lynch/USDA)Farmers and biofuel producers in Iowa are celebrating a proposal from U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin to reallocate renewable fuel requirements from which small refineries received an exemption. 
The move ensures that renewable fuel blending standards set by the EPA are maintained after small refineries — that prove they would receive “disproportionate economic hardship,” by complying with the renewable fuel standards — receive exemptions from EPA. 
At the end of August, EPA fully or partially exempted nearly 30 small refineries from the 2025 renewable fuel standard obligations, but also said it planned to reallocate 100% of the fuel exempted from the small refineries. 
Fuel producers satisfy EPA’s annual renewable fuel standards by either blending renewable fuels, like ethanol or biodiesel, into their products or by purchasing credits to offset the gas they produce. 
Zeldin, as part of his tour through Iowa, proposed two possible avenues to reallocate the renewable identification numbers, or RINs, while in Peosta Tuesday. 
The first option would spread the more than 770 million RINs worth of exempted renewable fuel equally across 2026 and 2027 compliance years, while the second option would add the exempted RINs to the 2027 compliance year. 
Zeldin’s visit, and the announcement, follows several stops in Iowa from Trump administration officials ahead of the November midterm election where Iowa has a slate of highly competitive races. The EPA news release on the proposal included statements from Iowa’s all Republican congressional delegation, the majority of whom are on the ballot.
Biofuel producers, and farmers growing biofuel feedstocks, have opposed the small refinery exemptions in the past. Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird has urged feds to investigate the refineries to ensure they aren’t manipulating the program. 
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, has said passing a law to allow year-round access to E-15 fuel would likely require compromises on small refinery exemptions to get enough votes to move forward. 
The Iowa Corn Growers Association said in a statement Tuesday that growers met with Zeldin while he was in Iowa to again ask for the exempted gallons to be reallocated. Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper said the move from EPA sends “a strong market signal that energy independence matters, while supporting farmers and biofuels producers.”
Lee Brooke, the Iowa Soybean Association president, also thanked EPA for the move toward reallocation, which he said comes as farmers are “navigating a challenging farm economy.” 
“This proposal offers the potential for greater certainty and much-needed domestic demand for soybeans if finalized later this year,” Brooke said in a statement. “We’re encouraged by this step forward and urge the EPA to finalize the rule swiftly to help provide the market certainty farmers need.”
Iowa Renewable Fuels Association President Monte Shaw also called for EPA to finalize the rule. 
“Today is a great first step, and we thank Administrator Zeldin and the EPA for sending a strong signal to farmers and biofuels producers that these gallons matter,” Shaw said in a statement. “Fully reallocating the lost gallons will ensure the robust 2026-2027 RFS blending levels remain intact, thereby supporting Iowa’s biofuels plants and providing the market certainty our industry needs to keep growing.” 
Iowa’s Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said a strong renewable fuel standard and reallocating the small refinery exemptions would be “an important step toward delivering the certainty our farmers and biofuel producers need to invest and grow.”
According to a news release from EPA, the agency is accepting public comments on the proposed reallocation rules until Dec. 4.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Gov. Wes Moore orders state agencies to target youth car thefts
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore's latest directive targets car thefts among youth in Montgomery County and Baltimore City. (Photo by WTOP)Gov. Wes Moore issued a directive Tuesday for the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services to immediately implement a pilot program for youth-involved car thefts in Baltimore City and Montgomery County, areas that have had an increase in motor vehicle thefts in the past year.
Moore’s directive, which will remain in effect until further notice, comes after a crash involving a motorcyclist and stolen car driven by a 12-year-old. The motorcyclist, 69, later died. 
“Public safety is my top priority and I am concerned by the recent frequency of motor vehicle thefts involving youth and young children,” Moore said in a statement. “Most tragically recent incidents have resulted in severe injuries and fatalities across our communities. We cannot wait for a tragic crash to be the first point of meaningful intervention. We must act decisively to interrupt this pattern of behavior before more lives are lost.”
In an emailed response to Maryland Matters, the Department of Juvenile Service said it plans to “strengthen coordination through existing Youth of Concern meetings to identify youth at risk, respond quickly to incidents, and connect youth and families with appropriate services and supports, including younger children who are served with community and/or residential services through the Child in Need of Supervision process.”
The governor’s office said the program can mirror one implemented in Minnesota in 2021. Part of the focus is to reduce youth and young adults committing vehicle thefts and direct resources toward intervention programs. The governor’s office said it hopes it will build on the juvenile services’ gun-violence prevention program known as Thrive.
The Democratic governor and Democratic-controlled legislature have focused on policies on youth reform such as a law signed in 2024 that requires youth charged for motor vehicle thefts to receive a Children in Need of Supervision petition. The petition would allow that youth and the youth’s family to qualify for a variety of services.
One of the top criminal justice reform policies went into effect Oct. 1, known as the Youth Charging Reform Act. It makes it more difficult to charge youth as adults and try them in adult court. However, serious charges such as first-degree murder or rape still go directly to adult court. 
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) questioned Tuesday whether the directive changes how the state addresses juvenile crime. In addition, he’s skeptical of the directive being released four weeks before the Nov. 3 general election.
“It announces an intervention strategy without establishing measurable outcomes, a clear deadline for demonstrating results, or additional funding and enforcement authority,” Hershey said in a text message. “Maryland families have serious concerns about juvenile crime and accountability, and this directive falls woefully short of addressing those concerns.”
An initial status report on the pilot program is due to the governor’s office by Dec. 1.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Lawmakers weigh more regulation amid mistrust in Oklahoma’s marijuana testing
text:
House lawmakers and medical marijuana industry stakeholders listen to a presentation on potential regulatory solutions at the Oklahoma Capitol on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The Oklahoma Legislature should hit pause on further regulating the state’s medical marijuana industry to allow recent laws to take full effect, one legislator said Tuesday. 
Rep. T.J. Marti, R-Broken Arrow, said lawmakers have created enough cannabis laws since voters first legalized medical marijuana in 2018, and everyone would benefit from waiting to pass any additional regulations. Marti has taken the lead on various marijuana regulatory bills over the past few years and currently chairs the House Alcohol, Tobacco and Controlled Substances Committee.
“I’ve been saying let’s see what shakes out from the things that we’ve done the first six years,” he said. “Give the industry a break and give it time to show us if the changes we made are beneficial.”
Still, House lawmakers heard from medical marijuana patients and industry advocates, laboratory testing businesses and the state’s regulatory agency at an interim study on Tuesday. They proposed over a dozen more ways the industry could be further regulated amid mistrust in cannabis testing and safety. The Legislature has retroactively passed regulations since voters approved legalization of the industry. 
The medical marijuana industry needs to work together to say what it needs from lawmakers, Marti said, because conflicting solutions are being proposed.
“We need you guys to come together with things that the industry wants help with solutions,” he said. “And we have a lot of offers today. I’m guessing if I posted, ‘This is what we’re going to take up this year,’ there would be at least 50% hate out there for all of these issues. So again, that’s not normal across any other industry, other than maybe oil and gas.”
Mistrust in medical marijuana testing
Marion McNabb, a cannabis and policy researcher, said a recent report on Oklahoma’s medical marijuana industry revealed that 30% of surveyed patients have some level of distrust in the accuracy of laboratory testing in Oklahoma. 
The surveyed business owners also said there’s a lack of transparency and communication on requirements and that testing can be unreliable, she said. 
Currently, the state relies on about a dozen independent labs to confirm safety and quality of marijuana products.
Rep. Jacob Rosecrants, D-Norman, said he thinks the Legislature needs to focus further regulation on expanding test labs’ capabilities to identify pesticides and other hazardous substances through new technology and approved methodology. 
Rosecrants, who hosted the interim study, also said the state needs to prepare itself for the federal government’s change in its classification of marijuana. 
These priorities could also potentially be achieved through the administrative rules process, he said. 
“We’ve got to get a hold of what we’re ingesting,” Rosecrants said. “Plus, not only have I spoken to patients that have ingested or smoked something that made them sick, it happened to me too.”
Barret Brown, chief administrative officer for the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority, speaks to House lawmakers Oct. 13, 2025 about the state’s marijuana testing. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Rosecrants said his constituents are questioning why it’s taken the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority so long to get its quality assurance lab fully up and running. 
Barrett Brown, the chief administrative officer for the agency, said the lab is operational but still awaiting accreditation for certain testing capabilities. The lab is intended to regulate the independent, licensed testing facilities. 
Suggestions on improving marijuana testing ranged from aligning testing criteria with existing national standards to targeting families of compounds when testing marijuana rather than listing out every harmful pesticide in state law. 
Gillian Schauer, executive director of the Cannabis Regulators Association, said the testing model in Oklahoma is high stakes because products are only tested at the end of the process, so failing a test means losing high quantities of a marijuana product. 
Testing ends up being the only marker of whether or not something is safe, she said. 
“There’s pressure on labs to falsify things, there’s pressure from licensees sometimes to try to get something through because they don’t want to lose the inventory,” Schauer said. “And this creates, again, some incentives that can be misaligned. We need better methods.”

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington man accused of killing his wife with a flashlight denies murder charge
text:
Bal Khadka is arraigned in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Khadka is charged with second degree murder in the death of his wife Lila. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A Burlington man is accused of killing his wife by beating her with a flashlight in front of young children, according to charging documents made public Tuesday. 
Bal Khadka, 44, through his attorney, entered not guilty pleas Tuesday morning during his arraignment in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington to a charge of second-degree murder in the death of his wife, Lila Darjee Khadka, in a residence on South Champlain Street.
Bal Khadka also entered not guilty pleas to three charges of child cruelty, with court records stating that the fatal beating took place with three children in the residence.
Attorney Stacie Johnson, a public defender, represented Bal Khadka at the hearing Tuesday. Johnson could not immediately be reached Tuesday for comment. 
A Nepali interpreter translated Tuesday’s court proceeding for Bal Khadka, who sat at the defense table next to his attorney.  
Judge Robert Katims granted a prosecution request to hold Bal Khadka in jail without bail.
“Mr. Khadka is charged with a brutal assault in which he bludgeoned his wife with a flashlight,” Chittenden County Deputy State’s Attorney Marykate Moore wrote in a motion seeking to hold Khadka without bail filed ahead of Tuesday’s hearing. “The act was witnessed by three juveniles and recorded by one of them.”
Police responded to the Champlain Street residence a little before 6 a.m. Saturday after receiving several 911 calls, with one of the callers reporting hearing a child screaming, Detective Cpl. Erica Schaller of the Burlington Police Department wrote in a charging affidavit.
Outside the residence, police said they found a 10-year-old child, frantic and crying, reporting that she and a friend, who both had been in the residence, had left the building through a window on the first floor, and her father was striking her mother and needed help. 
Officers at the residence found Lila Darjee Khadka on a bed unresponsive and suffering from head injuries, the affidavit stated. She was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington where she died Sunday evening, Schaller wrote in the filing.
Police said they saw Bal Khadka in the living room, trying to put shoes on a young child, and he said “Hello” in a low, calm voice, appearing unbothered by police there.
Police said three children were at the residence, all ages 10 or younger, including a friend of one of the Khadkas’ children who was there for a sleepover. 
One of the children, the charging affidavit stated, recorded audio of the incident on a cellphone, capturing the moments before the assault, during the assault and the arrival of police and emergency services, court records stated.
In the audio recording, according to the court filing, a girl could be heard saying what sounds like, “Dad no,” and then the girl starts screaming. 
Two of the children reported witnessing Bal Khadka repeatedly striking Lila Darjee Khadka with a large black and green flashlight, according to the court filings. Police reported later finding a large black and green flashlight in the top drawer of a dresser in a bedroom.
Bal Khadka was arrested and taken to the Burlington Police Department where he made no statements about the incident, though he repeatedly asked why he was in handcuffs, the charging document stated.   
The filing described Bal Khadka as “stone-faced” and “appeared unaffected by the incident.”
The children reported to police that Bal Khadka had been using drugs leading up to the incident, the records stated.
According to court records, Bal Khadka has prior convictions for drunken driving, violating an abuse prevention order and violating conditions of his release.
Also, court records show an aggravated domestic assault charge in Chittenden County stemming from an incident in 2020 against Bal Khadka that was dismissed by the prosecution.
“This was a charge that stemmed from an incident in October 2020 – at the height of COVID, and as the prosecution progressed Lila made the decision not to engage with the prosecution and indicated she was not interested in testifying and wanted the charge dismissed,” Chittenden County State’s Attorney State’s Sarah George stated in an email Tuesday in response to questions.
George added that the prosecution could not prove the case without her testimony so the charge was dismissed in 2021.
“This is very common and not meant to blame Lila for her decision. It’s truly a false choice,” George added. “Victims of domestic violence are not just exposed to and dealing with physical abuse, but also significant mental and emotional abuse, financial exploitation, and shared custody of children.”
George added that such cases are often one person’s word against the other.
That “means that the victim is almost always required to testify in order to prove the case – which actually puts her in a position to be cross examined by defense counsel, and puts her at greater risk of escalated abuse,” George stated.  
George, in the email Tuesday, said the Khadka children are “safe with family.”
Khadka was listed by the Vermont Department of Corrections on Tuesday afternoon as incarcerated at the Northwest State Correctional Facility in St. Albans.
If convicted of the murder charge alone, he faces up to life in prison. His next court date is set for Oct. 26.
