name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: PJM Interconnection issues alerts warning of tight electricity supplies
text:
PJM Interconnection alerted power plant owners and electric utilities Monday of the need to take steps to avoid rolling blackouts as the demand for power approaches the grid’s current maximum capacity. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The electricity grid operator for a broad swath of the mid-Atlantic and Midwest warned this week that warm weather and maintenance outages could push the system close to its limits.
PJM Interconnection alerted power plant owners and electric utilities Monday of the need to take steps to avoid rolling blackouts as the demand for power approaches the grid’s current maximum capacity. It called on them to suspend maintenance and keep generators online where possible to ensure the grid remains stable through Wednesday. 
Also on Monday, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued an emergency order at PJM’s request allowing it to order power plants to operate as needed, including exceeding limits on air pollution. Additionally, it allows PJM to direct data centers and other large users to switch to on-site back up generators before it is forced to institute rolling blackouts and  curtail electricity exports outside of the PJM coverage area.
“This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including backup power, available to use as needed,” U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He added the Trump administration is committed to using every available tool to prevent blackouts. He placed blame for current conditions on past leaders’ energy policies that he said have made the grid “more vulnerable to the risk of blackouts when the sun doesn’t shine or the wind doesn’t blow.”
PJM said Monday it has recalled or canceled transmission and generation outages to the extent possible. It expects generation capacity to be reduced by 62,000 megawatts during the alert. 
In a letter to the DOE on Sunday requesting the emergency measures, PJM warned that due to the combined effects of increased demand, maintenance and significant export obligations, the grid is expected to be within 900 megawatts of its reserve margin. That’s roughly the equivalent of a single large power plant.
Based near Philadelphia, PJM’s footprint includes 67 million electricity customers in 13 states and stretches from New Jersey to Illinois and from the New York-Pennsylvania border to North Carolina.
Spokesman Jeffrey Shields said the conditions PJM is experiencing have been felt by regional grid operators across the country. 
He said base load electricity demand is increasing faster than new generating capacity can be added to the system, while unpredictable weather patterns are reducing the time available for maintenance.
Power lines run across the ChesLen Nature Preserve in Chester County, Pa. (Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“This is the new reality that grid operators are facing, but PJM is confident that our procedures, along with the DOE orders, gives us additional tools to maintain our reserve margins and allow us to operate reliably,” Shields said.
Shields added that PJM is working with state and federal policymakers to address the conditions by increasing supply on multiple fronts, including accelerating the connection process for new plants and removing state permitting barriers that are outside of PJM’s jurisdiction.
Jon Gordon, senior director at renewable energy industry group Advanced Energy United, said it’s unusual to have an energy emergency in the autumn, when moderate weather causes electricity demand to ease. 
“What’s usually a routine maintenance season is now an emergency,” he said. “It’s all reflective of the tightening of supply on the PJM grid.”
Gordon said the blame lies in PJM’s handling of a flood of renewable energy projects seeking permission to connect to the grid. The organization was so overwhelmed that it closed the queue from 2022 until earlier this year while it cleared the backlog and reformed procedures for interconnection requests.
And, in July, it fell 6,800 megawatts short of its goal to procure standby capacity, needed to ensure supply during times of peak demand. PJM holds auctions each year, when power plant owners bid on contracts to supply that capacity.
“That’s a big chunk of generation that didn’t really show up that PJM wanted to contract with, so now we’re seeing the consequences of that,” Gordon said.
The state House Energy Committee recently advanced three bills addressing electricity company profits, data center infrastructure costs, and ensuring speculative developments do not skew electricity demand forecasts. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
In April, PJM announced that it had reopened its interconnection queue, accepting 811 new projects equivalent to 220,000 megawatts of new generating capacity. Under a reformed process, it said it would prioritize projects that were further along and better positioned to be completed by considering factors such as up-front financial commitments and ownership of land on which to build.
But David Masur, executive director of PennEnvironment, said the current crisis is the result of a lack of foresight by PJM. 
“This is emblematic of the old adage, “You make your bed and then you lie in it,’” he said.
While the interconnection queue was closed, older fossil fuel power plants continued to retire, reducing overall capacity, Masur noted. And manufacturing lead times for major components of new power plants, such as turbines and transformers, have increased, slowing their addition to the grid.
PJM has prioritized natural gas-fired power plants over renewable energy resources like wind, solar and battery storage, which are cheaper, faster and cleaner. 
“These are ideas that have been around for years and policymakers and advocates have been pushing them on this for years,” he said, adding that meeting demand on an emergency basis, “leads to decisions that are more expensive and dirtier for ratepayers.”
Monday’s alert is the second time this fall that PJM has asked plant and transmission operators to stay online during a forecast spike in demand. On Sept. 17, it issued a maximum generation alert and a load management alert. 
The tighter conditions were driven by electricity exports to regions in the south and west experiencing unseasonably hot weather in addition to planned outages as the maintenance season began, PJM said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Geothermal energy projects in New Mexico receive $17.3M in state funding
text:
The New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department announced on Oct. 8, 2026, that four projects, spread throughout the state, received nearly $20 million in grants to research viable areas for geothermal energy development. (Courtesy of Bureau of Land Management New Mexico via Flickr)Four geothermal energy projects across New Mexico recently received more than $17 million to evaluate potential “hot spots” across the state. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Geothermal energy taps into heat under the Earth’s surface to generate electricity. 
State leaders have eyed geothermal energy alongside renewables such as wind and solar as deadlines approach to comply with the landmark Energy Transition Act’s renewable energy goals. An academic report released last year indicated the state has the potential to be a leader in the field.
According to Rebecca “Puck” Stair, director of the New Mexico Energy Conservation and Management Division, these particular projects all address the “thorniest spot” of geothermal energy development: the lack of knowledge about the Earth’s subsurface. 
“All four of these grants are aimed at doing research on the subsurface in four different zones in New Mexico,” she said, “which we are pretty sure are hot zones and that’s what this research will confirm.” 
The grants come via the Geothermal Projects Development Fund created by state lawmakers in 2024. New Mexico Institute of Technology received the largest one: $10 million to drill a test well in Socorro County. Other recipients included New Mexico State University, which received $2.85 million to survey for geothermal potential around Las Cruces; the Jicarilla Apache Nation, which received $2 million to survey around Dulce; and $2 million to the San Ildefonso Pueblo to conduct geothermal modeling and exploration in the Pueblo, according to a New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department news release.
Stair said the state should know if the areas are viable for building further geothermal infrastructure by June 30, 2027, and will publish the data for the public.
From that point, the timeline will be in the hands of private developers, where there is “a lot of interest and that’s the reason the timeline is aggressive,” Stair said. Private developers “are ready to move as soon as we have an inkling of data.”
The state’s largest electric provider, PNM, has already tapped into a southern New Mexico geothermal plant.
Entities eligible for Geothermal Development Projects include municipalities, counties, state agencies, public schools, universities, and Native American Nations, Tribes and Pueblos. When asked if there are additional projects pending fund approval, Stair told Source NM that there is a “wait list.”
New Mexico is well poised for continued geothermal energy development, Stair said, because “we already have the workforce here and we already have the equipment” from drill rigs and crews from the state’s oil and gas industry. “It’s a great opportunity for them to continue being employed and continue using their skills as they crosswalk over into clean energy,” she said.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Appeals Board Orders DNREC to Revisit US Wind Project Approval
text:
Photo: Delaware’s Environmental Appeals Board voted 5-1 Tuesday to send a key regulatory decision involving the US Wind Maryland Offshore Wind Project back to the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC), finding that the agency failed to follow regulations governing its review. Photo was created on 10/13 using AI.
In a 5-1 ruling, the board found state environmental regulators failed to follow required procedures, ordering a new public notice and regulatory review of the controversial offshore wind project.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s Environmental Appeals Board voted 5-1 Tuesday to send a key regulatory decision involving the US Wind Maryland Offshore Wind Project back to the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC), finding that the agency failed to follow regulations governing its review.
The Oct. 13 decision represents a significant development in the continuing dispute over the offshore wind project, which has generated opposition from coastal residents and local officials concerned about its potential environmental impacts and planned transmission infrastructure in Sussex County.
The ruling stems from an appeal filed by Edward Bintz, a coastal Sussex County homeowner who challenged a decision by former DNREC Secretary Shawn Garvin that the project was consistent with applicable coastal management requirements.
Bintz argued that DNREC’s review was inadequate and that US Wind’s application did not contain all the information required under state regulations.
Board finds problems with regulatory process
According to M. Jane Brady, a partner with Halloran Farkas + Kittila who represented Bintz, the board agreed that DNREC had failed to comply with its regulatory requirements.
The board ordered DNREC to reconsider its determination, issue a new public notice, ensure US Wind’s application complies with applicable requirements and follow the regulations governing the review process.
The ruling does not automatically cancel the offshore wind project or permanently prohibit its development. Rather, it requires the state agency to revisit the process used to reach its earlier decision.
The board indicated that it would issue a formal written decision explaining its findings and the requirements imposed on DNREC.
Brady is lead counsel in several other matters related to the Maryland Offshore project, including challenges to the beach construction and subaqueous lands permits. Those permits are pending review in the Superior Court and the EAB, respectively.
Why the consistency determination matters
The dispute centers on a process known as a federal consistency determination, which evaluates whether certain federally authorized activities affecting Delaware’s coastal resources comply with the state’s federally approved coastal management policies.
Although the wind turbines would be located offshore in federal waters, US Wind’s plans include transmission infrastructure affecting Sussex County.
The project proposes bringing underwater transmission cables ashore at 3R’s Beach in Delaware Seashore State Park and connecting them to electrical infrastructure near the former Indian River Power Plant.
Those plans have prompted questions about coastal land use, environmental protections and the extent of state oversight over infrastructure associated with federally approved offshore energy projects.
Bintz’s challenge focused on whether DNREC had sufficient information to make its determination and whether the agency followed the procedures intended to protect public participation and ensure regulatory compliance.
Attorney praises decision and public oversight
Brady argued that US Wind’s application was incomplete and that DNREC’s analysis failed to address issues specifically required by state regulations.
Following Tuesday’s ruling, she praised the board for recognizing the importance of the regulatory process.
“I am pleased the Board recognized how important a properly informed public is to environmental regulation, and that the members appreciated how important careful compliance to the regulations, that were so carefully crafted, can be,” Brady said.
The appeal has been part of a broader legal and regulatory dispute involving the proposed offshore wind development.
Tuesday’s decision addresses DNREC’s handling of the consistency review rather than determining whether offshore wind development itself should proceed.
What happens next for US Wind?
The ruling returns the matter to DNREC, which must address the regulatory concerns identified by the board.
The agency will be required to issue another public notice and examine whether US Wind’s application satisfies the applicable regulations before reaching a new determination.
It remains unclear whether the additional review will affect the project’s construction schedule, federal approvals or other regulatory proceedings.
The board’s forthcoming written decision should provide greater clarity about the deficiencies identified and the actions DNREC must take.
Responses from DNREC and US Wind to Tuesday’s ruling were not immediately available.
The decision also highlights the importance of procedural requirements in environmental permitting, particularly when projects involve overlapping federal and state authority.
For coastal communities, the ruling potentially provides another opportunity to review information about the project and participate in the regulatory process.


THE TO-GO BOX: US WIND ENVIRONMENTAL APPEAL


What happened? Delaware’s Environmental Appeals Board voted 5-1 on Oct. 13 to return a US Wind regulatory determination to DNREC for further review.
Who challenged the decision? Edward Bintz, a Sussex County coastal homeowner, represented by attorney M. Jane Brady.
What did the board find? DNREC failed to follow applicable regulatory requirements in reviewing the project’s consistency with Delaware’s coastal management policies.
What must DNREC do? Issue a new public notice, ensure the application complies with regulatory requirements and conduct its review in accordance with those regulations.
Is the project canceled? No. The ruling requires additional state regulatory action but does not itself cancel the project.
What’s next? The board is expected to issue a written decision detailing its findings. DNREC must then address the deficiencies identified by the board.

title: Vermont Supreme Court closes case in Westmore residents’ fight against telecommunications tower
text:
A photo of Lake Willoughby in Westmore shows the location proposed for a 140-foot tall telecommunications tower. Photo courtesy of Donna Dzugas-Smith.

Approval for a 140-foot telecommunications tower near Lake Willoughby remains in place after the Vermont Supreme Court on Tuesday formally closed residents’ legal challenge over its impact on the scenic landscape.
Tuesday’s notice certified the case back to the Public Utility Commission following an appeal by seven Westmore residents who said the commission did not give proper consideration to input from the town’s planning commission, select board, town plan or neighbors in approving the tower’s construction.
Industrial Tower and Wireless, based out of Massachusetts, filed a petition to construct the tower, proposed to be installed just northwest of Lake Willoughby, a national natural landmark, in June 2024. They were met with local concerns over how the tower would impact the scenery of Lake Willoughby and surrounding forest, despite the tower improving radio and cellular service in the Northeast Kingdom.

READ MORE

The three-member Public Utility Commission granted approval for the project in September 2025. 
The group filed a notice of appeal to that decision the next month in the Vermont Supreme Court. 
On Sept. 4, the state’s Supreme Court upheld the Public Utility Commission’s decision, and the group of residents rebutted on Sept. 16, filing a motion for the Court to hear the case again. 
The motion for reargument was denied Sept. 29, the Newport Daily Express reported. Tuesday’s notice formally closed the Supreme Court case, leaving the tower’s approval in place.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Morningside University to expand nursing training and support with federal grant funds
text:
Morningside University's Nylen School of Nursing and Health Sciences received a federal grant to expand simulation training and nursing student support. (Photo courtesy of Morningside University)Morningside University will use federal grant funding to expand simulated experiential learning and help those hoping to instruct in the health sciences field one day, with the goal of supporting nursing education and workforce needs in its communities.
The Sioux City private university announced this week it has received the largest grant in its history — $2.97 million over four years from the Health Resources and Services Administration — to fund an underserved community nursing initiative.
Project CONNECT CARE, or Community-Oriented Nursing, Navigation, Engagement, Clinical Training, and Career Advancement through Rural Experiences, will help Morningside further its outreach and draw in partners in need of educational resources and facilities, said Nylen School of Nursing and Health Sciences Dean Jackie Barber.
“We need a strong healthcare nursing workforce to take care of all of us, and Morningside wants to be that partner in that space,” Barber said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The majority of grant funding will go toward expanding simulation equipment and training for the faculty and outside nurses who will work with students in simulated healthcare situations, Barber said. Morningside will also use funding to establish a certified nursing assistance program, with Barber calling it a good first step into healthcare careers.
Currently Morningside houses a four-room patient simulation suite, which will see additions of an intensive care unit and emergency care simulation suite. Barber said the university will also duplicate simulations it has in maternal, pediatric and primary care to accommodate multiple student groups simultaneously — a helpful expansion after Morningside acquired St. Luke’s College last year.
Morningside will also establish immersive role-play and virtual reality simulation rooms for further training, and simulation spaces with wearable equipment for students to work through different situations together with their peers.
“It gives a very, very real experience of doing those types of care on patients,” Barber said. “We can do things like these wearables that are wound care, maybe even IV care … we have one that’s like a chest tube, so all these different things that just really give a very true, real-life learning component to it that you just don’t get every day.”
Expanded simulation areas will serve more than just Morningside students, Barber said, but the university’s “practice partners” as well. Healthcare practices in the rural areas surrounding Sioux City often don’t have the opportunity to provide simulated learning to train and upskill nurses, but Morningside hopes to be a “regional resource center” for them to send employees who want to further their education.
The grant will also support mentoring, tutoring and other resources for students in need as they complete their education. With these new experiential learning opportunities and new curriculum the university has switched to “to meet the national call for preparing our nurses to be competent and confident and just ready for practice,” Barber said the nursing school wants to ensure that students have strong outcomes and are able to achieve them outside of the classroom once they graduate.
A separate, one-year grant of $95,000 from the Health Resources and Services Administration will provide student loan reimbursement to doctor of nursing practice program students who go on to become faculty in their field.
Describing the second grant as “small but huge,” Barber said nursing programs can’t be successful in graduating enough practice-ready professionals to meet demand without a strong faculty group teaching them. Morningside students who go on to become faculty will have up to 80% of their student loans forgiven.
“We know that strategically we have been a good resource for our practice partners, all the facilities out there, and they have been such a great resource to us too,” Barber said. “We just want to make sure that we can continue to expand that beyond our area, and then just (ensure) that we’re really doing our part to have practice-ready nurses out there, nurses that are ready for practice, but most importantly, that they stay in practice and stay in those careers.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island officials seek to reassure voters ahead of midterm elections
text:
Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore looks through a binder during a press conference at an early voting site in the community room of the Warwick Police Station on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) Voting booths were lit, ballots were stacked, and ID scanners were in place inside Warwick’s police headquarters the day before early voting begins in Rhode Island for the 2026 midterms.
The setup offered a preview of the preparations underway across the state, as election and public safety officials Tuesday outlined their efforts to get voting sites ready and assure voters they will be able to cast their ballots safely and securely whether in person or by mail. 
“Get out there and vote,” Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore told reporters gathered inside Warwick’s early voting location. “This is a precious and sacred right and nothing will impede that ability to cast a vote.”
The state’s Board of Elections has tested and sealed hundreds of voting machines, deployed more than 600 machines and electronic pollbooks statewide, and trained more than 2,200 poll workers who will work on Nov. 3.
State and local police leaders said they are working with election officials to prepare for potential problems at polling places, even if they don’t expect any major incidents.
“Our goal is for an election day to be uneventful from a public safety standpoint,” said Col. Michael Correia, chief of the Barrington Police Department and president of the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association.
Amore, a Democrat running unopposed as the state’s top election official, said the preparations were part of the routine work election officials undertake every election cycle. But he said a steady stream of national headlines about election administration, White House executive orders and federal court decisions prompted him and other officials to publicize their efforts.
“We want to make sure Rhode Islanders are comfortable with all aspects of voting,” Amore said.
Miguel Nuñez, executive director of the Rhode Island Board of Elections, said voters can return mail ballots through the U.S. Postal Service without restrictions or interference, despite the Trump administration’s efforts to impose new limits.
The U.S. Postal Service sought to impose new requirements on ballot envelopes and require states to submit lists of eligible mail voters to the federal government, but the plan was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court in September.
The deadline to request a mail ballot in Rhode Island was 4 p.m. Tuesday. More than 27,000 Rhode Island voters had applied for one as of early Tuesday afternoon, Nuñez said.



Quotation







Get out there and vote. This is a precious and sacred right and nothing will impede that ability to cast a vote. Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore


Amore urged voters to mail their completed ballots by Oct. 27, or return them to one of the state’s 41 secure drop boxes outside either their local board of canvassers, the Secretary of State’s Office on West River Street in Providence, or the Board of Elections’ Cranston headquarters by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3.
Election officials are also working to ensure municipalities have enough poll workers to keep voting locations running smoothly on Election Day.
Staffing shortages contributed to delayed openings at some Providence polling places during the Sept. 9 primary. The capital city saw an unusually high rate of poll worker no-shows, with some polling places opening more than an hour late. Nuñez said the Board of Elections has been working with universities, state agencies and local election officials to recruit additional workers.
1 in 7 Providence poll workers called out sick or did not show

Nuñez said he expects the recruitment efforts should create a reserve pool of poll workers equal to 10% to 15% of the state’s staffing needs, ensuring municipalities have enough people to cover last-minute absences. The call-outs in Providence on Primary Day were not part of a coordinated effort to disrupt voting, he said.
“It was simply just individuals who had gotten sick who committed to it and decided at the last minute not to show up at the polling location,” Nuñez said.
Officials said they’re also preparing for the possibility of federal involvement at polling places, particularly concerns about immigration officers showing up at voting sites. A law passed by the Rhode Island General Assembly in June bars U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers from coming within 200 feet of a polling place while voting is underway.
In August, the Board of Elections issued guidance directing local officials to notify police and document any interactions with federal agents or observers at voting sites, Nuñez said. 
Officials said they have received no indication that federal law enforcement agents will be present at polling places on Election Day.
Federal election observers are expected in Pawtucket on Nov. 3 under an agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice stemming from a 2024 consent agreement — just as they did during the September primary. The agreement requires the city to provide Spanish-speaking voters with election assistance and materials in their native language.
Should federal officials interfere with voting, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha said his office would take the Trump administration to court.
“The team will be ready at a moment’s notice,” Neronha told reporters.
Early voting runs through 4 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 2.

name: VTDigger
title: Manufacturing leaders tackle Vermont workforce challenges
text:
Business and community leaders gathered for the Brattleboro Development Credit Corp.’s Brattleboro Regional Manufacturing Event in Brattleboro on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The event highlighted the importance of manufacturing to Southern Vermont’s economy and workforce. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Charlotte King was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 11, 2026.
The Brattleboro Development Credit Corporation (BDCC) brought together employers, educators and government officials for a roundtable discussion about manufacturing on Thursday, ringing in October as Manufacturing Month.
The event featured presentations from educators at the Windham Regional Career Center (WRCC) and from the state’s Economic & Labor Market Information Director Mathew Barewicz, as well as panel discussions with state officials and educators and an open discussion with all present brainstorming about how to streamline the process of educating and employing people in the regional manufacturing industry.
BDCC Executive Director Adam Grinold said the goal was to get people from all sides of the matter in a room to start conversation about why manufacturing matters in southeast Vermont, what problems are facing the industry and how to find some shared solutions to those problems.
“We recognize our role in trying to bring everybody together,” Grinold said. “We have a real opportunity to lead as we see manufacturing start to decline, largely around some closures, but there’s opportunity, there’s need, and we need to make sure we’re following all of those.”
Barewicz’s presentation focused on data concerning changes in employment and population rates over the past 20 years. He said Vermont, adjusted proportionally to compare against the United States, surpasses the nation in its share of industry that is manufacturing. He also said one of the major contributing factors to the state’s population growth has been immigration.
“Seventy-five percent of our population growth over these last decades has been from people coming from abroad,” Barewicz said. “When you have a change in the federal policy about how many people are coming into this country, states like Vermont are going to feel problems.”
Barewicz said Brattleboro holds the biggest share of manufacturing industry in Windham County, and he emphasized the need to make the profession seem accessible to young people.
“When we’re talking to kids today, we’re changing the conversation, from not just finding a job or getting a career, but, ‘Hey, do you want to run your own business?’” Barewicz said.
He said there was a need for passion to drive successful employment.
“We have to get them excited about either the work they’re going to do or the mission of the organization,” Barewicz said.
Some discussion covered preconceptions about manufacturing, like involving lots of dangerous work or having limited upward mobility. WRCC Director Nancy Wiese said a lot has changed in the industry over time.
“We need students to buy into the fact that manufacturing is now really cool,” Wiese said. “Now, manufacturing is so clean, and it has so much to offer students.”
After hearing from leaders in both government labor relations and regional education, several attendees voiced a need to streamline and simplify.
“We need to have one door to knock on,” said Richard Normandin of Northrich, Inc. “A common goal as a region is really important.”
Commissioner of Economic Development Lyle Jepson said the limited population growth of Vermont makes every potential new employee important.
“When we’re only graduating four or five thousand kids, we’ve got to make sure that we keep all the kids in the state, going to our schools,” Jepson said. “Maybe we need to change how we work things, but we all need to meet them, shake their hands, tell them how important they are, create relationships to keep them in the state of Vermont. It’s a harder thing to do, because you can ski in Colorado [or] you can ski in Vermont, but it’s the relationships that are going to keep people here.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Three weeks out, Foulkes is 9 points ahead of Block in WPRI poll
text:
WPRO host Bill Bartholomew, standing, interacts with Rhode Island gubernatorial candidates Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, seated far left, and Republican Aaron Guckian, second from left, and independent Ken Block, seen from the back at far right. (Photo courtesy of Cumulus Media)Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes continues to lead the five-way race for governor, even as independent Ken Block has narrowed the gap, according to a WPRI-TV 12 poll published Tuesday.
The survey of 800 likely voters, conducted by Emerson College from Oct. 8 to 11, puts Foulkes 9 points ahead of Block — compared to the 27 points between the two candidates in a survey conducted in August. The margin of error is 3.5%.
While Foulkes still has the support of more than 4 in 10 likely general election voters — nearly identical to two months ago — Block has gained ground, with more than 1 in 3 voters backing him now, compared with 1 in 5 in August.
Meanwhile, the share of undecided voters shrank from 14% to 9%. Also on the decline: enthusiasm for Republican nominee Aaron Guckian. 
Only 10% of survey participants said they supported Guckian, compared with 18% backing an unnamed GOP nominee in August before he won the Sept. 9 primary.
Could Block come from behind and win the election?
“Nothing is impossible,” said Joe Fleming, a political analyst for WPRI. 
But Block will have to broaden his appeal beyond undecideds and conservatives to pull from Foulkes’ Democratic base. That could prove challenging, Fleming said.
All three candidates have traded barbs on debate stages and in political ads and mailers over their ideology. The Rhode Island Democratic Party spent $300,000 to send out mailers on Foulkes’ behalf, accusing Block of secretively being a Republican.
Block, who has run for governor twice before, once as a Moderate and then again as a Republican, came out with two new TV ads Monday leaning on his work fighting the political establishment, including disproving the Trump campaign’s allegations of voter fraud in the 2020 election. 
But Block’s statement on reproductive rights during an Oct. 30 gubernatorial forum, pledging to sign any bills passed by the General Assembly, drew fierce rebukes from Foulkes and from all 68 Democratic state lawmakers. 
Another potential turnoff for Democratic voters: Block’s opposition to the Affordable Care Act, a position he restated when asked during a WPRO debate Tuesday morning, citing the cost to small business owners. 
Pocketbook problems top voter concerns 
Health care access and costs remain a concern of voters, though the survey found taxes and spending were the top problem respondents want state officials to tackle.
Block’s pragmatic focus on improving government efficiency, drawing from his work as a software engineer helping other state governments and private companies improve operations and root out waste, appeals to voters, Fleming acknowledged.
“The pocketbook issues really stand out a lot,” Fleming said. “For Ken Block, I would stay on that message.”
Key to getting the message out is raising money. Block had $263,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5, the highest of any candidate, though his balance includes a $190,000 personal loan.
Foulkes, having depleted her campaign account with more than $5 million spent in the primary, had nearly $215,000 cash on hand. But Democratic groups came through with financial support, including the state party covering the cost of anti-Block mailers, plus $500,000 from the Democratic Governors Association.
The three candidates appear with moderator Bill Bartholomew, far left, in a debate pre-recorded at WPRO in East Providence on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Screenshot)
No independent expenditures for Block or Guckian had been reported to the Rhode Island Board of Elections as of Tuesday.
Guckian, who narrowly defeated Elaine Pelino in the Republican primary, continues to struggle with lack of name recognition and donations. He had just $7,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5.
After Block released an internal poll last month showing he could defeat Foulkes in a two-way race, calls mounted for Guckian to drop out of the race. Guckian’s campaign rejected the pressure, in turn suggesting Block should be the one to drop out.
More than half of Republican voters surveyed by WPRI picked Block, compared with 3 in 10 who backed Guckian. Block also drew support from nearly half of the independent voters included in the poll, while one-third supported Foulkes.
Block was the only one of the three who more voters viewed favorably than unfavorably, with a plus 27 rating. Guckian’s net rating was minus 20, while Foulkes was essentially neutral at minus 1, a signal to Fleming that McKee’s attacks on Foulkes have stuck with voters.
“His negativity on her paid off in the primary,” Fleming said.
Debate, take 2
Block remained immune from scrutiny until the general election cycle, a point Guckian raised during the pre-taped debate at WPRO’s offices Tuesday morning.
“You cut the line,” Guckian said to Block, criticizing Block’s changing party identity while touting his own “right to be here” having survived a primary.
The hourlong event hosted by Bill Batholomew rehashed many of the same disagreements that unfolded seven days earlier in an Oct. 8 debate organized by NBC 10 and Coastal ABC.
On Tuesday, Guckian continued to attack Foulkes for her willingness to work with Democratic Providence mayoral nominee David Morales, a socialist.
“I have never seen someone who benefited from capitalism so much, and now she stands for socialism,” Guckian said, referencing Foulkes’ corporate career that includes 25 years at CVS Health.
Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, most recently served as head of the Rhode Island Dental Association. A former aide to then-Gov. Don Carcieri, Guckian touted his ability to work with Republicans in Washington to yield funding for Rhode Island.



Quotation







I have never seen someone who benefited from capitalism so much, and now she stands for socialism.


– Aaron Guckian on his opponent Helena Buonanno Foulkes


Foulkes, 62, of Providence, reprised similar criticisms of Block over the lack of detail in his housing and education policies, while Block denounced both his rivals.
“Aaron’s plan is to have the federal government swoop in to save the day, and Helena’s plans are heavy on empathy but light on fact-based solutions,” Block, 61, of Barrington, said in closing statements. 
Much of the debate focused on housing — the second most-pressing issue among voters surveyed by WPRI and the top issue for registered Democrats.




Quotation







Aaron’s plan is to have the federal government swoop in to save the day, and Helena’s plans are heavy on empathy but light on fact-based solutions.


– Independent Ken Block on his two opponents



Foulkes has proposed a public revolving fund to encourage private developers, using money from the state millionaire’s tax. Block emphasizes an individual approach tailored to each municipality, while Guckian suggested creating communities of modular homes specifically for veteran and frontline workers. 
Criticizing her opponents, Foulkes said, “My takeaway from both of these folks is they don’t really think there’s a housing crisis.” 
Foulkes was also vehement in her pledge to fight federal immigration authorities “with every bone in my body,” while Guckian warned that failure to cooperate with ICE and law enforcement would lead to increased crime.
“You defund police, and socialism is going to attract more and more bad actors and people who are not documented,” Guckian said.
Block did not wade into the immigration debate, focused on pragmatic solutions to cut red tape and improve government efficiency. 
All three candidates said they would lean into Rhode Island’s blue economy to boost jobs and suggested higher reimbursement rates for government and commercial health care as a solution to the primary care doctor shortage.
None of them wanted to keep Rhode Island Commissioner of Elementary and Secondary Education Angélica Infante-Green in her cabinet position, and each stressed the need to overhaul management in the Rhode Island Department of Transportation. 
While Foulkes’ housing plan leans on a tax on income over $1 million, Block and Guckian both opposed the tax, which took effect July 1 as part of the state’s fiscal 2027 budget. 



Quotation







My takeaway from both of these folks is they don’t really think there’s a housing crisis. 


– Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes on her two opponents


The three will meet for a third, and final debate, hosted by WPRI-TV at Rhode Island College, on Tuesday, Oct. 20.
The gubernatorial race also includes two other independent candidates, Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds, who have not qualified for any of the debates under station criteria. 
LG race a ‘nail-biter’
In the lieutenant governor’s race, WPRI’s poll put Democratic incumbent Sabina Matos tied with Republican challenger John Loughlin. The findings echo results of a University of New Hampshire survey from Sept. 25, though more voters, 12%, were undecided in the WPRI poll.
Despite defeating four challengers in the Sept. 9 primary, Matos remains haunted by the signature fraud scandal from the 1st Congressional District Democratic primary in 2023, Fleming said. Matos finished a distant fourth in the race that elected now-U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo, and was never linked to the forgeries that led to criminal charges against two campaign workers.
Loughlin, a former state representative from Tiverton and former talk radio host, enjoys modest name recognition helping boost his campaign, Fleming said.
Neither candidate has significant campaign cash — Matos had $43,000 in the bank as of Oct. 5 while Loughlin had $22,800 — though Fleming speculated Matos may benefit from independent expenditures on her behalf, as she did in the primary. 
“It’s going to be a nail-biter,” Fleming said of the lieutenant governor’s race.
WPRI is set to release a second round of poll results at 10 p.m., focused on Rhode Island’s congressional races and Trump’s approval rating. There will also be more results published Wednesday morning.
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont to bolster heating assistance using CT contingency fund
text:
The policy and political impacts of skyrocketing home heating oil prices came together Tuesday as Gov. Ned Lamont announced the planned release of $12.7 million from the $500 million contingency fund created last year to address the impact of federal cuts since Donald J. Trump’s return to the White House.
At a press conference at a community action program in New Haven, the governor and other Democrats outlined plans to address rising oil prices attributed to the war on Iran, one of the issues angering voters in the approach to midterm elections expected to deliver a blow to the president and his party.
With oil prices jumping about 80% from a year ago to nearly $6 a gallon, the confluence of the heating season and start of early voting next week gave the Democratic governor and members of Congress and the General Assembly an opportunity to score political points.
“Everybody needs to show up at the polls. Everybody needs to make their no’s and their yeses known,” said state Rep. Toni Walker, D-New Haven. “We need to make sure that we bring back the strength of the people in Washington and in Connecticut, and make sure that they are seen and understood.”
Connecticut’s heating assistance plan anticipates serving 94,291 households, including 32,893 that rely on heating oil. The majority of the aid still comes from the federal government through LIHEAP, the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
Trump repeatedly has proposed ending LIHEAP, only to be rebuffed by bipartisan opposition. U.S. Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, D-3rd District, the ranking Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said $75.3 million of the $94 million in federal LIHEAP funds the state hopes to get was released this week.
Energy assistance funds typically are paid out in three payments — a base level of $355 to $705, depending on need, followed by two crisis payments of up to $430 each. The $12.7 million will allow a fourth crisis payment, once the federal funds are exhausted.
Connecticut households may qualify for energy assistance if their annual gross income is at or below 60% of the state median income, which is $93,681 for a family of four. Households receiving means-tested benefits such as SNAP, Temporary Family Assistance, and Supplemental Security Income may qualify automatically. 
The state also for the first time will “bundle” the base and crisis payments, allowing eligible recipients to fill their oil tanks at the beginning of the season, avoiding price increases expected over the winter. With an average oil tank of 275 gallons, a fill up will cost about $1,600.
“It makes a lot of sense financially, because the CAA’s will drop their administrative costs because they’re not trying to figure out parsing out a little bit here and a little bit there. It gets it out there. Let’s get it out to people,” said state Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chair of the General Assembly’s Appropriations Committee, referring to the Community Action Agencies that help administer the heating assistance program.
About $250 million remains in the contingency fund created to give the Lamont administration flexibility in responding to federal funding and policy changes. Lamont is required to notify the legislature leaders, who have a veto that never has been used. 
“We’re all talking to legislative leaders right now,” Lamont said. “Let’s do $12 million. Let’s make sure that not only do we have the base case that we got from the federal government, which is hopefully going to be as much as we had last year, at least we can make good for those folks, especially when it comes to home heating.”
There was no shortage of political gibes at the president.
“A year ago, look, we didn’t know what that master of mischief and chaos in Washington was going to do, but we knew he was going to do something, and that’s why we stood up and worked with the governor to create the $500 million federal emergency response fund to help manage the chaos,” state Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, said.
“Because of this misguided war in Iran, it’s difficult for the benefits to get to people through the winter. That’s why I am so grateful to Gov. Lamont,” DeLauro said. “His decision to help fund seniors and their families, it will mean that they can fill their oil tanks without worrying about how they’re going to find the money.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Challengers call Arkansas governor’s policy priorities misplaced in debate
text:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders participates in the debate against 2026 gubernatorial candidates Sen. Fred Love (D), and Colt Shelby (L) on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Democrat Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby sharply criticized Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ school voucher program, state spending priorities and prison plans in a debate Tuesday where the three gubernatorial hopefuls did not offer specific plans for the future of the state’s Medicaid expansion.
Sanders touted her record on tax cuts and school choice during the debate hosted by Arkansas TV, while Love and Shelby said her priorities were misplaced. 

﻿ 
Love, a state senator from Little Rock, repeated his promise to end the state’s school voucher program with an executive order if elected and supported suspending the state’s gas tax amid high fuel prices. Shelby said he would resume executions and push for legislation allowing for execution by firing squad.
This was the first debate of the 2026 election cycle featuring all three candidates. Shelby and Love debated in June at the Arkansas Press Association’s annual conference.
Sanders, White House press secretary for President Donald Trump during part of his first term, is running for reelection in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to a statewide seat since 2010. She won 62% of the vote in 2022; Trump won 64% of the vote in 2024.
Trump’s low approval numbers have raised Democrats’ hopes in the state, though political forecasters Larry Sabato and the Cook Political Report have rated the race as safely Republican.
Sanders’ office said in July that the Trump administration rejected the state’s request to renew its hybrid Medicaid expansion program, which purchases private insurance for low-income residents. The state has requested a temporary two-year extension as it works on a replacement.

Sanders said Medicaid expansion would be one of the most important issues addressed during next year’s legislative session but did not say what approach she’d favor as a replacement. Sanders also hailed the new work requirements for the expansion program, which take effect next year.
“We have to make sure we have accessibility. We also have to ensure that we have affordability. It’s why I fought so hard to make sure that Arkansas has a work requirement,” Sanders said. She said it was “outrageous that somebody should be able to confiscate your hard-earned tax dollars” because they “choose not to work.”
According to the health policy research group KFF, the vast majority of Medicaid recipients under the age of 65 already work, attend school, are caregivers or are unable to work due to an illness or disability. 
The Congressional Budget Office in 2022 found that work requirements for Medicaid and SNAP “reduced benefits more than they have increased people’s earnings,” while recent research found that nearly 20% of people currently enrolled in Medicaid would likely be unable to meet the work requirements even though they already work due to variable hours or hours that don’t meet the 80 hours requirement under the law.
More than 200,000 people were covered by Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program, ARHOME, as of July.
Love said the state had to invest more in Arkansas hospitals and Medicaid. Shelby said the state needs “better Medicaid programs.” 
Love and Shelby attacked the school vouchers known as the Educational Freedom Account program and Sanders’ opposition to expanding Medicaid to cover mothers for 12 months postpartum, pointing both as examples of her having priorities that did not align with the state’s needs.
Arkansas gubernatorial candidate Sen. Fred Love (D) participates in the debate against 2026 candidates Colt Shelby (L), and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
“For us to be a pro-life state, we’re doing a bad job in protecting our moms and protecting our children,” Love said. “The governor has refused to — refused to — actually pass 12-month postpartum care.” 
Sanders responded that “Democrats think that the government is the answer to all of our problems.”
“I want to empower people so that they can live their best lives,” she said. “You don’t do that by forever trapping them on government welfare.”
Medicaid eligibility for postpartum mothers would be limited to 12 months if Arkansas expanded the program to cover them. Arkansas is the only state that hasn’t done so.

Shelby called the LEARNS Act, Sanders’ signature 2023 education law that created the voucher program,  “the biggest failure of this administration.” He said teachers are unhappy while the educational gains cited by Sanders were based off a test “that the state made, that’s not nationally-recognized.”
“We need to scale it back, get it where we can afford it, and make the schools accountable for what’s going on,” Shelby said.
Sanders, however, said that LEARNS was working and improving outcomes for students. She pointed to literacy coaches that have been provided to struggling schools and increasing teacher pay as examples.
“What’s not fair is trapping kids in failing schools,” she said. “LEARNS is not just about educational freedom. While that is a key part of the legislation, it’s only a small part.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump administration seeks to rescind approval for Revolution Wind
text:
The Trump administration is once again seeking to interrupt the development of Connecticut’s first offshore wind project, Revolution Wind.
In a federal court filing on Friday, attorneys representing the U.S. Department of the Interior sought permission to rescind the agency’s three-year-old approval for the construction of the Revolution Wind project, which is now nearing completion.
The filing was made in a lawsuit filed in 2024 by Green Oceans, an anti-wind energy group, challenging the federal government’s approval of permits for Revolution Wind and its sister project, South Fork Wind.
“The Department of the Interior agrees that remand of its prior approval of the construction and operations plan (“COP”) for the Revolution Wind Project is warranted so that the agency can reevaluate its compliance with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act,” the filing states. “Given that remand, the Court need not reach Plaintiffs’ other claims challenging Interior’s COP approval.”
A spokesperson for the project’s developer, Ørsted, declined to comment on the filing Monday. The Department of Interior did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Revolution Wind’s 65th and final turbine was installed in September, and developers say the project is on track to begin producing its full, 704-megawatt output by the end of this year.
The project is located off the coast of Rhode Island, with onshore assembly taking place at the State Pier in New London. The project began supplying power to the New England electric grid in March, and is supported by contracts with utilities in Connecticut and Rhode Island. (South Fork Wind, which was not mentioned in the filing, was completed in 2024). 
The move also comes as Congress is mulling bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects, including offshore wind farms. A vote on that bill is not expected until after the midterm elections. 
National Ocean Industries Association President Erik Milito released a statement on Monday calling for Congress to vote on that legislation in response to the Trump administration’s latest efforts to interfere with Revolution Wind. The NOIA represents companies involved in offshore energy development for the wind, oil and gas industries.
“Predictable regulatory processes and timely decisions are important for offshore energy development of all kinds,” Milito said. “We recognize the federal government’s responsibility to review projects and ensure compliance with applicable requirements, and we hope the remaining process can move forward efficiently while Revolution Wind continues progressing toward full operations. The second-guessing of federal approvals that have already gone through a lengthy review process is precisely why Congress must pass comprehensive permitting reform legislation, specifically the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”
Friday’s filing did not cite any specific concerns that prompted officials to reverse their stance on the Revolution Wind project. However, the filing criticized the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s original 2023 record of decision for failing to “adequately explain” how potential impacts fit within the agency’s mission to provide for other uses within U.S. waters, including fishing and recreation.
Previously, the Department of Interior has cited concerns about the impact turbine blades can have on military radar in its efforts to halt offshore wind development.
Those arguments, however, have failed to gain much traction within the courts. The judge overseeing the Green Oceans case, Royce C. Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, has twice sided with the developers of Revolution Wind in blocking the Trump administration’s efforts to halt work on the project.
Lamberth has yet to rule on Interior’s latest request to reconsider the project’s construction permit.
The Trump administration has had greater success stopping wind projects that have yet to begin construction. On the first day of his second term, Trump issued an executive order withdrawing all areas of the outer continental shelf from further leasing to wind developers, while also pausing permiting on any new projects.
Since then, several wind developers have reached agreements to relinquish their leases for areas of the U.S. coast, in exchange for billions in refunds and promises to develop oil and gas projects instead. Those agreements have prompted lawsuits from several state attorneys general, including Connecticut’s William Tong.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lawmakers concerned corrections agency may skip hearing on prison healthcare
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Lawmakers will hold a hearing on Thursday to look into dire problems with healthcare in Mississippi prisons and allegations of systemic failure to stop preventable deaths and illness.
Prison healthcare problems have been exposed through news investigations, legislative watchdog reports and first-person accounts from those working inside.
But apparently the Mississippi Department of Corrections will be a no-show at the hearing, a letter obtained by Mississippi Today shows.
In a letter on Tuesday to Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain, Public Health Chairs Rep. Sam Creekmore and Sen. Hob Bryan, along with Corrections Chairs Rep. Becky Currie and Sen. Lydia Chassaniol said they were “disappointed to learn that the Department of Corrections will not take part in Thursday’s joint hearing.”
“We want to be clear about the purpose of this hearing. It is not meant to assign blame. It is meant to help members of both chambers understand how health care is delivered behind the walls today, where the gaps are, and what the Legislature can do to help,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Department’s perspective is essential to that conversation. No one knows the day-to-day challenges better than the people responsible for meeting them.”
The letter does not say whether MDOC officials provided lawmakers with a reason for their avoidance. A department spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about the matter.
The hearing comes after Mississippi Today’s Behind Bars, Beyond Care investigation documented potentially thousands of people living with hepatitis C going without treatment, amputations from delayed care and inmates having trouble getting cancer screenings. Such findings, as well as handwritten letters sent to lawmakers by prisoners seeking care and panicked messages from their family members, have drawn bipartisan condemnation in the statehouse and numerous hearings this year at the Capitol.  
In an interview, Currie, who has led the charge to improve healthcare in Mississippi’s prisons, said many prisoners are not getting cancer treatment in time to recover and are forced to languish for lengthy periods without care for ailments such as diabetes and hepatitis C, even as spending on prison healthcare has risen for taxpayers.
“Treatment could be less expensive and have better outcomes when treated early. Diabetic care is almost nonexistent. Many inmates complain to me that they have sugar drops when their blood sugar gets low, but they don’t have anything but the canteen to get a candy bar to get their sugar up, and then (prison medical staffers) put in the chart that the inmates are noncompliant.”
MDOC has the fourth-highest funding of any Mississippi state agency, set to receive over $430 million in the next fiscal year. The high costs for taxpayers can be attributed in part to its medical care contract and increased payments to private prisons, according to Rep. Currie, a top budget writer for corrections in the state Legislature.
The largest single chunk of the corrections budget goes to a prison medical contract currently held by Kansas-based VitalCore Health Strategies. The Kansas-based company was initially awarded four no-bid emergency contracts, for hundreds of millions of dollars, before securing a three-year contract worth over $357 million.
Mississippi Today’s investigation revealed that the same year the state agreed to keep paying VitalCore, a top official at the MDOC, remarking on a prisoner’s rotting leg, said the company “sucks.”
After she took over as House Corrections Chairwoman, Currie, a Republican from Brookhaven, began to notice what she described as disturbing instances of inadequate care under VitalCore’s contract. She embarked on a tour of Mississippi’s prisons and said she couldn’t believe what she found.
Currie encountered a wheelchair-bound man so jaundiced he appeared to glow in the dark. She met a 23-year-old woman with a lump growing out of her breast from untreated cancer. Other women were denied pap smears and mammograms. She met men with untreated HIV. Many more inmates were charged for care they never received.
“Since I began trying to hold VitalCore accountable to the contract they signed, they are doing somewhat better,” Currie told Mississippi Today. “They are now treating HIV, which they weren’t doing. They are treating 50 hepatitis C inmates a year, which is far below the necessary numbers if they want to eradicate (the illness), but better than they were doing. We still have a long way to go on many things.”
Currie said she wants to make it possible for other entities to compete for Mississippi’s prison health contract after Gov. Tate Reeves leaves office in 2027. 
As the healthcare problems roiling Mississippi’s prisons began to surface, Reeves dispatched Kenny Ellis, his former policy director, to keep an eye on the corrections committees in the Legislature. Cain then appointed Ellis as MDOC’s chief of staff in early 2026.
After numerous bills to reform prison healthcare passed the House unanimously, most of the measures were killed in the Senate by former Corrections Chairman Juan Barnett, a Democrat from Heidelberg and Vice Chair Chassaniol, a Republican from Winona. 
Rep. Justis Gibbs, a Democrat from Jackson, advanced the only prison health care reform to survive legislative negotiations last session. His measure requires that prisoners be provided with protective equipment while handling cleaning chemicals. The measure was inspired by the story of Susie Balfour, a Mississippi woman, who died of breast cancer last year at the age of 64.
In a lawsuit that her family eventually settled, she said her exposure to cleaning chemicals in prison might have led to her cancer, and that prison health providers delayed or failed to schedule follow-up cancer screenings for Balfour even though they had been recommended by prison physicians. 
In a statement ahead of Thursday’s hearing, Gibbs urged the Legislature to pass more legislation on prison healthcare in 2027.
“Meaningful, large-scale reform will require the commitment, collaboration, and support of an overwhelming majority of our Legislature,” Gibbs said. “We are talking about human rights here. It shouldn’t be such a hard lift.”
Creekmore, a Republican from New Albany, said he urged MDOC officials to participate with the hearing given the steady stream of stories emanating from Mississippi’s prisons about inadequate healthcare.
“There are very sad, unsuccessful stories about healthcare in prisons,” Creekmore said. “So I just hope that we can put everybody in the same room and figure something out.”
In the letter lawmakers sent to Cain, they said the issues of prison healthcare impact the state as a whole. 
“The health of the people in our correctional facilities is a public health issue for every Mississippian,” the lawmakers wrote. “Nearly everyone who enters our prisons will one day come home. Whether they return healthier, treated for addiction and mental illness, and ready to work, or return sicker and more likely to reoffend, affects our communities, our hospitals, our Medicaid program, and our public safety. A strong, rehabilitative corrections system is in everyone’sinterest, and we cannot build one without the Department at the table.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Secret deal with feds moves Iowa church closer to use of controlled substances
text:
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy has agreed to award the Iowaska Church of Healing the state certification that is needed to clear the way for the issuance of federal certificates to not only import a controlled substance, but also to manufacture from it a tea that is to be used in religious ceremonies. (Photo via Getty Images)After years of litigation over its nonprofit status and use of a hallucinogenic controlled substance, an Iowa-based church is one step closer to being able to import the drug.
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy has agreed to award the Iowaska Church of Healing the state certification that is needed to clear the way for the issuance of federal certificates to not only import a controlled substance, but also to manufacture from it a tea that is to be used in religious ceremonies.
State records indicate the church was formed in Iowa in September 2018 and is run by Admir Dado Kantarevic and by Shaman BaBa DaDo, the latter of whom the church describes as “an internationally renowned healer and clairvoyant.” For a time, the church’s official headquarters was Kantarevic’s former home in Des Moines.
Iowaska’s teachings are built around the use of ayahuasca, a tea that is brewed from the leaves of shrubs and vines found in the Amazon. The church has acknowledged that under the federal Controlled Substances Act, an ingredient of ayahuasca called dimethyltryptamine or DMT, is a Schedule I drug and a hallucinogenic alkaloid, and that there is no statutory exemption allowing for its use in religious ceremonies.
Church fights IRS and DEA in court
In January 2019, Iowaska filed an application with the IRS seeking tax-exempt status and was denied because, in the IRS’ view, the church’s use of the Sacrament of Ayahuasca in its religious practices was illegal.
In 2021, the church sued the IRS in U.S. District Court, challenging the federal agency’s decision. In court papers, the church argued the IRS was violating the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 and noted that the church’s mission was “to help individuals attain healing of the mind, body and spirit through the sacred Sacrament of Ayahuasca under the guidelines of North and South American indigenous traditions and cultural values. Ayahuasca is consumed in the form of a tea during religious ceremonies.”
At the same time, the church was asking the federal Drug Enforcement Administration for a religious exemption from the federal Controlled Substances Act. In court, the church argued the DEA never responded to its request, which then resulted in the IRS refusing to grant nonprofit status.
In March 2023, a federal judge at the district court level ruled in favor of the IRS and dismissed the church’s lawsuit. The church, the court noted, “has had as many as 20 members living in different states and foreign countries, and generally holds its ceremonies on weekends, with members staying in frequent contact with ‘healers’ to help guide them through their daily struggles.”
Organizations may be denied tax-exempt status if their activities violate public policy, the court ruled, adding the church’s activities violated public policy in that the use of ayahuasca remained illegal under the federal law for which the DEA had yet to grant an exemption.
In the meantime, the church continued to seek that exemption from the DEA. Earlier this year, the church went to federal court and argued the DEA and federal government had failed to discharge their duties for more than five years, thereby imposing a “clearly unjustified prior restraint on religion.”
Lawyers for the DEA argued the government “continues to act diligently in reviewing Iowaska’s request for an exemption,” but acknowledged its lack of a decision in the matter.
Confidential agreement reached with DEA
In June 2026, lawyers from the U.S. Department of Justice informed the court that the DEA and the Iowaska Church of Healing had settled their differences and signed a “memorandum of agreement” on the church’s request for a religious exemption to the Controlled Substances Act.
The DEA and the church then filed a joint motion to provide the court with a copy of their agreement only under seal, making the contents of the agreement inaccessible to the public.
“The parties agree that maintaining the memorandum of agreement under seal is necessary to protect important public and privacy interests,” lawyers for the DEA and the church told the court.
The agreement, they said, contained confidential information such as “personal identifying information” of church members, the names of individuals responsible for handling the controlled substances, security measures for storing the controlled substances and the manner in which the controlled substances were to be imported to the United States for the church’s use.
The agreement, they said, recognized the church’s “right under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act to practice its Sacrament of Ayahuasca, subject to agreed conditions.”
That agreement, they said, resolved only the first stage of the DEA’s two-step process for obtaining a religious exemption to the Controlled Substances Act. Step two, they said, involved the Iowa Board of Pharmacy awarding the church an Iowa Certificate of Registration, after which the DEA would “expeditiously” process the necessary exemption, registrations and permits.
On Oct. 5, 2026, the Board of Pharmacy agreed to provide the church the certificate of registration. In its order, the board stated the confidential agreement between the DEA and the church “effectively grants” the church a federal certificate to not only import “concentrated paste of ayahuasca,” but also a federal certificate to manufacture, in bulk, the ayahuasca tea used in ceremonies.
According to Board of Pharmacy records, the board-issued state certification will be placed on probationary status for one year. In addition, the church will be required to report to the board any “adverse events that occur with any participant in (the church’s) religious ceremonies using ayahuasca” if those events require some sort of off-site medical intervention.
