name: Maryland Matters
title: Rutledge faces steep climb to unseat Brown in low-key attorney general’s race
description: He's outnumbered in voter registration, outraised in campaign funds and is in a low-key race against an incumbent with decades of name recognition, but GOP attorney general nominee Jim Rutledge still sees a path to victory in his bid to unseat Anthony Brown (D).
text:
Republican attorney general nominee James Rutledge, left, is challenging first-term Attorney General Anthony Brown, a Democrat, in November. (Photos courtesy Rutledge campaign; Danielle Gaines/Maryland Matters)He’s outnumbered in voter registration, likely outraised and outspent in campaign donations and is running in a race that’s getting little exposure against an incumbent with decades of name recognition.
But Republican attorney general nominee Jim Rutledge still sees a path to victory in his bid to unseat Attorney General Anthony Brown.
“We believe that the independent vote and the Republican vote, and the Democrats that are disappointed with his [Brown’s] record on basic law enforcement, like the Fraternal Order of Police, will not back Anthony Brown this time,” Rutledge said in an interview Friday. “That is our analysis, and we’ve taken our case to the people.”
But Brown is counting on his record, running on it in what he acknowledges has been a low-key campaign. Neither man had a primary opponent, so Nov. 3 will be the first chance voters have had to have their say on either candidate this year.
“We speak through our actions — the lawsuits we file or defend. The comments we propose. Marylanders, they hear us and they’re listening,” Brown said Friday. “I’m confident that Marylanders are going to come out. I ask them to come out and vote and give me another four years so we can continue the good work we’re doing.”
Analysts say the race is Brown’s to lose in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans about 2-1.
“There’s just really no contest to speak of. Anthony Brown will cruise to reelection,” said St. Mary’s College political science professor Todd Eberly, who expects Rutledge will get about 36% of the vote from the “Republican baseline,” compared to about 60% of the vote from Democrats for Brown.
Both Rutledge and Brown are 64. Both are lawyers. Both say they respect the rule of law and both love their children and Maryland.
That’s about where the similarities end.
Someone different
If elected, Rutledge ensures the attorney general’s office would stay out of the business of suing the federal government.
Rutledge, an attorney of four decades with a law office in Harford County, said the state shouldn’t be suing the federal government over policy disagreements. One main reason, he said, is the state constitution declares the federal government is supreme in Maryland, or that “all federal law is Maryland law.”
“We need to focus on Maryland, and litigating against Washington, D.C., or the powers that be in Washington, shouldn’t be a knee-jerk reaction,” he said.
Since Trump began his second term in 2025, Brown has been an active member of a group of Democratic attorneys general that have taken legal action against administration policies, with Maryland leading or signing on more than 150 lawsuits, court briefs and advisory letters with other states.
Brown compiles ‘voluminous’ record of legal challenges to Trump administration policies

“The attorney general shouldn’t sue the federal government just because of a policy disagreement, or because the attorney general feels like the policies of Washington hurt Marylanders,” Rutledge said. “I’m not going to take my direction from any president, any political party. I’m going to look out for Marylanders.”
Rutledge, who was endorsed by the Fraternal Order of Police, said the attorney general’s office should show more support for law enforcement. He said he backs an FOP-endorsed legislative proposal that would prohibit officers being placed on “do not call” lists without their knowledge.
Prosecutors keep the lists of officers who may be deemed untrustworthy to testify in court, because of prior false statements, pending charges or other reasons. The lists became public after the 2021 passage of Anton’s Law, which made police administrative, misconduct and personnel records subject to the Maryland Public Information Act, and available for public inspection.
“They get placed on the do-not-call list without any opportunity to challenge the underlying accusation on why they should be banned from testifying,” Rutledge said. “They could witness a murder in broad daylight on Redwood Street in Baltimore, and the murderer gets away because they [listed officers] can’t testify against them.
“Why are they out there with a badge and a gun if they are worthless as a witness? Basically, it’s gutted their career,” he said.
Rutledge said the current attorney general’s office should do more to protect Maryland’s environmental resources, taking a stronger stance against states like New York and Pennsylvania, to stop dumping waste into the Susquehanna River, the source of the Chesapeake Bay.
“That’s been going on for decades and it’s time to stop that,” he said.
Rutledge said he’s fought for environmental protections during his career as an attorney and his recent time as a Bel Air Town commissioner. He was elected in November 2023 and served until October 2025 to handle a family manner.
“So, the question is, do they [voters] want someone who’s basically spent a career in elected office, or an attorney that has spent a career and has put their money where their mouth is when it comes to environmental protection” and supporting law enforcement, Rutledge said.
“He [Brown] is distracted in some way, shape, or beholden to greater political powers, and I am not.”
‘Not politically motivated’
Brown is in his first term as attorney general, but he has a political career spanning almost 30 years.
He was elected to the House of Delegates in 1999 from Prince George’s County, serving two terms before becoming lieutenant governor under Gov. Martin O’Malley for eight years. After being upset in his 2014 bid for governor by Republican Larry Hogan, he was elected to Congress from the 4th District in 2016 and served three terms before running for attorney general.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Brown, the state’s first Black attorney general, continued a massive investigation of abuse by Catholic priests in the Archdiocese of Baltimore, releasing a 463-page report of “horrendous” abuses just weeks into his term. His office won expanded authority to pursue class action suits in civil rights cases, and it received approval for the office’s Independent Investigations Division to prosecute police-involved deaths.
But the investigations division didn’t bring its first charges against officers until December 2024, when Anne Arundel County Police Cpl. Eddie Vasquez and Cpl. Kieran Schnell were indicted for a high-speed chase a year earlier that ended in a fatal crash. Both officers were cleared of charges in September 2025.
Brown declined to comment on that case specifically, but said criminal culpability is just one level of accountability. Loved ones can file civil complaints against officers, he said, and under legislation approved last year, the investigations division can request administrative changes within an agency, such as enhanced training to the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission.
“There are different levels of accountability,” Brown said. “I think a lot of the reforms in Maryland, including body-worn cameras, has resulted in fewer incidents of excessive force. It’s part of the accountability and oversight that’s necessary. I’m pleased with how the unit’s evolved and developed.”
As for the many lawsuits against the Trump administration, Brown said he is pleased with the office’s work fighting administration policy. He recognizes that some people may criticize the office for challenging the Trump administration, but said the president continues to usurp the role of Congress, especially when it comes to money already approved for various programs.
“We continue to see sort of like this onslaught of executive orders, proposed agency regulations from this administration that look to roll back some of the rights that we as Americans have extended to more and more people,” Brown said. “It’s never ending with this administration.”
Brown said his office’s actions have preserved millions of dollars that were at risk by administration actions, including $110 million in education funding for the state that the White House tried to freeze.
“We only bring actions that involve the things that Marylanders talk about around the kitchen table. We’re not bringing politically motivated actions,” he said. “If our transportation dollars are being threatened, if our education dollars are being threatened … then we’re going to bring an action, and we’ve been successful.”
A numbers game
Even though Brown and Rutledge both ran unopposed in the primary, there are other differences. Brown received 568,685 votes in his primary and Rutledge got 161,800. That largely reflects voter registration in the state: 2.2 million Democrats to just over 1 million Republicans and 1 million unaffiliated voters as of September.
That doesn’t mean a Republican can’t win, as Brown well knows: He lost a statewide governor’s race to Republican Larry Hogan in 2014.
But Hogan was not a typical Maryland Republican, Eberly noted. And Rutherford doesn’t have the money or the name recognition that Hogan did, which makes the challenge all the more difficult for the GOP nominee.
“Republicans, if they’re not named Larry Hogan, just do not do well statewide in Maryland, and don’t have the ability to raise the kind of funds that would be necessary to mount a truly effective campaign,” Eberly said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: One of the best reasons for nonpartisan judge elections? KY law requires it.
description: A recent column said nonpartisan judicial elections present a problem for voters, namely, “How can voters know how judges may rule on the cases that come before them?” The key word in that sentence is “may.” Judges should not commit to ruling one way or the other, but to decide cases based on the law […]
text:
Kentucky has nonpartisan judicial elections for many good reasons, the writers argue. (Getty Images)A recent column said nonpartisan judicial elections present a problem for voters, namely, “How can voters know how judges may rule on the cases that come before them?”
The key word in that sentence is “may.” Judges should not commit to ruling one way or the other, but to decide cases based on the law and the facts. Voters must remember that judicial elections are not like elections for legislative or executive offices, in which candidates make pledges to get support. Judges must keep an open mind and avoid obligations beyond their duty to follow the law and the facts.
Why have nonpartisan judicial elections? The simple answer is that the Kentucky Constitution requires it and has for more than 50 years.
A deeper dive into the role of the judiciary in our system of government also suggests why, if we are to select judges by popular election, we should do so in nonpartisan elections.
The judicial determination of what the law is should not depend on what is most popular. That may be an appropriate consideration for the legislature, and even the executive branch of government. However, that is not what judges do. Courts and judges resolve disputes by deciding facts, interpreting rules, statutes, ordinances, constitutions, and the common law. That determination is not based on popular opinion. Occasionally the courts must disagree with the other branches of government.
Perhaps this is an oversimplification, but it may be a helpful reminder:
The legislature makes the law.
The judiciary interprets the law
The executive enforces the law.
The judicial process works best when judges approach cases with an open mind and not committed to prior positions taken for partisan reasons. The judicial process is also at its best when it is the result of a formal, orderly procedure of hearings and trials devoted to fairness and informed decision making. It may not be perfect, but we submit it is the best we can devise.
We believe it would be appropriate for judicial candidates to discuss societal and legal issues if all sides of a controversy were presented. However, opinions should not be expressed in such a way that suggest the candidate already has determined what the outcome should be.
Other areas of inquiry also may be helpful. Retired Judge Julia Adams of Winchester, who has served both as a circuit and district judge, has suggested the following questions that could be properly asked of judicial candidates.
1 .What do you see as the challenges facing our judicial system?

 What changes would you advocate in our system, if elected?
 What do you see as the challenges facing our circuit/district?
 Have you ever represented a litigant in a jury trial? How many defendants and how many plaintiffs?
 Would you agree to serve as a specialty court judge, those courts which focus on drug, mental health, and veterans treatment issues?
 Have you received any training with participants who suffer addiction issues, mental health issues, etc.?

One final point: Our nation and Kentucky are deeply divided by excessive partisanship. Why would we make judicial selection more partisan, especially now? If we need to make changes, let’s do so thoughtfully. Kentuckians deserve a fair and open-minded court system committed to the rule of law.
This piece was also signed by Kate Hendrickson, a  former commonwealth’s attorney for Mason, Fleming and Bracken counties, and Julia Adams is a retired circuit and district judge in Clark and Madison counties.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: The secret sauce to keeping KY election problems to a minimum
description: Being an election official isn’t easy these days.  In recent years, local election officials across the country, including poll workers, have faced an increase in threats and harassment.  According to a 2024 survey released by the Brennan Center for Justice, 38 percent of local election officials experienced threats, harassment or abuse for doing their job.[...]
text:
A poll workers carries his lunch into the Scott County Public Library precinct in Georgetown on Nov. 5, 2024. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)Being an election official isn’t easy these days. 
In recent years, local election officials across the country, including poll workers, have faced an increase in threats and harassment. 
According to a 2024 survey released by the Brennan Center for Justice, 38 percent of local election officials experienced threats, harassment or abuse for doing their job. The survey also reported more than half of local election officials reported being concerned for their and their colleague’s safety. 
But as other states have experienced alarming situations at the polls in past elections, Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams said Kentucky poll workers haven’t faced those same kinds of threats while on the job. 
“The vast majority of our poll workers are people who do it every single election,” Adams said. “They love it, and whenever I go around the state election day, poll workers are always in a great mood. They’re very comfortable. They’re very relaxed.” 
Poll workers help make sure polling places run smoothly, which can include checking voters in, issuing ballots and setting up polling locations among other responsibilities. 
The problem with battleground states 
Some Kentucky election officials attribute a lack of non-competitive races to why temperatures are dialed down on election day. 
Adams said in swing states, like Arizona and Georgia, tempers around the election typically tend to run hotter. So while there sometimes is misbehavior at the polls in Kentucky, Adams said it hasn’t appeared to be related to angst about the elections. 
“There’s (also) just a lot less emotion in a non-presidential year, and this is not a state that’s seen as especially competitive, at least not at the statewide level,” Adams said. “So, there’s certainly downsides to that. You want interesting races to draw people to go vote, but the upside of complacency is that the temperature is just a lot lower.” 
Kentucky Secretary of State Michael Adams sits at his desk in Frankfort behind the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award that he received in 2024 for increasing voting days in Kentucky and protecting election integrity. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Trey Grayson, a former Kentucky Secretary of State, expressed similar thoughts to Adams, saying most problems arise in battleground states and during presidential election years. He has also been a poll worker since 2023 and said people are typically friendly and proud to participate in the Democratic process. 
“I think that Kentucky, not being a big battleground state, has probably shielded us a little bit from some of the pressures,” Grayson, who is now a lobbyist for the County Clerks Association, said. 
Adams said Kentucky has also taken preemptive measures to protect election officials. In 2021, the General Assembly passed House Bill 574, which significantly reformed the state’s election system. A provision in the bill included legal protections of election workers from harassment and intimidation. 
“I also feel that the very careful approach that we take, the very nonpartisan approach that we take, we don’t lend people to think that the elections are rigged,” Adams said. “We don’t make election administration partisan. I feel like just taking the drama out of it helps assure voters that there’s no rigging here.” 
Meanwhile, some county clerks say confidence in the election system and strong laws are reasons why county clerks can adequately staff precincts. 
Fayette County Clerk Susan Lamb said Kentucky has a transparent election process, which helps boost the community’s confidence in the state’s elections. For the general election, she said Fayette County will have 1,100 election officers across 285 precincts. 
She added Fayette County has not had any turmoil or major issues that cause concern for safety at the polls. 
“What we need to understand is that there’s a lot of noise out there, and a lot of people want people to be up in arms,” Lamb said. “They want to put the fear into (elections) so that they might think second guess about going and voting, and I don’t want people to think that here in Fayette County.” 
Clinton County Clerk Nathan Collins said he has filled the 24 poll worker spots needed in his county, and the same people typically have come back year after year. 
“I’ve never really had any trouble in the past with poll workers being intimidated by people,” Collins said. “But in the case that they are, we’ve got procedures in place in our sheriff’s office that controls our three voting centers day and during early voting.”
Improvements still needed
Politicians still think there’s ways to improve the system. 
While election threats and safety concerns haven’t impacted Kentucky’s elections, Adams said there’s still room to improve the system. 
One idea Adams mentioned is to increase the base funding counties receive to run elections. He said county budgets pay for around 85% of the costs for running elections and believes there should be an equal sharing of costs. 
In the base funding formula, Adams said counties receive 25 cents per registered voter and $255 per precinct. 
“At the very least, we should be inflation-adjusting these numbers, and those numbers were in the 80s, and they’ve just not been raised,” Adams said. 
For poll workers, they are paid at least $10 for attending a mandatory training session and at least $60 per election day, but the exact rate is determined at the county’s discretion, according to the State Board of Elections website.  
Grayson said if the state gave more money to help offset the costs counties have to pay to run elections, counties could increase poll worker pay to help incentivize the job. 
“Nobody’s getting rich being a poll worker, but an extra $50, that’s a night out, dinner out. It’s a Christmas present for somebody,” Grayson said. “It’s the kind of thing that might make a little bit of a difference on the margin.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY Supreme Court review of judge’s decision in murder case could renew impeachment quest
description: While the Kentucky Supreme Court isn’t reconsidering its decision in last spring’s impeachment of Fayette County Judge Julie Goodman, it does plan to weigh in on her decisions in a controversial hit-and-run case at the center of the legislative proceedings.  Two legal experts who spoke to the Kentucky Lantern said that while those cases are […]
text:
Rep. John Blanton, R-Salyersville, delivered articles of impeachment against Judge Julie Goodman to the Kentucky Senate on March 24, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley) While the Kentucky Supreme Court isn’t reconsidering its decision in last spring’s impeachment of Fayette County Judge Julie Goodman, it does plan to weigh in on her decisions in a controversial hit-and-run case at the center of the legislative proceedings. 
Two legal experts who spoke to the Kentucky Lantern said that while those cases are separate, the high court’s decision may further future political action against Goodman. 
Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Muth Goodman (Kentucky Court of Justice photo)
Last month, the Kentucky Supreme Court declined to review its decision at the behest of Republican lawmakers in the impeachment case, which said the matter “encroaches upon the inherent powers of the Judicial Branch” and violates the separation of powers among branches of government. 
After the House forwarded articles of impeachment against Goodman during the legislative session this year, the Senate paused its proceedings and allowed the Judicial Conduct Commission to review the matter. The legislature’s process frequently prompted questions about the power it has over impeachments versus the commission’s authority under the Judicial Article adopted in the 1970s.  
Laura Hendrix, the executive secretary of the commission, told the Kentucky Lantern earlier this month she could not confirm or deny the existence of investigations as they are confidential until 15 days after a notice of formal proceedings or an answer is filed in response under Kentucky Supreme Court rules. 
An attorney who represented Goodman in the impeachment matter declined to comment on this story. 
Separate cases
Sheryl Synder, a state constitutional lawyer, said the 2020 hit-and-run case is “totally separate” from the impeachment “but politically, they’re related.” 
“Theoretically, if the Supreme Court criticized the judge in the opinion, that could add political fuel to the fire, so to speak,” he said. 
The Kentucky Supreme Court granted discretionary review on Sept. 16 in a criminal case against Cornell Denmark Thomas II, who was charged with wanton murder for a June 2020 car crash in Lexington that killed Tammy Botkin. Media reports said Thomas had allegedly been driving nearly 100 miles per hour and fled the scene on foot. In 2023, Goodman dismissed the case against Thomas, saying he had been overcharged because of his race as he is a Black man. The county prosecutor’s office is led by a Black woman, Fayette Commonwealth’s Attorney Kimberly Baird. 
The Thomas case is the first listed of the six cited by former state Rep. Killian Timoney’s impeachment petition against Goodman. Timoney later said on social media he filed the petition on behalf of Botkin’s family. Her widower, Doug Botkin, also briefly testified before the House Impeachment Committee and said he and other family members were shocked when Goodman dismissed charges in the case. 
Timoney, a Republican, is currently seeking reelection to the House. The incumbent, Democratic Rep. Adam Moore, was the only Democrat to vote in favor of the articles of impeachment. 
The Kentucky Court of Appeals said Goodman’s order in the Thomas case was “fraught with legal errors and abuses of both its discretion and its authority” in a December 2025 108-page ruling written by Appeals Judge Glenn Acree. 
Joe Dunman, a law professor at the University of Louisville, said Acree often “doesn’t pull punches when he thinks somebody in the court below, either an attorney or the judge, has messed something up.” If Judge Acree’s interpretation is correct, Dunman continued, “she essentially ran a bench trial and said that this guy can’t be guilty at the very beginning of the case, which is just not done in criminal court.”
Dunman said he would not expect the Supreme Court to reverse the appellate court ruling in the case, but justices may provide clarity on Kentucky law regarding motions in criminal proceedings. 
“A big chunk of (Acree’s) opinion is about what kind of motions can be made in a criminal court at that point, and he mentions that there’s no Kentucky case law on that topic, and that’s why Judge Goodman relied on federal law,” Dunman said. “She looked to federal law to help guide what Kentucky courts can do. And Acree says, ‘Well, you just misinterpreted that federal law, but what would be really handy to have is some Kentucky law on that topic.’”
If the high court sides with the appeals court, then the matter goes back to Goodman to restart the criminal case, Dunman said. However, the Supreme Court does have the power to discipline judges and recuse or reassign them. 
“Judge Goodman being wrong on the law and getting reversed is not all that big of a deal on its face,” Dunman said. “But if the Supreme Court upholds the Court of Appeals opinion here, then it’s one more maybe one more political reason to be mad at her if the legislature just wants to point at her and say, ‘See, we told you she was bad.’”
Impeachments are rare
The Kentucky General Assembly returns to Frankfort in January. A Republican member of the House wasn’t available for comment on this story. A Senate Republican spokesperson provided a statement saying the Senate “will refrain from public comment on the merits of a case, or potential case, in order to preserve the integrity and impartiality of a trial” as the Senate has the power to try impeachments, similarly to a jury hearing a lawsuit. 
Snyder said a new citizen petition would not be needed for the House to enact new articles of impeachment against Goodman, “but in my view, the House would need to pass new articles of impeachment because once they adjourned, that House legally ceased to exist.” 
In modern history, the House of Representatives has never questioned a judge’s decision as a reason for impeachment to Snyder’s knowledge. He pointed out that one reason for creating the Judicial Conduct Commission was to “add a constitutional procedure for dealing with misconduct by judges that doesn’t rise to the level of an impeachable offense.” 
“Impeachments have been exceedingly rare in Kentucky history,” Snyder said. “There’s certainly not many, if any, prior impeachments of judges.” 
Goodman was last elected to the Fayette County Circuit Court in 2022. Her current term ends in 2031.

title: Subramanyam questions Loudoun transmission line route process, offers new paths for SCC to consider
description: The debate over the final path for Dominion Energy’s controversial high-voltage transmission line project in Loudoun County continues, with U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun, now urging the State Corporation Commission to consider three new routes that avoid cutting through residents’ yards and encroaching on two schools. The Golden to Mars transmission[...]
text:
Transmission lines for a data center in Prince William County, Va. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The debate over the final path for Dominion Energy’s controversial high-voltage transmission line project in Loudoun County continues, with U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun, now urging the State Corporation Commission to consider three new routes that avoid cutting through residents’ yards and encroaching on two schools.
The Golden to Mars transmission line project is the final piece of a “reliability loop” in Loudoun designed to send more power to Data Center Alley in Ashburn. Residents of the Loudoun Valley Estates neighborhoods have fiercely opposed the 500-250 kilovolt project, which would partially transverse some private properties.
Those residents and others in the region have rallied to keep the power line away from homes, Rock Ridge High School and Rosa Lee Carter Elementary, which sit near one of the proposed routes. Subramanyam has also spoken against the planned location of the line and on Oct. 9, penned a letter to state regulators proposing alternative paths.
The congressman’s route options would place the line on Old Ox Road/Route 606 or west of Dulles International Airport’s runways, cutting through National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) property.
An alternative route for the high-voltage transmission line Golden to Mars proposed by U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun. (Map provided by Subramanyam)
An alternative route for the high-voltage transmission line Golden to Mars proposed by U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun. (Map provided by Subramanyam)
An alternative route for the high-voltage transmission line Golden to Mars proposed by U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun. (Map provided by Subramanyam)
These routes “would minimize impacts to homes and communities,” Subramanyam wrote to commissioners.
Subramanyam wrote that he was told routes along Route 606 or directly west of Dulles Airport would not be feasible because federal agencies like the NOAA would likely not allow right-of-way for transmission lines on their property.
“I sat down with NOAA Administrator Dr. Niel Jacobs on July 20, 2026, and I was surprised to hear that NOAA did not have a technical objection to a route on their land or near the WSR-88D Doppler radar such as New Route #1,” Subramanyam said in his letter. “In fact, Dr. Jacobs seemed open to working with the community to find a feasible route for a transmission line even if it were to go through NOAA property.”
The congressman also said that the Federal Aviation Administration is producing an obstruction evaluation on a route Dominion submitted that could cross the center of two runways. He also asked if commissioners would be willing to meet with these agencies to better assess route options.
U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun, attends a rally outside the Office of Management and Budget, at a press conference held across the street from the offices on Tuesday, Oct. 14, 2025. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
He supports ensuring grid reliability, Subramanyam wrote, “but we cannot place the data center industry’s need for electricity on the backs of Virginians.”
“Ignoring community input and calls for better routes is eroding the public’s trust in regulators, utilities, this entire public engagement process, and even transmission infrastructure itself,” Subramanyam warned.
 How the transmission line battle began

Dominion proposed the transmission line project in March 2025, laying out several route options for the line. It faced widespread public backlash almost immediately.
The SCC ruled in June that Dominion’s proposed Route 4 would be in the public’s best interest, but because a portion of that route would have to be placed on school property, Loudoun County Public Schools would have to approve it.
If the school board rejected that idea, commissioners wrote, then Route 3a would be selected. In July, the board did just that, which kicked off a slate of appeals to the SCC’s decision.
However, Route 3a cuts into the backyard of residents like Vicky Hu, who has lived in her home for over 20 years and has been fighting the transmission lines for months. In the 3a plan, a 165 foot monopole would be placed in the center of her back yard and all surrounding trees would be cut down. 
Hu has filed an appeal of the final order to the Supreme Court of Virginia.
There was a push by residents of Loudoun County to get the lines buried. But the SCC sided with Dominion in blocking that idea, saying that the process would be too expensive and it would take up more space for the transition sites.
Legislation passed during the regular General Assembly session to allow for cost sharing of the burying of lines between the utility and impacted localities but it didn’t change the SCC’s decision.
The Golden to Mars project, estimated to cost $513 million, will complete a trio of major transmission line projects in the area. 
Dominion previously stated that if the line isn’t complete by June 2028, they could face violations from the regional grid operator PJM and infrastructure could be damaged.

title: Study provides a remedy for coal dust in Newport News. Good luck getting terminal operators to pay.
description: Coal dust, a decades-long scourge for thousands of residents of Hampton Roads cities where mammoth coal terminals operate, could be less of a menace in Newport News if local officials and businesses follow the recommendations in a new study. But getting funding from the wealthy terminal operators? Don’t hold your breath. Dust Solutions Inc., a […]
text:
This coal transfer terminal in Newport News sits close to many homes in the majority Black East End neighborhood. (Photo courtesy of Cornell Watson for the Southern Environmental Law Center)Coal dust, a decades-long scourge for thousands of residents of Hampton Roads cities where mammoth coal terminals operate, could be less of a menace in Newport News if local officials and businesses follow the recommendations in a new study.
But getting funding from the wealthy terminal operators? Don’t hold your breath.
Dust Solutions Inc., a South Carolina-based company that designs and manufactures equipment to battle the residue, recommended erecting an 80-foot-tall, semi-porous fence in Newport News to block wind from blowing dust off the terminals’ massive coal piles near Interstate 664, WHRO recently reported. 
Kinder Morgan and Dominion Terminal Associates separately own the two Newport News coal terminals.
The study, sought by city officials but paid for by private donors, noted that a fence could reduce the amount of some particles escaping the piles by 89%. Kinder Morgan currently uses wet suppression to lower dust – basically hosing down the towering piles with water. Dominion Terminal Associates didn’t respond to my questions about its operations or the study.
Coal dust has long been a nuisance – and a possible threat to human health – for residents of the Southeast Community, a largely African-American neighborhood also known as the East End.
The price tag for the fencing is a not-insignificant $12 million to $22 million, WHRO reported. Nor did either terminal company tell me they were willing to foot the bill – though that amount is a relative pittance to their bottom lines.
That means taxpayers would have to pick up the cost if the city or state eventually oversees the construction.
I’m usually wary of studies in which the authors might benefit financially from the prescribed solution. That poses a conflict of interest in the study’s design and conclusion.
Yet, it’s reasonable to think anything that could significantly lower the dispersal of dust would be a good thing. Some residents attribute their family’s health problems, especially cancer or pulmonary-related conditions, to the proximity of coal terminals and the uncovered trains that transport the stuff.
“The clouds of dust contain heavy metals such as arsenic, lead, and mercury, as well as silica,” the Southern Environmental Law Center noted in an article in May. “The dust is known to cause and worsen respiratory issues such as asthma, COPD, and to increase the risk of cancer.”
Yugonda Sample-Jones, founder and CEO of the East End Civic Association in Newport News, believes her son’s asthma years ago was linked to the terminals. 
“We see the coal terminal over there … It’s the backdrop of all our health issues,” Sample-Jones, 47, told me in an interview.
“We’re not benefiting from this billion-dollar industry,” she added.
“I wipe coal dust off my mailbox often,” said Joni Ivey, a local resident and retired chief of staff for U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Newport News.
Coal from Appalachia has been coming to Hampton Roads since the 1880s. As news articles and businesses note, the terminals in Newport News and at Lamberts Point in Norfolk together export more coal than anywhere else in the country.
If the terminal owners wanted to be better corporate citizens, they could certainly pay for this solution or an alternative. They seem more concerned, though, about their shareholders than the residents they’ve impacted negatively for so many years.
Kinder Morgan, with its 11,000 employees and 136 terminals across North America, has an enterprise value of nearly $102 billion. (“Enterprise value” measures a company’s total value by combining its market capitalization with debt and subtracting the cash.)
Dominion Terminal Associates’ website says it operates as a Virginia limited liability partnership. However, it’s owned by Alpha Metallurgical Resources and Core Natural Resources. AMR’s enterprise value is nearly $2 billion; Core Natural’s enterprise value is just under $4.6 billion.
It’s not just that the dust is a nuisance. Concerns about health are always near the surface for residents living near the terminals. 
As a Virginian-Pilot editorial noted last month: “Health studies suggest residents suffer from asthma at a significantly higher rate than elsewhere in the region or state. Other chronic diseases are also found at noticeably high rates.”
Residents, though, complain there have been more than enough studies over the decades; I found one that the state conducted 39 years ago. How many are needed? 
Besides, residents know folks who have gotten sick, and they know how much coal residue lands on their homes, cars and in their air filters.
Nor should the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality evade scrutiny. Activists have long considered the agency too timid in enforcing current air and water quality regulations and being too deferential to Big Business at the expense of residents’ health. A 2019 report said the agency’s programs had been hamstrung by outdated state regulations.
Environmental activists often battled with David Paylor, agency director from 2006-2022, saying he regularly sided with polluters over the environment. They also criticized the agency for its minimal $27,000 fine against Norfolk Southern in 2020 for an earlier train derailment. The derailment caused 16 boxcars to spill almost 1,400 tons of coal into the Roanoke River.  
DEQ is finally embarking on a long-delayed project to study and reduce the potential health risks associated with dust coming from coal storage and transportation facilities in Newport News and Norfolk. It’s called the Tidewater Air Monitoring Evaluation project and will measure and analyze toxic metals and particulates in the air. 
Regarding the Newport News coal terminals, Irina Calos, a DEQ spokeswoman, said by email that Dominion Terminal Associates has one air permit, issued July 17, 2012, and Kinder Morgan has two air permits, issued Sept. 12, 2013, and April 29, 2021.
“Both facilities are classified as synthetic minor sources, and permits for minor sources remain effective until there is an event that would require a change to a permit, e.g., the facility makes a physical or operational change that would increase its air pollution or there is a violation of air quality standards,” Calos added.
Mark Sabath, senior attorney at the SELC, told me in an interview the permitting process should be more robust. “There are facilities all over the country and abroad that are doing more” to fight coal dust blowing off properties into neighborhoods, he said.
“It’s fair to call this an example of environmental injustice,” Sabath noted. The term refers to disproportionate hazards and pollution borne by minority and low-income neighborhoods.
Taylor Smith, a Kinder Morgan spokesman, told me the company continues to evaluate dust-control practices. “Third-party railcars received at the facility are unloaded within a fully enclosed building,” he said by email.
The  company also remains “committed to operating in compliance with all applicable regulatory requirements.” If those requirements are weak, though, residents feel the fallout – literally.
The clincher: “We are not currently pursuing a wind-fence project at the facility,” Smith said.
As I said earlier, Dominion Terminal Associates never responded.
The proposed wind fence is no panacea. Some environmental advocates have acknowledged as much.
It would go a long way, however, to helping a long-suffering community fight coal dust. It definitely would lead to a better outcome than the persistent dust that now wafts over everyone in the Southeast Community.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Get to know Indiana’s comptroller candidates
description: A little-known statewide office responsible for disbursing and reporting how Indiana’s state tax dollars are spent is on the ballot this election season. Three candidates are vying to be Indiana’s next comptroller: Incumbent Elise Nieshalla, a Republican, is seeking re-election against Democratic nominee Jessica Bailey and Libertarian John Schick.  The compt[...]
text:
Pictured from left: Elise Nieshalla, Jessica Bailey and John Schick. (Courtesy photos)A little-known statewide office responsible for disbursing and reporting how Indiana’s state tax dollars are spent is on the ballot this election season.
Three candidates are vying to be Indiana’s next comptroller: Incumbent Elise Nieshalla, a Republican, is seeking re-election against Democratic nominee Jessica Bailey and Libertarian John Schick. 
The comptroller, formerly known as the state auditor, is responsible for accounting, disbursing and reporting how Indiana spends its $26 billion in annual state general fund revenues.
Former Gov. Eric Holcomb appointed Nieshalla to the position in 2023.
Holcomb names Nieshalla as new State Comptroller

The comptroller compiles an annual financial report for lawmakers and governors to plan future budgets, pays the state’s 30,000 employees, disburses funds to state agencies and local governments and administers Indiana’s deferred compensation fund.
She also manages the state’s transparency portal, intended for Hoosiers to know how their tax dollars are spent, and is a member of the State Board of Finance.
Nieshalla describes her ascent to the position as a natural progression from president of the Boone County Council and Indiana County Councils Association.
She spent the previous two decades in economic development and real estate acquisition for the Indiana Department of Commerce, now known as the Indiana Economic Development Corporation. 
The role taught her the basics of state government — “it’s all about jobs,” she said.
“For a long time, I’ve known that it’s my responsibility to do my part to keep the republic,” Nieshalla said, adding: “And here I find myself now as a leading financial officer for the state of Indiana, and doing my utmost to keep Indiana fiscally strong, disciplined, responsible and transparent.”
Beau Bayh celebrates after winning the Democratic secretary of state nomination at the Indiana Democratic Convention on June 6, 2026, in Indianapolis. The party also formally nominated Coumba Kebe, left, for state treasurer, and Jessica Bailey, right, for state comptroller. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Democrat Bailey is finishing her second term as clerk of courts for Porter County, where she manages marriage licenses, traffic and criminal records and oversees county elections. She also spent six years with the Porter Township school board.
The apolitical nature of the comptroller’s office is attractive to Bailey, who said she was inspired to seek the nomination to make Indiana’s transparency portal more accessible to the average Hoosier.
As clerk of courts, Bailey said she started a mobile voting center out of a single-wide trailer for Porter County residents whose community polling centers had closed, so early voting wouldn’t be so inconvenient.
“I think if we just put some of that out-of-the-box thinking into the comptroller’s office, it’ll make it much easier and more accurate for Hoosiers to get information functions like the transparency portal,” she said.
Schick, a Northwest Indiana management consultant now in his fourth campaign for comptroller, joined the Libertarian Party in 2002. He rose through the ranks as secretary for the state central committee and now district leader for Congressional District 1.
Schick sees his political outsider status as an asset for the office, which he said would benefit under the direction of a comptroller who is not a member of either major political party.
“An independent state comptroller would make it clear that it’s run independently (of the governor and legislature),” he said, “and isn’t there just to have the same set of priorities as the legislature that’s making the decisions.”
Inside the transparency portal
Nieshalla is proud of Indiana’s transparency portal, an online database of state assets, contracts, employees, finances, local governments and vendors. “It’s a phenomenal tool,” she said.
In May, Nieshalla launched a new dashboard dedicated to federal expenditures in Indiana.
Federal funding surged from an average of between $12 billion and $14 billion a year to $26 billion at the peak of the coronavirus pandemic and has remained elevated since then, she said.
“When you have that much money coming into a state so quickly … those dollars are vulnerable to fraud, waste and abuse because of the administration and assimilating those funds in so quickly,” Nieshalla said. “So we needed to have the brightest sunlight on those dollars to be able to look back and look forward and say, ‘Are those dollars being spent as they were intended?'”
The federal number is now dropping each year.
National debt advocacy
Nieshalla and state Treasurer Daniel Elliott formed a coalition of 37 state financial officers who lobby lawmakers to take action on the $40 trillion national debt, leaning on Indiana’s balanced budget amendment as a model for the federal government.
Failure to act could result in national bankruptcy — eroding the U.S. dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency, she said.
Max Engling, right, celebrates winning the Republican secretary of state nomination alongside state Treasurer Daniel Elliott, left, and state Comptroller Elise Nieshalla at the state party convention in Fort Wayne on Saturday, June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Nieshalla worked with Hoosier lawmakers as chair of the National Debt Crisis Task Force for the State Financial Officers Foundation on a resolution asking the federal government to act. Other states are doing the same.
“They’re working to get it passed in as many states as possible to build this movement from the states, because what we’re asking the federal government to do is some of the most difficult work,” Nieshalla said, as it will require reforms of America’s most popular social programs: Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security.
“We’ve got to get back to basics and understand that resources are finite and that there are consequences for a debt load of $40 trillion … and $1 trillion in annual cost of interest.”
Bailey and Schick each said the national debt is concerning, but they would prefer to focus their attention on state issues where they could have more impact.
Opponents push to improve portal
Bailey and Schick each said they’d like to make the portal more user-friendly to the average Hoosier.
“Republicans talk a lot about the state transparency portal, but it’s not very transparent,” Schick said. “When you get into it, you realize it’s not really giving you very much information about how much money is being spent.”
A search of state expenditures in his home Porter County shows “60% of all spending goes into a single account called settlements,” he said, “and it doesn’t describe at all how all that money is being spent.”
If elected, Schick said he’d “completely” rework the site and issue regular press releases about how state monies are spent on issues of the day like Flock cameras. “It’s spending of public money and should not be hidden behind a wall of opacity,” he said.
Bailey said there are practical solutions to site glitches — case sensitive searches requiring the exact spelling of an employee or contractor’s name, which she said could be corrected to function more akin to Google by generating suggested names and search terms.
She’d like to add other information too about the prevailing wage and minimum standards for state contractors.
“It’s a very good tool, and I think it’s a good starting point,” she said.
Bailey wants more focus on State Board of Finance
The three-member State Board of Finance supervises state funds — authorizing loans, appropriations and transfers made between accounts that don’t require legislative approval.
Bailey said she’d like to see the board engage in more public discussion, so Hoosiers aren’t left out. The meetings often last only a few minutes.
“As a county official, if I need more money in my budget, or if I need to transfer money within my (accounts), I go to the county council,” she said. “They are the fiscal stewards of the county money. … They want to know why it wasn’t high enough. They want to know where the money went, what the expenses were, what cost went up and what I plan to do with the additional money.”
The State Board of Finance should do the same, she said. “But there’s no discussion at a public meeting, so how are taxpayers across the state supposed to know what’s happening with their money?”
Nieshalla said board members review information in advance to “make sure it’s on the up and up.” Many requests are routine, she said. Others are subject to additional scrutiny: “We do our due diligence to make sure we understand the request, why, what it’s going toward and then we vote yea or nay.”

name: National
title: Trump immigration policies could turn away much-needed foreign doctors, critics say
description: As the nation’s physician shortage worsens, some fear the Trump administration’s immigration policies will dissuade or prevent doctors who earned their medical degrees in foreign countries from practicing in the United States. Among all U.S. doctors, an estimated one quarter were educated abroad. But they make up an even larger proportion of physicians in ma[...]
text:
Dr. Sindhura Manubolu, the director of the family medicine program at the Long Island City Health Center in New York, received her medical degree in India. Some fear the Trump administration’s immigration policies will dissuade or prevent doctors who earned their medical degrees in foreign countries from practicing in the United States. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)As the nation’s physician shortage worsens, some fear the Trump administration’s immigration policies will dissuade or prevent doctors who earned their medical degrees in foreign countries from practicing in the United States.
Among all U.S. doctors, an estimated one quarter were educated abroad. But they make up an even larger proportion of physicians in many specialties, including internal medicine (41%), endocrinology (46%) and geriatrics (52%).
The U.S. has long welcomed foreign-educated physicians as a way to ameliorate its doctor shortage. Already, an estimated 102 million Americans live in communities that don’t have enough primary care providers, according to the federal Health Resources and Services Administration. The agency projects a shortage of 141,160 full-time physicians by 2038.
Foreign-educated doctors are slightly more likely than American ones to work in areas with a shortage of primary care providers. And doctors who are here on H-1B visas — a federal program that allows U.S. employers to temporarily hire non-citizen workers for health care jobs and other positions requiring specialized knowledge — are more likely to work in high-poverty areas.
But last August, the Trump administration issued a rule increasing the fee for employers hiring workers through the H1-B visa program to $100,000, up from between $2,000 and $5,000. It also has issued a travel ban on residents of 39 countries. And earlier this month, the U.S. State Department broadened its “online presence review” of applicants for H1-B and other visas to ensure that they do not “pose a threat to national security or public safety.”
“The United States remains vigilant throughout the visa issuance process to confirm that applicants do not intend to cause harm to Americans or threaten U.S. interests,” the State Department said in its announcement of the expanded vetting.
Dr. Tarun Ramesh, a physician at Massachusetts General Hospital and a health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School, said Trump’s policies will make it more expensive for hospitals and other healthcare employers to hire foreign physicians and might dissuade many international doctors from coming here at all.
“We’ve created a system where we depend heavily on physicians trained abroad, and at the same time, we create immigration policies that make it harder for those physicians to enter, to train, to remain in the country,” Ramesh said. “And that intersection of both the health workforce and immigration workforce and immigration policy makes it a clear tension.”
Both left-leaning and conservative states have taken steps to attract foreign physicians.
As of the middle of this year, about two-dozen states of every political bent had enacted laws to make it easier for foreign nationals to get their U.S. medical licenses.
Georgia Republican state Sen. Dr. Ben Watson, who co-sponsored a law in his state, said there simply aren’t enough U.S. medical school graduates to keep pace with population growth. He said one of his main goals is to increase the number of doctors in rural areas.
“We did it in several different stages to assure quality,” Watson said. “Hopefully we can encourage rural migration from that standpoint, also.”
Since 1994, states also have used the federal Conrad 30 Waiver Program to boost the number of doctors in underserved areas. The law allows a limited number of foreign medical school graduates who have trained in the U.S. using a J-1 visa to waive the normal requirement that they return to their home countries for two years before applying to come back — as long as they practice in an underserved area.
In increasing the H-1B visa fee, the Trump administration argued that some employers, especially tech companies, have abused the program by using it to replace native-born workers with foreigners who will work for less, rather than using it to fill jobs they can’t find Americans to do.
“American IT workers have reported they were forced to train the foreign workers who were taking their jobs and to sign nondisclosure agreements about this indignity as a condition of receiving any form of severance,” President Donald Trump said in the executive order he issued in September 2025. “This suggests H-1B visas are not being used to fill occupational shortages or obtain highly skilled workers who are unavailable in the United States.”
But 20 Democratic-led states sued to stop the fee increase, and in June a federal judge ruled in their favor. The administration was thwarted again in September, but it isn’t giving up: its latest proposal is to levy a $103,265 fee for a subset of H-1B applicants.
Even as the legal wrangling continues, the administration’s proposal has had an effect. In November survey of its members, the American Hospital Association found that 64% of hospitals that utilize the H-1B program had paused, deferred or limited recruitment because of the possibility of the $100,000 fee.
Andrew Wizner, an attorney who represents medical institutions that hire foreign medical school graduates, said the onslaught of new rules, legislative holdups, and confusing court decisions almost certainly has dissuaded some H-1B and J-1 visa applicants from applying to practice or train here.
“If you’re outside the U.S. and loosely following, (you might think) ‘Oh, there’s this rule, and I heard a court may have set it aside, but I don’t really know how their system works, their judicial system, and what that means,’” Wizner said.
He said the message that foreign-educated doctors are receiving is a simple one: “Don’t come here.”
Bradley Cunningham, a regulatory affairs and policy analyst at the Association of American Medical Colleges, said most hospitals simply can’t afford to navigate the new legal challenges and fees associated with H-1B visas.
“There’s a tremendous amount of confusion and misinformation about what’s going on,” Cunningham said. Like Wizner, he said he suspects the uncertainty swirling around H-1B visas is causing many would-be applicants to think twice about coming to the U.S.
“We can’t determine causality, but I can’t imagine that that is helping the situation any more when you’re talking about having to commit your family to come overseas to train at an institution and not having security or assurance that you can complete your training.”
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

title: Indiana shows states how to stop the Medicaid abuse, protect the care
description: Medicaid dollars intended for vulnerable children and families are not a slush fund. Every dollar lost to fraud, waste, inflated billing, or care that was never properly delivered is a dollar taken from a child who genuinely needs help. And when government fails to protect those dollars, honest providers are undercut, taxpayers are forced to […]
text:
Applied behavioral analysis is a therapy that helps kids with autism, but Indiana has had to strengthen guardrails on the expensive service. (Getty Images)Medicaid dollars intended for vulnerable children and families are not a slush fund. Every dollar lost to fraud, waste, inflated billing, or care that was never properly delivered is a dollar taken from a child who genuinely needs help. And when government fails to protect those dollars, honest providers are undercut, taxpayers are forced to foot the bill, and the families Medicaid was created to serve are left with less.
Gov. Mike Braun has decided Indiana will not accept runaway spending and weak oversight as the price of providing care. The reforms his administration is putting in place offer other states a model for protecting care without abandoning the children who depend on it.
Indiana’s experience with applied behavioral analysis, or ABA, shows what that approach looks like in practice. ABA can help children with autism develop communication, social, and daily living skills. It can be a life-changing for families, which makes abuse of the system all the more troubling. According to the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, annual Medicaid spending on ABA rose from roughly $17 million in the program’s early years to $611 million in 2023, prompting the state to take a much closer look at how the program was operating.
Rapid growth alone does not prove wrongdoing, but it demands scrutiny. The Department of Health and Human Services inspector general found that all 100 sampled enrollee-months contained at least one claim line that was improper or potentially improper. Auditors estimated that Indiana made at least $56 million in improper fee-for-service payments during 2019 and 2020 alone.
State coming down on autism therapy providers that potentially abused system

An “improper” payment is defined as one that should not have been made or was made in the wrong amount. All fraudulent payments are improper payments, but not all improper payments are fraud. When the state cannot verify who delivered a service, whether it was medically necessary, or even whether it occurred as billed, that is more than a paperwork problem. It creates an opening for deliberate abuse and puts dollars meant for vulnerable children at risk.
Braun’s response was to listen to those navigating the system firsthand. He convened families, clinicians, educators, and providers to hear how Indiana could rein in spending and strengthen oversight without sacrificing care. The state then turned those recommendations into targeted safeguards.
One of the first changes was basic accountability. Previously, ABA providers did not have to be accredited. Now, agencies must begin the accreditation process, with full accreditation required by October 2027. Indiana also secured federal approval for a temporary moratorium on new ABA agency enrollments and changes of ownership, with exceptions for underserved areas.
Indiana also strengthened clinical oversight. Registered behavior technicians must receive at least one hour of supervision from a qualified clinician for every eight hours of technician-driven therapy.
Braun also closed obvious, common-sense loopholes. Providers can no longer bill Medicaid for telehealth when a service requires direct, in-person observation. A video call is not a substitute for treatment that requires a provider to be physically present. Parents should not be sold inadequate treatment for their children and taxpayers shouldn’t pay for it.
The deeper problem, though, is incentives. The state tackled this by reducing maximum fees for individual therapy, requiring billing modifiers that identify provider credentials, and establishing group-payment tiers based on group size. But the goal should be even simpler: pay for results, not volume. Medicaid should reward better care and outcomes for children, not more billable hours.
Indiana’s reforms offer a roadmap for other states confronting the same pressures from explosive ABA spending and weak oversight. National Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program spending on ABA grew 421% between 2021 and 2025. Runaway spending has become impossible to ignore, and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services is responding with a new ABA toolkit to help states strengthen oversight and protect care. The toolkit gives states practical options on provider qualifications, supervision, payment, utilization, enrollment, and fraud prevention.
The federal guidance reinforces what Indiana is already proving: states can protect access to ABA while demanding greater accountability from the programs that provide it. Fiscal discipline is not the enemy of compassion, it’s what sustains it. Other states should follow suit before more taxpayer dollars are lost and the families Medicaid was built to serve are left with less.

title: ‘No Kings’ events return to Rhode Island Saturday with a new focus: early voting
description: A fresh round of “No Kings” events is happening across the state on Saturday, Oct. 17. This time around, organizers of at least 10 events planned so far across Rhode Island are emphasizing voting early. The focus is aligned with a push by national organizers to highlight early voting and protect voting rights, Rob Vitello, […]
text:
Participants in a No Kings rally at the Rhode Island State House on Oct. 18, 2025, are seen perched at the feet of a statue of Revolutionary War Maj. Gen. Nathanael Greene. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)A fresh round of “No Kings” events is happening across the state on Saturday, Oct. 17. This time around, organizers of at least 10 events planned so far across Rhode Island are emphasizing voting early.
The focus is aligned with a push by national organizers to highlight early voting and protect voting rights, Rob Vitello, the Newport Democratic City Committee’s treasurer who has helped organize previous No Kings outings on Aquidneck Island, said via email Monday.
“These are meant to be small events as opposed to a big rally/march as we’ve done in the past,” Vitello wrote.
Vitello said the Newport event will take place outside Newport City Hall from 10 a.m. to noon Saturday. The event page describes it as “a day of nonpartisan voter participation” meant to encourage early voting and ensure “every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard.”
Early voting starts on Wednesday in Rhode Island. The deadline to request a mail ballot is Tuesday. The General Election will take place on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
North Kingstown’s event will take place on the sidewalk outside 80 Boston Neck Road, with organizers describing it as “a hyper-local gathering site where neighbors can double-check their voter registration, locate polling places or ballot drop boxes, organize rides to the polls, and connect with voter protection networks ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.” 
“Our communities, our rights, and our future are shaped by the choices we make at the ballot box,” Jennifer Lima, the president of Transformative Action for North Kingstown (TANK), which is organizing the town’s Saturday event, said in a statement. “Don’t leave your vote to chance.
TANK is also encouraging attendees to bring a non-perishable donation for the North Kingstown Food Pantry.
The No Kings rebrand is national, with many of the events subtitled “Vote Early.” Compared to the mass protests of earlier No Kings events, the new emphasis is on helping voters with registration, understanding options and making a voting plan — in contrast to the colorful, raucous rallies that began last summer. 
In Providence, the first rally drew roughly 3,000 people in June 2025, while organizers estimated more than 30,000 attended a second rally outside the Rhode Island State House last October. Those October numbers weren’t independently verified, although Providence police estimated as many as 20,000 people attended another State House demonstration in March.
No events were listed on the No Kings site for Providence as of Monday.
National organizers could not immediately be reached for comment Monday, but an autoreply email contained an FAQ detailing the retooled approach as “the critical next step in our strategy.”
“This is an urgent, massive day of voter participation and election protection,” the email stated. “We’re going to turn people power into voter power while also building a network of election defenders.”
“October 17 is a celebration, an orientation, and an activation — all designed to drive mass early vote participation and build the nationwide capacity we’ll need to ensure the countless efforts to undermine our elections are met with the overwhelming nonviolent people power needed to defeat them,” the email continued.
 



 Here are where No Kings events are planned for Saturday

Rhode Island events listed as of Monday include:

Barrington: noon to 1 p.m. at Barrington Town Hall at 283 County Road.
Block Island: noon to 1 p.m. at Esta’s Park on Water Street.
Bristol: 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. outside Rogers Free Library at 525 Hope Street. 
Cranston: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Cranston City Hall.
East Greenwich: 1 to 2:30 p.m. at Main Street and 1st Avenue.
Newport: 10 a.m. to noon at Newport City Hall at 43 Broadway.
North Kingstown: 10 a.m. to noon at 80 Boston Neck Road.
North Smithfield: 1 to 2:30 p.m. at 900 Victory Highway.
Portsmouth: 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. in front of Clements’ Marketplace, at the corner of East Main Rd. and Turnpike Avenue. 
Westerly: noon to 2 p.m., at 14 Canal St.
