name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: What girls hear when a Pennsylvania lawmaker calls women ‘more costly to hire’
description: While hanging out in the social media universe the other day, I grazed over a clip with a short shelf life. It spread through X posts and outlets like Jezebel. I happened to see it on Instagram, and the feed moved on. The logic behind the post should not. When a Pennsylvania lawmaker said he would choose a […]
text:
Rep. Melissa Shusterman (D-Chester) wears pins claiming there's "No Time for a Pause" on menopause legislation. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)While hanging out in the social media universe the other day, I grazed over a clip with a short shelf life. It spread through X posts and outlets like Jezebel. I happened to see it on Instagram, and the feed moved on.
The logic behind the post should not.
When a Pennsylvania lawmaker said he would choose a mid-40s man over an equally qualified woman to avoid possible menopause accommodations, he revealed more than just hiring bias.
He exposed a social bargain: Women may enter the workforce, excel and build expertise, but their bodies can be used to strip them of economic independence.
That is why the debate over Pennsylvania House Bill 2135 matters beyond the state. The bill would require reasonable accommodations for pregnancy and menopause related conditions. At a Sept. 29 House Labor and Industry Committee meeting, Republican Rep. Scott Barger put it in dollars and cents, “Speaking as someone who’s signed the front side of a paycheck, I think that this bill is going to make women more costly to hire.”
Employers, he argued, would compare a mid-40s woman and a mid-40s man and “find reason not to hire the woman.” He added, “I would.”
Pregnancy accommodations are not new to the workplace. The federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act has been in effect since June 2023. Menopause accommodations are already available in Pennsylvania.
Starting Jan. 1, 2027, a Philadelphia ordinance will require employers to reasonably accommodate perimenopausal and menopausal symptoms that substantially interfere with their jobs. Barger’s “hassle” may soon become routine in Philadelphia, too.
Menopause is not a professional defect, and an accommodation is not proof that a woman cannot do her job. But when a normal bodily process is framed as a cost, complication or “problem,” it can become a weapon, another excuse to deny women jobs, promotions, income and the autonomy that income makes possible.
Untreated symptoms already cost money. A Mayo Clinic study estimated that $1.8 billion was lost in work time in the US, not counting lost jobs or early retirement. When an employer passes on the woman, that cost does not disappear. It moves on to her.
This should concern every young woman deciding what kind of future she can build.
A woman in her mid-40s is not old. For women, these are the years when their accolades and financial stability should increase. This is true for careers that require long preparation. By the time a woman has completed her training and gained the experience to lead, she may be in her late 30s or 40s.
What does a high school girl aspiring to be an astronaut hear when a lawmaker suggests that women her age may be troublesome to hire? What do college students preparing for medicine, law or engineering hear?
She hears that even after studying, training, persevering and excelling, her body may be used as evidence against her. She hears that ambition has an invisible expiry date. Girls absorb these messages early. Researchers Lin Bian, Sarah-Jane Leslie and Andrei Cimpian found that at ages  6 and 7, girls were significantly less likely than boys to associate being “really, really smart” with their own gender.
Laws are not created in a vacuum; when lawmakers consider a bill, they respond to the visible demands of their constituents. Rep. Morgan Cephas, the bill’s sponsor, told the Capital-Star that the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission had received menopause-related complaints.
The House voted 159–44 to have the Joint State Government Commission study menopause-related workplace policies. The Pennsylvania bill does not establish that every employer views midlife women as being unreliable. Yet, it reveals a conflict in our culture.
One position states that a woman who needs an individualized, reasonable workplace adjustment should be able to request it without risking her livelihood. The other treats the possibility of an accommodation as a reason to view her as a liability before she is even hired.
No one has to say that women belong back in the home for workplace practices to push them toward dependence. It is sufficient to make their employment conditional and their request for ordinary support a reason to choose a man instead.
The consequences extend beyond a paycheck. A paycheck shapes where a woman lives, with whom, and when she leaves. Being shut out of work costs a woman more than her salary. Work exclusion can mean loss for career women. Independence does not guarantee safety, nor does unemployment destine women for abuse or crime.
However, financial strain, employment sabotage, and economic abuse can restrict a survivor’s ability to leave an abusive relationship. In a study of survivors, Rutgers researcher Judy Postmus found that 78% experienced employment sabotage.
The lesson is not that women must hide their menopause to remain employable. A humane workplace should make room for women at this stage of their working lives.
Girls deserve to know that their dreams will not be crushed in the future. They deserve a workforce that views menopause not as a hiring problem but as a normal part of life.
 
Andrea Hagain
Andrea Hagan is a criminologist, an adjunct instructor of criminology and justice at Loyola University New Orleans, and the founder of Pattern Hunters, LLC, a public scholarship and accountability research platform.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: GO-NORTH ‘cautiously optimistic’ ahead of federal rescoring of rural health program
description: When the federal government revealed how much money it was giving New Hampshire as part of its Rural Health Transformation Program, Granite State leaders bragged that the state secured more funding than any other New England state (though Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont received more per rural resident, according to a KFF analysis). Howe[...]
text:
Donnalee Lozeau, GO-NORTH director, speaks to the New Hampshire Public Health Association at the McAuliffe-Shepard Discovery Center in Concord on April 23, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)When the federal government revealed how much money it was giving New Hampshire as part of its Rural Health Transformation Program, Granite State leaders bragged that the state secured more funding than any other New England state (though Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont received more per rural resident, according to a KFF analysis).
However, that could all change soon as the federal government rescores each state based on their first-year performance. 
When Congress established the program, it mandated an annual reassessment. If states hit the appropriate marks and make progress in distributing the money effectively, the government will continue providing funding. If not, the funding will be cut. According to the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, continued funding relies on “program authority,” “satisfactory performance,” “compliance with the terms and conditions of the Federal award,” and “compliance with reporting requirements.”
New Hampshire received roughly $205 million from the program late last year and hopes to receive the same amount each year until 2030 when the program concludes. According to CMS guidance materials, rescoring takes place across September and October.
Donnalee Lozeau, director of the Governor’s Office of New Opportunities & Rural Transformational Health (GO-NORTH), addresses the Executive Council, March 4, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Donnalee Lozeau is the director of GO-NORTH, the office established to manage New Hampshire’s funding. She told the Bulletin her team is “cautiously optimistic.”
“We feel like if we follow through on what we told them that we would do, which was part of our notification of funding award, that we should be fine to continue the work,” Lozeau said. “We have not had any indications that we need to change our approach. We’ve had no indication that something is amiss. Everything has fortunately been going as we’ve planned.”
Lozeau pointed out that New Hampshire was one of the first states to be deemed “fully obligated” by the federal government in June. That means CMS approved the state’s budget well ahead of the October deadline. She called that “a really strong indicator” of CMS support.
Lozeau credits GO-NORTH’s “hub” model for its speedy approval. That model designates five “hubs” throughout the state to distribute money to different projects:

The Foundation for Healthy Communities was tasked with distributing $283 million to projects aimed at expanding access to primary care, behavioral health and specialty services.
The New Hampshire Community Development Finance Authority received $223.2 million to initiate capital infrastructure projects for rural hospitals, health centers, EMS providers, telehealth and more.
The New Hampshire Behavioral Health Association received $132 million to distribute to community mental health initiatives.
The University System of New Hampshire received $96.9 million to improve the higher-education-to-healthcare-workforce pipeline.
The Community College System of New Hampshire received $37.8 million to work on other workforce development efforts.

“With the five hubs, we’re able to launch our initiatives concurrently,” Lozeau said. “You know what I mean, so it’s like it’s not just one entity doing something. It’s multiple entities.”
Lozeau said CMS officials visited in May and were supportive of GO-NORTH’s efforts and progress. CMS did not respond to the Bulletin’s questions or request for comment.
The financial landscape for rural healthcare across New Hampshire and the United States is rough. The New Hampshire Hospital Association reported last year that four rural critical access hospitals in the state were operating on negative margins. It also reported a 44% rise in operating expenses from 2019 to 2024 across all hospitals in the state and a 36.1% increase in labor costs.
With the Rural Health Transformation Program, Congress called on states to create “a transformational, long-term, sustainable health access solution” to the challenges facing rural healthcare, Lozeau said. Asked whether the threat of funding being revoked complicates GO-NORTH’s ability to create something transformative, long-term and sustainable, Lozeau said she doesn’t think so because she’s not concerned about losing the funds. She said the rescoring hasn’t changed the approach to disbursing the money.
Congress created the program as a counter-measure to cuts it made to several public health programs, including Medicaid and SNAP. In its One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Congress cut an estimated $991 billion of federal Medicaid spending over the next decade, per KFF. The Rural Health Transformation Program, which the Republicans behind the legislation said was designed to mitigate the Medicaid cuts, is providing states $50 billion over five years.
In April, the Bulletin asked Lozeau if she believes the federal government has given her enough resources to meet the lofty goal of mitigating Medicaid cuts. She said “the jury’s still out on that.” Last week, the Bulletin asked if she’d gotten a clearer picture in the months since.
“If your question is, what have we got that is out there that’s transformational,” she said, “I think some of the partnerships that are starting to develop in a way that they haven’t before will result in us seeing things that we can point out that are more transformational. I really can’t point at anything in particular right now. I mean, our most recent meeting was with the high school CTEs (Career and Technical Education centers) and the community college system and CDFA (Community Development Finance Authority) to talk about how all of those interconnections can work, which was very productive. 
“The community college system already works with all the CTEs,” she said, “but for our group to hear from the CTEs about where they think they fit in this work, I think is information that we’re coming back with and looking at. So if we can save some steps for people as they go, I think that that will be transformational. If we can find a way to get more primary care in the North Country and make it sustainable, I think that’ll be transformational.”
She added that there’s “so many things happening at one time” and that leaders need to “see how some of these work to then say, ‘oh, you know, we could make this better,’ or ‘if we did this, it would have a bigger impact.’”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Medicaid provider might end its coverage for Ochsner network, affecting 70,000
description: One of Louisiana’s four Medicaid plans might no longer cover treatment at the state’s largest healthcare network, Ochsner Health System, after Dec. 1, potentially affecting 70,000 people.
text:
Louisiana Healthcare Connections, a private Medicaid plan the Centene Corp. manages, told Ochsner Health System on June 1 it was considering ending coverage for its hospitals and clinics. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)One of Louisiana’s four Medicaid plans might no longer cover treatment at the state’s largest healthcare network, Ochsner Health System, after Dec. 1, potentially affecting 70,000 people. 
Louisiana Healthcare Connections, a private Medicaid plan the Centene Corp. manages, told Ochsner on June 1 it was considering ending coverage for its hospitals and clinics. The two companies have been in negotiations for a new contract since that time but haven’t reached an agreement yet, according to a letter sent from Ochsner to the Louisiana Department of Health last week. 
Louisiana Healthcare Connections was the largest of what were then six privately managed Medicaid plans at the end of 2025. It provided health insurance to 377,000 of the 1.4 million people in Louisiana on Medicaid plans last November, according to the state health department.  
Ochsner described itself as the largest healthcare provider for Medicaid recipients in the state of Louisiana in a letter from Mary Armstrong, the hospital system’s vice president of managed care, to state Medicaid director Seth Gold last week. Unlike any other medical system in Louisiana, Ochsner owns facilities in nearly every region of the state. 
Armstrong asked Gold for help in Ochsner’s negotiations with Louisiana Healthcare Connections, specifically requesting the Dec. 1 end date for the Louisiana Healthcare Connections plan be withdrawn.  
“This would give LHCC and Ochsner additional time to reach an agreement and preserve continuity of care for members,” Armstrong wrote. 
She also asked the health department to ensure Louisiana Healthcare Connections would fully pay Ochsner for all services it has rendered if the two sides can’t reach a deal. 
Gold said in an interview Monday that Medicaid recipients enrolled with Louisiana Healthcare Connections who are worried about losing access to Ochsner providers can switch to one of the other plans available. 
Given the current disruptions, state legislators said they will monitor the impasse between Ochsner and Louisiana Healthcare Connections.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
“You’re talking about 70,000 patients. That’s my concern,” Sen. Patrick McMath, R-Covington, said during an interview after Monday’s meeting of the Senate Health and Welfare Committee, which he chairs. 
It’s not clear what issues have stopped Ochsner and Louisiana Healthcare Connections from coming to an agreement. 
Ochsner released a written statement Monday that said it is working with state health officials to minimize disruptions for Louisiana Healthcare Connections enrollees who see Ochsner medical providers. 
“Like LDH, we are focused on helping ensure Louisiana’s Medicaid beneficiaries have access to the care they need, and we are appreciative of the shared commitment to support patients and communities across our state,” the healthcare network said in its statement. 
In a public post on its website Sept. 22, Louisiana Healthcare Connections said it still hopes to reach an agreement with Ochsner but described its current contract with the healthcare system as outdated. Staff at the Medicaid plan could not be reached for followup questions Monday.

“We believe our members deserve a provider partnership that reflects how healthcare is delivered today, not terms established about 15 years ago that no longer reflect advances in technology, care coordination, quality measurement and member expectations,” its statement reads. 
Even though Ochsner asked health officials to assist with the negotiations, Gold said the agency doesn’t know the details of its dispute with Louisiana Healthcare Connections. 

“We’re not privy to the specifics of the contract that they, Ochsner and LHCC, have with each other. So I don’t think I could speak to either what is currently in there or what they’re asking for,” Gold said. 
Since Louisiana Healthcare Connections is funded entirely with public money, the Medicaid plan must also contract with the state. The 2027 extension of its current agreement, worth $5.8 billion, is up for review and approval Thursday with the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget. 
Gold said a termination of Louisiana Healthcare Connections arrangement with Ochsner might put the Medicaid plan at risk for failing to provide enough medical providers in various regions of the state. If it violated that portion of its contract with Louisiana, the department could assess the plan penalties, he said. 
“If LHCC was to do this, they better be able to ensure that in South Louisiana or North Louisiana … that there is availability of providers that are Ochsner providers that make up the difference for them,” he said. 
The standoff between the two entities comes at a time of upheaval for Medicaid, which provides publicly funded health insurance to people with low incomes or who are pregnant or have disabilities. 
UnitedHealth pulled its Medicaid plan from Louisiana in April. A second plan, Healthy Blue run by Elevance Health and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Louisiana, also announced last month it would exit Louisiana in January. 
The number of people participating in Medicaid has dropped dramatically since Gov. Jeff Landry took office at the beginning of 2024. The program has gone from 1.6 million enrollees to 1.3 million over the past two years as the Landry administration imposed a more aggressive review of its participants’ qualifications.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: In Maine’s 1st District, Pingree and Russell square off again
description: The election in Maine’s 1st Congressional District may have fallen to the wayside amid more contentious statewide races, but the names on the ballot are still familiar — it’s the same two candidates who ran for the seat two years ago.  Republican Ron Russell is back again to challenge incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree won nearly 59% of the vote in 2024 against independent Ethan Alcorn and Republican Ron Russell, who is challenging her again to represent Maine's 1st Congressional District. (Pingree photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star; Russell photo courtesy of campaign) The election in Maine’s 1st Congressional District may have fallen to the wayside amid more contentious statewide races, but the names on the ballot are still familiar — it’s the same two candidates who ran for the seat two years ago. 
Republican Ron Russell is back again to challenge incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree for her seat in Congress. Pingree had a solid win in 2024, beating Russell and independent Ethan Alcorn. 
Russell, 72, grew up in Fort Fairfield, and is a retired Army colonel. He served for just over 30 years as an airborne ranger Green Beret, and was in combat in Panama, Somalia, Afghanistan and other crisis response operations. 
After retiring, he founded the North Carolina-based defense contractor Far Ridgeline Engagements, and returned to Maine in 2021. Russell said he knows he’s a repeat candidate for voters, but hopes it will work in his favor. 
“There’s certainly nothing different in the way I feel about the issues, probably have refined them somewhat,” Russell said. “But I’m the same person I was back then, and I think, unfortunately, the issues facing the nation and Maine are the same.”
Pingree has represented the district since 2009, and is currently the ranking Democratic member on the Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies under the Committee on Appropriations. 
“I never take any campaign for granted,” Pingree said. “The voters deserve to both see us and hear from us, and know that you’re taking it seriously.”
She also served in the Maine Senate from 1992-2000, and was majority leader in her final four years in the state Legislature. 
“We all know this is an extremely critical election,” Pingree said. “This has been one of the most challenging two years in our country, and it doesn’t matter which side of the aisle that you’re on.”
The two will meet for one debate, on Oct. 29 in Portland, jointly hosted by Maine Public, NewsCenter Maine and the Portland Press Herald.
President Trump
Like most federal races across Maine and the country, even if President Donald Trump’s name is not on the ballot, he is very much still a central factor in the race, and the 1st District is no exception. 
Pingree said in her latest term in office, she has spent a lot of time pushing back against Trump’s actions. 
“Especially in the last two years, unfortunately, much of our focus has just been on fighting back from an out of control administration,” Pingree said. “I mean, the amount of things they have done that are illegal or unconstitutional or just extremely damaging to Maine is greater than anything I’ve ever seen before.”
But she said constituents have been incredibly engaged in the issues, and want to see Maine’s congressional delegation protect their interests — and Pingree hopes to do more of that if Democrats can regain a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
“So I think this year people want to know that we’re fighting for them, that our goal is if I’m reelected to do everything we can to undo the damage that they’ve done, particularly if we’re in the majority and we have more power to do that,” Pingree said. 
Russell has a very different approach, and while he hopes to bring an independent mindset to Congress, he doesn’t disagree with Trump’s priorities. 
“I said before I’m not going to be a rubber stamp for President Trump, but I really kind of agree with the things that we are doing and in getting our nation back on board,” Russell said. 



Quotation







I said before I'm not going to be a rubber stamp for President Trump, but I really kind of agree with the things that we are doing and in getting our nation back on board.


– Ron Russell, Republican nominee for Maine's 1st Congressional District


But Russell said he doesn’t agree with the way the president goes about enacting his agenda. 
“Sometimes how he does what he does, I’m not a big fan of,” Russell said. 
Russell added that he thinks Congress can do more to assert its authority to be on par with the president.
“We have three equal branches of government, and I think, to a degree, he does things the way he does because a couple of the branches of government have abdicated their responsibilities,” Russell said. 
That point is one Pingree agreed with, and said many Republicans have relinquished a lot of Congress’s constitutional responsibilities. 
“As much as I have good friends on the other side of the aisle and I like working with them, uniformly the Republicans have stopped using the power of Congress,” Pingree said. “They forgot we’re a co-equal branch.”
Immigration 
Immigration has been a major issue in the 1st District during Trump’s second term, and came to the forefront in July when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford.
“The officer was unqualified,” Pingree said. “They literally shot a person who they weren’t even intending to pick up.”
Pingree has been vocal about her opposition to ICE activity around the country, and participated in two ‘shadow’ hearings on the shooting with fellow Democrats. 
The federal government has so far declined to investigate or reveal any information about the fatal shooting of Guerrero, a pattern seen across the country in response to violence and wrongful detentions by ICE. 
“It’s not what anybody believed that the president was talking about, and he said he was only going to pick up the worst of the worst, the murderers and rapists, and it’s not how you want your tax dollars spent,” Pingree said.
Russell said he doesn’t know if the results of the federal investigation into the Biddeford shooting would be made public, but he said will push for that information to be released. 
“Releasing the results of that investigation would be very, very valuable for obvious reasons,” Russell said. “People want to know, and people should know.”
Russell said he thinks that a lack of coordination between federal, state and local agencies has contributed to the death in Biddeford and other shootings by ICE agents around the country. 
“You can’t have it both ways,” Russell said. “You can’t insist upon cooperation during the investigation when you’re not coordinating and cooperating before the investigation. And if you did, the investigation would be necessary, from my perspective.”
More broadly, Russell said he opposes sanctuary cities and supports immigration enforcement.
“The fact that the border is closed, our southern border, I think, is a great accomplishment,” Russell said. “And we are having to deal with the millions of illegal immigrants who came across the border during the last administration, and that is what has been problematic.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On the other side, Pingree said she strongly opposes the quotas in place for ICE agents, and called the agency’s actions unconstitutional. 
“It’s just an outrageous use of the taxpayer dollars,” Pingree said. “It doesn’t make us safer, and it goes against what people think is fundamental in a democracy.”
Pingree said her staff regularly hear from constituents struggling to navigate the immigration system, and are confused about the enforcement actions.
She said her Portland office “has a steady stream of new Mainers who come in there, sometimes just looking for a work permit to be renewed.” 
“Sometimes it’s employers saying, ‘Hey, I have a whole carload of roofers and I can’t figure out where they’ve been taken,’” she said. “Family members who say to us, ‘Someone was picked up and now they’ve been moved.’”
Pingree pointed to her efforts to get Olivia Andre, a 19-year-old asylum seeker and Portland resident, released from detention after six months. Pingree and other Democratic members of Congress traveled to the detention center in Texas where Andre was held.
“But it took a congressperson to visit all the way to Texas to get them moving on that,” Pingree said. “But that happens every single day.”
Heating costs and the Iran War
As temperatures begin to drop, many Mainers are watching the cost of heating oil, which has reached historic levels this fall as the war in Iran drives up prices. 
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.97 per gallon on Oct. 5, up roughly 79% from last year. That is down slightly from Sept. 21, when the average price reached a record high of $6.02. 
Pingree called the latest prices “unthinkable,” and said she is particularly concerned about programs like the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, known as LIHEAP, going far enough for Maine residents this year. 
“It’s a bad picture to start,” Pingree said. “And if we get a cold winter, even without a cold winter, this will be a strain on a lot of people there.”
According to a press release from U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office on Friday, Maine is set to receive more than $36 million through LIHEAP, one of the earliest releases of funds in the program’s history.
“We need to end the war on Iran to try to bring down that price, but there’s no good reason not to up the amount of money in LIHEAP,” Pingree said. 
Pingree has repeatedly voted for War Powers resolutions in Congress, and said the war in Iran is a clear example of Trump abusing the limited exception for the president to defend the country from an imminent attack.
Russell agreed that the war is driving up heating oil, gas and diesel prices, but said he still supports the U.S. military action.
“I think that war was necessary, and I support President Trump doing it,” Russell said. “I’m dismayed that it’s taken as long as it has, for obvious reasons. It’s having a significant impact on gas prices around the world, but I think eventually, and fairly soon, actually, those prices will get back into normal parameters. I think prices will drop precipitously once that situation is resolved, and I think that will resolve itself within a month.”
Russell said he thinks another factor in the price spikes is the lack of natural gas refineries in the country. 
“Until we get those up and running again, where we are self-sufficient in terms of refining our own heating oil and diesel fuel, then we’re catching up once again,” he said. 
Russell said he would support building those refineries in Maine or other parts of the country, to be less reliant on other countries for processing. 
“I would not shy away from not doing it in our backyard because it’s going to be beneficial to the United States,” Russell said. “It will be beneficial to Mainers, and it will get us back on track fixing a lot of the problems that are broken right now.”

title: If Willie Sutton were still here, he’d look for loot in ridiculous immigration enforcement spending
description: William “Willie” Francis Sutton Jr., the robber who plundered banks and jewelry stores during a 40-year career, said he targeted banks because, “That’s where the money is.” He stole an estimated $2 million and spent more than half of his adult life behind bars. Were Sutton alive today however, he’d likely target the Department of […]
text:
Officers from the Tennessee Highway Patrol and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security at a traffic stop in Memphis in October, 2025. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)William “Willie” Francis Sutton Jr., the robber who plundered banks and jewelry stores during a 40-year career, said he targeted banks because, “That’s where the money is.” He stole an estimated $2 million and spent more than half of his adult life behind bars.
Were Sutton alive today however, he’d likely target the Department of Homeland Security. That agency has doled out tons of federal money to local law enforcement here in Kansas, and the Shawnee County Sheriff’s office has inked just such a deal. Kansas Reflector obtained a redacted copy of a memorandum of agreement between the federal government and the sheriff’s office.
Under the signed MOA, each “trained and credentialed TFO (task force officer) will receive up to $7,500 for essential equipment including a laptop and a mobile phone with cellular service upon becoming operational.” 
“Operational” means the LEA (law enforcement agency) having “a signed MOA, trained and credentialed TFOs, and the LEA making 287 (g) arrests in accordance with the MOA.”
Qualified law enforcement agencies “receive up to $100,000 for the purchase of new vehicles for each signed MOA upon becoming operational.” 
“This partnership is more than a program — it’s a shared mission,” said an official with a redacted name. “By working together, we are building a safer, stronger America. Your dedication and professionalism inspire us every day, and we are proud to stand with you as we take the 287(g) program to the next level.”
What is 287(g)?
It’s a section of federal law allowing local officials to work with the federal government on immigration enforcement.
President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14159, or the “Protecting the American People from Invasion Act,” the day he took office in January 2025. It authorized state and local law enforcement officials, as determined by the secretary of Homeland Security, to be “qualified and appropriate under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.”
According to the MOA, “several states, including but not limited to Florida and Georgia, have passed or are considering state legislation mandating LEAs to seek out and enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.” 
The outlay here would have left Willie Sutton salivating. 
According to federal spending analyses, Congress has dumped $268.9 billion into this administration’s mass deportation and detention agenda across DHS, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and other related agencies.
That number includes funds from H.R.1, or Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which contributed $175.6 billion. The Secure America Act chipped in $52.5 billion, and the DHS appropriations for fiscal year 2025 added 33.5 billion.
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican seeking reelection against Democrat Chris Mann, has told news organizations that the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, 35 counties and 10 cities have implemented collaboration agreements with ICE — so far.
Kobach said the federal agency needs local assistance.
Mann argued that Kansas sheriffs and police chiefs manage departments already stretched thin, without adding immigration enforcement responsibilities.
This spending has occurred along with ruthless cuts to the social safety net. Trump cleaved $186 billion from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which provides monthly food benefits to low-income individuals and families, serving more than 42 million people each month.
His administration also slashed $990 billion from Medicaid over 10 years, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s analysis. It’s the largest reduction to Medicaid in U.S. history.
But there’s more to this than money.
This spending feels like both a jobs program for the president’s base and a way of reducing hunted human beings into salaries for those jobs. Skewed budget choices threaten the survival of rural hospitals while also demonstrating that there really was enough money for social uplift efforts.
It was the will to help people that went lacking.
The money in these agency budgets would have left Sutton plotting on how to pinch some for himself. He was one of the first ever fugitives named to the FBI’S Ten Most Wanted List.
According to the FBI’s website, despite robbing banks, “Sutton had the reputation of a gentleman; in fact, people present at his robberies stated he was quite polite. One victim said witnessing one of Sutton’s robberies was like being at the movies, except the usher had a gun. When asked why he robbed banks, Sutton simply replied, “Because that’s where the money is.”
Sutton acquired the nicknames “The Actor” and “Slick Willie” for his various disguises.
Had he not died at age 79 in Spring Hill, Florida, DHS might have been on the lookout for a smartly dressed but suspicious centenarian casing the joint, looking for one last big score.
Mark McCormick is a journalist and a nonprofit executive. He’s also the author of four books including “Barry Sanders: Now You See Him” (a New York Times bestseller), “Some Were Paupers. Some Were Kings: Dispatches from Kansas,” and his latest, “Kansas Matters: America’s Social Faultlines.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Court of Appeals and Tax Court judges are on the ballot for retention
description: As Hoosier voters head to the polls this election, they will find on their ballots the Court of Appeals of Indiana judges and the Indiana Tax Court judge who are up for retention, but many of those voters may struggle to decide whether to retain them or not. Retention questions are difficult for the electorate, […]
text:
The Court of Appeals of Indiana was created by the Indiana General Assembly in 1891. (Photo by Marilyn Odendahl/Indiana Citizen)
As Hoosier voters head to the polls this election, they will find on their ballots the Court of Appeals of Indiana judges and the Indiana Tax Court judge who are up for retention, but many of those voters may struggle to decide whether to retain them or not.
Retention questions are difficult for the electorate, especially for those who are not lawyers. Some voters may even be uncertain as to what the judges on the Court of Appeals and Tax Court do and, therefore, feel unable to make an informed decision.
However, former Court of Appeals Judge Linda Chezem has some simple advice for Hoosier voters: read the opinions the judges have written. She acknowledged reading through the rulings will take time, but she pointed out the decisions made by the appellate and tax court judges impact the entire state, regardless of whom the litigants are and where the case originated.
Chezem brushed off the notion that nonlawyers would have trouble understanding the written opinions from the appellate court.
“You don’t need a law degree to have common sense,” Chezem said. “I just think it’s really important that people not be intimidated, ‘Oh, that person’s a judge, I can’t understand it.’ No law degree ever made anyone smart.”
How does retention work?
This year, three judges from the Court of Appeals of Indiana and the judge from the Indiana Tax Court will be on the ballot for retention. Appellate Judges Mary DeBoer and Paul Felix will be on every Hoosier voter’s ballot, while Judge Dana Kenworthy will only be on the ballots of voters from the counties in the Court of Appeals’ second district, which includes Marion, Hamilton, Tippecanoe, Delaware and Howard counties.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
The 15 judges on the Court of Appeals of Indiana represent five districts in the state. (Graphic/Court of Appeals of Indiana)
Tax Court Judge Justin McAdam will also be on every ballot.
The voters will be asked to answer “yes” or “no” as to whether each judge should be retained. The judges just need a simple majority to remain on the bench.
If any of the judges are rejected by the electorate, that judge’s tenure on the bench will end when the Indiana secretary of state issues a certificate verifying the judge has not been retained by the voters. No later than the first Friday after Election Day, the secretary of state has to issue a certificate stating whether each judge was retained or removed.
Judges who lose the retention vote can ask for a recount. Consequently, the judge’s term will continue and only end if the Indiana Recount Commission certifies the electorate did vote against retention.
Should one of the judges not be retained, the vacancy on the court will be filled through the same merit selection process that is used to fill any open seat on the Indiana Supreme Court, Court of Appeals or Tax Court. The Judicial Nominating Commission will take applications, interview the applicants and then submit the names of three nominees to the governor no later than 70 days after the vacancy occurred. The governor will then appoint one  of the nominees to the bench.
What assistance is available to help voters?
The Indiana Supreme Court’s Office of Judicial Administration has created a judicial retention website, which includes biographical information, videos of oral arguments and links to each judge’s written opinions.
Also, the Indiana State Bar Association has released the results of its survey that found a sizable majority of its members support retaining all four judges. The members of the ISBA, which includes lawyers, judges, law school professors, court administrators and paralegals, were asked whether each judge from the Court of Appeals and Tax Court should be retained in the general election.
The survey results are as follows:
Indiana Court of Appeals

Judge Mary A. DeBoer: Yes – 89.5%; No – 10.5%
Judge Paul A. Felix: Yes – 86.5%; No – 13.5%
Judge Dana J. Kenworthy: Yes – 91%; No – 9%

Indiana Tax Court

Judge Justin L. McAdam: Yes – 88%; No – 12%

As Indiana’s second-highest court, the Court of Appeals hears most cases that are appealed from the trial courts and some state agencies. It was created by the Indiana General Assembly in 1891 to help with the backlog of cases waiting for adjudication at the Indiana Supreme Court.
Today, 15 judges serve on the appellate court. Each case that comes before the court is randomly assigned to a three-judge panel, which will consider the facts and the law and then make a ruling. Oral arguments are rarely heard at the Court of Appeals. A majority of the opinions are decided based on the briefs the parties file and the trial court record.
Some appellate courts in other states only issue short opinions, stating whether the lower court’s ruling was affirmed or reversed. Conversely, the judges on the Indiana Court of Appeals write substantial opinions, diving into the case and explaining how the panel reached its decision. The court issues more than 2,000 written opinions each year.
The Indiana Tax Court was created by the legislature in 1986. It has one judge.
That court hears any cases that are appeals of decisions made by the Indiana Department of State Revenue or the Indiana Board of Tax. Also, it has jurisdiction over some appeals from the Department of Local Government Finance.
Any advice for determining who to retain?
Chezem advised voters to not only read the judges’ opinions but also do some additional work and find any dissents they may have written. Judges typically write a dissent when they do not agree with the majority on the panel, because they have a different interpretation of the law or of court precedent.
(Courtesy of Indiana Court of Appeals)
A dissent, she said, could entice the Indiana Supreme Court to take a look. The justices might see the dissenting opinion as bringing forth a valid point and something they should consider.
“I consider dissents to be very important,” Chezem said. “The dissents often point the way to the future.”
Joel Schumm, a professor at Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law, who has represented more than 100 indigent clients in the appellate court, cautioned voters against basing their retention decision on a single written opinion. The Court of Appeals judges, he said, decide hundreds of cases every year, so looking at only one ruling might not be enough to make an informed choice.
Rather, Schumm said the decision on whether to retain should be based on the answers to such questions as does the judge work hard, treat people with respect, and write well-reasoned opinions.
Schumm said voters should pay particular attention to the state bar association’s survey, which he called a “useful tool.” The respondents would have included lawyers who have appeared before these judges and have the professional expertise to determine whether the judges are following the law and making logical and rational decisions.
”I don’t think it’s a bad thing that the default is ‘yes’ for a lot of people,” Schumm said of voters choosing to retain judges. “If there is a problem (with a judge’s behavior or rulings), hopefully the message will get out more.”
Who are the Court of Appeals judges on the ballot?
Judge Mary DeBoer was appointed to the Court of Appeals by Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2024.
While on the Porter County bench, DeBoer created two problem-solving courts for juveniles: a truancy court and a transformation court focused on mental illness. She also developed an Immersion Through the Arts Program to help get youths struggling with delinquency connected with mentors in the local community.
Court of Appeals Judge Mary DeBoer
DeBoer has served on the Indiana Judges Association Board of Managers and is currently on the Appellate Practice Section Council of the Indiana State Bar Association. Also, she chairs the Criminal Case Flow Management project, which examines and identifies strategies that can improve criminal case processing throughout the state.
A native of Kalamazoo, Michigan, DeBoer graduated with honors from Western Michigan University and earned her J.D. degree from Valparaiso University School of Law in 1993.
Judge Paul Felix was appointed to the Court of Appeals by Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2023.
Felix served as a deputy prosecuting attorney in the Johnson County Prosecutor’s Office for more than a decade, where he created the county’s first Domestic Violence Unit and led the prosecution of domestic violence cases for three years. He was subsequently appointed to the Carmel City Court by Gov. Mitch Daniels in 2007 and then elected as a Hamilton County Circuit Court judge in 2009. During that time, he helped create the Youth Assistance Program, which is one of the state’s only judicial programs that focuses on prevention of crime by providing youth with mentors, tutors and other services.
Court of Appeals Judge Paul Felix
Currently, Felix is the chair of the Indiana Juvenile Detention Alternative Initiative and co-chair of the Marion County Judicial Selection Committee. Also, he serves on the State Board of Law Examiners Committee on character and fitness, interviewing graduating law students to ensure they are fit to practice in Indiana.
Born in Elkhart and raised in Greenwood, Felix earned both his undergraduate and law degrees from Indiana University Bloomington.
Judge Dana Kenworthy was appointed to the Court of Appeals by Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2022. With her appointment, the COA had a majority of women judges for the first time in its history.
Kenworthy started her career as a deputy prosecutor in Grant County from 2001 to 2010, handling cases involving child abuse, sexual assault, domestic violence, computer-facilitated crimes and juvenile delinquency. In 2025, she received the Outstanding Prosecutor Award from the Indiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence and in 2006, she received the Randall T. Shepard Award from the Indiana Pro Bono Commission.
Court of Appeals Judge Dana Kenworthy
As judge for Grant Superior Court 2, Kenworthy presided over a variety of cases, including criminal, civil, juvenile and family. In 2015, she established the Grant County Family Recovery Court, which is considered one of the best in the state and in 2021 was named as one of eight Peer Learning Courts in the country.
Kenworthy currently serves on the Commission on Improving the Status of Children in Indiana and is chair of the Youth Justice Oversight Committee.
A graduate of Ball State University, Kenworthy holds a J.D. from Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law.
Who is the Tax Court judge on the ballot?
Justin McAdam was appointed by Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2023, becoming the third judge to preside over the Indiana Tax Court.
After serving as a law clerk to now-retired Justice Brent Dickson of the Indiana Supreme Court, McAdam joined The Bopp Law Firm, founded by prominent conservative attorney Jim Bopp.
Tax Court Judge Justin McAdam
Prior to his judicial appointment, McAdam was deputy director and chief legal counsel for the Indiana Office of Management & Budget. Also, he served as chair of the Indiana Distressed Unit Appeal Board and the Indiana Board for Depositories as well as a trustee of the Indiana Public Retirement System and the Next Level Indiana Trust Fund.
McAdam is a past chair of the Indiana State Bar Association’s Tax Section and serves on several committees established by the Indiana Supreme Court, including the Innovation Committee and the Records Access and Management Committee.
Born in California and eventually settling with his family in Terre Haute, McAdam started his college studies at Purdue University before transferring and earning a bachelor’s degree at Indiana University. He earned his J.D. from Harvard Law School.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Criminal justice advocates disappointed by GOP attacks, Crowley’s cancellation of  jail tablets
description: For weeks, a stream of ads has attacked Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, for allowing  access to tablets in the Milwaukee County Jail. In some high-profile cases, incarcerated people used the tablets to harass people on the outside. The ads, which recycle footage of a disgruntled local judge, have kept […]
text:
David Crowley, Milwaukee County Executive, speaks to media after he relaunches his campaign to become Wisconsin's next governor. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)For weeks, a stream of ads has attacked Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, for allowing  access to tablets in the Milwaukee County Jail. In some high-profile cases, incarcerated people used the tablets to harass people on the outside. The ads, which recycle footage of a disgruntled local judge, have kept Crowley on the defensive while casting his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, as a protector of crime victims. 
The ads focus on individual cases of people using their jail-issued tablets to harass witnesses and victims. Many feature Milwaukee County Circuit Court Judge David Borowski, who asked,  “Why is the sheriff’s office handing laptops and iPads to defendants?” Borowski was presiding over a hearing involving Thomas Zollicofer, who is accused of killing three people in a spree. Zollicofer used his tablet to tell a witness to “stop lying,” WISN 12 News reported. Some of the ads also mention Ameir Jones, who is also accused of homicide and of attempting to call a victim in his case over 1,500 times, with prosecutors saying 300 of those calls were answered.
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Over a short span of time, the anti-Crowley ads have made tablet access a big issue in the governor’s race. Late last week, Crowley suspended instant messaging on digital tablets at the Community Reintegration Center. The facility, formerly known as the House of Correction, is under more direct oversight by Crowley and the county board than the jail, which is overseen by the sheriff’s office. 
On Monday Brian Schimming, chairman of the Wisconsin Republican Party, issued a press release accusing Crowley of protecting himself from a scandal. “This program should’ve never been allowed in the first place, and Crowley resisted ending it for months after victims were threatened and laws were broken,” said Schimming, going on to call Crowley “a craven politician who only cares about his own political future, not the safety of our state’s citizens.”
Milwaukee-based Black Leaders Organizing Communities (BLOC), which supported Crowley when he re-entered the race for governor and won the primary race, expressed disappointment at the suspension of messaging services. “We have to be careful in giving in to the narrative of Republicans and their methods to make incarcerated people as uncomfortable as possible,” their statement warned. The group added that “this form of communication seems to be the best and safest form that there is currently.”
As the political controversy over tablets grew, the sheriff’s office attempted to clear the air. Joshua Briggs, director of the Milwaukee County Jail, said that the devices are not iPads but a “generic tablet.” Briggs explained that the tablets cannot be used to make calls out of the jail, and are not connected to the internet. The devices use a network maintained by the vendor, ICSolutions, which allows for keyword flagging and other guardrails. Briggs estimated that 98% of the people held in the jail use the tablets responsibly.
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany speaks to reporters after his launch event in Wausau in September. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
The ads don’t mention that Republican-dominated counties including Waukesha and Ozaukee also give people housed in their jails access to tablets. 
The tablets are important, advocates say, because they allow incarcerated people to maintain connections with loved ones and others on the outside. 
“I understand what it means to have a connection to home,” Marianne Oleson, co-executive director of Ex-Incarcerated People Organizing, told the Wisconsin Examiner. Oleson, who spent four years in prison before being released in 2017, explained that tablets give incarcerated people access to recovery resources, employment preparation, parenting classes, and other rehabilitative services. 
Tablet use  has become commonplace in jails and prisons tablets. “This technology is being used on a significant scale,” Oleson said. “Edovo reports that its educational platform was available in 1,483 correctional institutions across 47 states in 2025, with participants completing 46 million hours of learning. Those are the provider’s reported numbers, but they show how much programming can be delivered through these tools.”
Shannon Ross, a founding member of Justice Forward, wrote in August in an op ed for Wisconsin Watch, that tablet-type devices are used in 48 state prison systems, the federal prison system and in county jails nationwide. “Correctional officials have credited tablets with reducing violence and disturbances inside correctional facilities,” Ross wrote in the August op ed. “Some jurisdictions have reported declines of up to 40%, and the director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons described the agency’s tablet program as reducing administrative burdens and allowing staff to focus more on institutional safety, not as a security risk it was forced to accept.”
The Milwaukee County Jail. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“Providing tablets is an established practice today,” Oleson told the Examiner. “Wisconsin DOC says that each person residing in an adult facility will be issued an ICS tablet as its transition moves forward. Ozaukee County’s own website says that personal letters, pictures and drawings are delivered digitally through tablets available in all living units. This is happening across jurisdictions, regardless of politics.”
Other criminal justice advocates raised similar points about the use of tablets in jails and prisons. “Allowing tablets inside jail facilities is particularly important because it allows more in-depth communication with family and friends,” BLOC said in a statement to the Examiner. “Inmates can see messages and pictures from their families and loved ones. It enables them to maintain a closer connection than that of regular phone use. Sometimes, persons in custody need their families to advocate for them for their health, treatment and more that the jail staff cannot assist with immediately.”
Oleson was also disappointed by Crowley’s move. “My reaction to Crowley’s decision is concern for the people and families who are losing legitimate communication because of someone else’s misuse,” she wrote. “Victim harassment and witness intimidation are serious, and they must be addressed. We support holding people accountable for that behavior and holding facilities and vendors accountable for enforcing protections.”
Roy Rogers, a minister, board member of the Wisconsin Justice Initiative, and leader of the Onesimus Group of Milwaukee, wrote in a statement to the Examiner that electronic communication is one of the main ways his ministry can keep in touch with incarcerated people. “For us, a message is an opportunity to encourage someone, share our faith, or help them think through their next steps,” wrote Rogers. “For families, it means maintaining a connection with a parent, spouse, or child. We say ‘reentry begins with relationship’ because those connections need to grow before someone comes home.” 
 Getty Images
Rogers said that he cares about the safety and security of victims. “No one should have to fear threats or harassment through this technology,” wrote Rogers. “My understanding is that Crowley’s action pauses messaging at the CRC until stronger safeguards are in place, rather than eliminating tablets altogether. My hope is that those protections allow safe communication to continue. These tools have a meaningful place in family connection, ministry, daily facility operations, and preparation for reentry.”
“If a suspension is necessary while those changes are made, there should be a clear timeline and an explanation of what must happen for access to resume,” wrote Oleson. “I am concerned when the needs of incarcerated people and their children become talking points in a political campaign. These decisions affect real families. They should be guided by evidence, safety, and what will help people return home successfully.”

title: Ohio voters are deeply concerned about corruption, poll shows
description: As the midterm elections near, another poll is showing that Ohio voters and Americans generally are deeply concerned about corruption. In Ohio, respondents said they didn’t particularly trust either party to fix the problem. And huge majorities said they’d consider voting for candidates who said they’d fight corruption in specific ways. The survey was an […]
text:
Getty Images.As the midterm elections near, another poll is showing that Ohio voters and Americans generally are deeply concerned about corruption.
In Ohio, respondents said they didn’t particularly trust either party to fix the problem. And huge majorities said they’d consider voting for candidates who said they’d fight corruption in specific ways.
The survey was an online poll of registered voters conducted between Sept. 8 and Sept. 23. It was conducted by YouGov on behalf of the reform group End Citizens United.
When asked, “How much of a problem do you think corruption in government is in the United States today?” two-thirds of Ohio voters said it was a very serious problem. 
Another 28% said it was a somewhat serious problem. That’s 94% of voters who think it’s a problem.
Zero said it wasn’t a problem at all.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio has its own recent history of corruption, but the poll didn’t ask specifically about it.
When Ohio voters were asked to pick three of eight issues they found most pressing, “corruption in Washington” came in at No. 2. “Economy and rising costs” was No.1, and “threats to democracy and elections” was No. 3.
The Ohio results roughly matched those in an identical national poll.
While the Ohio poll didn’t ask respondents to define corruption, another national poll conducted this spring did. 
The Brennan Center for Justice, which sponsored the poll, said respondents “understand corruption broadly, centered in part on the perception that government primarily works for the ultrawealthy and well-connected and doesn’t prioritize the interests of most voters.”
Other survey data show that Americans see partisan gerrymandering as another form of corruption because it also thwarts the will of the voters.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The portion of respondents to the Brennan Center poll who said corruption is a major problem was similar to that in the Ohio poll that was conducted in September.
When it comes to solving corruption, the Ohio respondents in September appeared to view both parties with suspicion. 
Thirty five percent said they trusted Republicans more to address the issue than Democrats. That compares to 32% of Ohioans who said they trusted Democrats more to clean up corruption.
That leaves a full third of respondents in the “neither” camp. And this appears to create opportunities for reform-minded candidates.
Asked if support for certain reforms would make them more likely to support a candidate, huge majorities said they would. The reforms:

Ban Congressional stock trading — Seventy percent said it would make them more likely to support a candidate, 10% said it would make them less likely and 20% were uncertain.
Ban corporate political action committees from giving to campaigns — Sixty four percent said it would make them more like, 9% said it would make them less likely and 27% were undecided.
Require donor disclosure, or get rid of dark money — Seventy two percent said they were more likely to support that candidate, 8% said they were less likely and 19% were undecided.

Election Day is Nov. 3. Military and overseas absentee voting, as well as early in-person and mail-in voting, have started. 
The deadline to register to vote has passed.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin doesn’t have to accept new gas plants as inevitable
description: Wisconsin is facing another major test of how it plans its energy future. We Energies has proposed a new 750-megawatt natural gas plant in Wrightstown, the Fox North Energy Center. If approved, it could begin operating around 2032 and run for 30 years or more. With Fox North added to the queue, We Energies now […]
text:
The XTO energy oil and gas plant is seen at night on March 24, 2024 in Coyanosa, Texas. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Wisconsin is facing another major test of how it plans its energy future.
We Energies has proposed a new 750-megawatt natural gas plant in Wrightstown, the Fox North Energy Center. If approved, it could begin operating around 2032 and run for 30 years or more. With Fox North added to the queue, We Energies now has roughly 4.25 gigawatts of methane gas generation awaiting Public Service Commission approval.
The utility says the buildout is needed to meet rapidly growing electricity demand and maintain reliability. Data centers are a major part of that growth.
But projected demand does not make new gas plants inevitable.
Wisconsin is being asked to make decades-long energy decisions based on electricity demand forecasts that are changing faster than our regulatory system. That is exactly why new methane gas plants must first prove they are the cleanest, lowest-cost, lowest-risk option before customers are committed to paying for them.
Before Wisconsin commits customers to decades of fuel costs and long-lived infrastructure, regulators should ask a more important question: What combination of resources can meet that demand reliably, affordably and with the least long-term risk?
That means comparing new gas plants not just with one solar farm or one battery project, but with complete portfolios of solar, wind, storage, energy efficiency, transmission, distributed resources, nuclear power and demand flexibility.
Other states, including Minnesota and North Carolina, have already shown that regulators can challenge utility assumptions and require closer examination of alternatives rather than treating new gas plants as the default response to projected load growth.
Wisconsin can do the same.
That approach is already gaining support in Wisconsin, including among labor leaders who see comprehensive energy planning as an opportunity to create good-paying jobs.
Climate Jobs Wisconsin, whose leadership includes representatives of Wisconsin building trades and construction unions, recently advanced a “35 by ’35” clean-energy and good-jobs agenda. The proposal envisions roughly 35 gigawatts of new clean-energy resources by 2035, including storage, utility-scale solar, wind, nuclear generation and networked distributed power. A plan  developed by the PSC would map what gets built, where and when, establish resource targets and create a grid-investment roadmap.
That is exactly the kind of planning Wisconsin needs.
Whether policymakers ultimately adopt those exact numbers is less important than the principle behind them: Evaluate the whole system before locking customers into decades of costs.
And expanding clean energy does not have to mean sacrificing Wisconsin’s best farmland or open space.
Renewable development can be directed toward brownfields, marginal and previously disturbed lands, rooftops, parking structures, industrial parks, sites near substations and existing infrastructure. Solar can also be integrated with agricultural production through agrivoltaics, allowing farming and energy production to coexist rather than compete.
Wisconsin should be able to protect prime agricultural land while dramatically expanding clean energy. Those goals are compatible if we plan carefully.
The jobs case matters, too.
Climate Jobs Wisconsin’s agenda is built around creating clean-energy careers with prevailing wages, registered apprenticeships and local hiring. It proposes tying those labor standards to PSC approvals and expanding Wisconsin’s ability to build new energy infrastructure with skilled union labor.
That is important because Wisconsin’s energy transition should not be framed as a choice between workers and the environment.
Done well, it is an industrial green growth strategy.
It can create careers for electricians, operating engineers, laborers, carpenters, pipefitters and other skilled trades while reducing exposure to volatile fuel costs and strengthening Wisconsin manufacturing.
The rapid growth of data centers makes this kind of comprehensive planning even more important.
Wisconsin families, farmers, manufacturers and existing businesses should not become the financial backstop for those investments.
If a gas plant is justified largely by projected data-center demand, regulators should determine how certain that demand really is, what alternatives were considered, who will pay for the plant and who bears the stranded-cost risk if forecasts change.
Transparency is equally important.
That means disclosing projected electricity and water use, infrastructure requirements, tax arrangements and long-term impacts before commitments become difficult to reverse.
It also means using transparent Community Benefit Agreements, so benefits are public, measurable and enforceable.
Transparency is not anti-development. It is how responsible development earns trust.
Wisconsin does not have an electricity shortage. It has a planning challenge.
The choice before us is not new gas or reliability. It is whether Wisconsin evaluates all available resources together before committing customers to another generation of long-term fossil fuel infrastructure costs.
The Fox North proposal gives Wisconsin another opportunity to get that right.
A new gas plant should have to prove it is necessary. It should not be treated as inevitable.

title: Ramaswamy loans campaign $5 million more as Acton outpaces him with donors

text:
Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. (Photo by WEWS.)Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton out-raised her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy nearly 2-to-1 in September. She outpaced him in July and August as well.
However, Acton’s success with donors got swamped by Ramaswamy’s personal wealth. In August and September, Ramaswamy made $5 million-plus in loans to his campaign.
In all, Ramaswamy has staked more than $36 million of his personal fortune on his bid for governor. Because those funds are structured as loans, he can pay himself back with money from donors.
Ohio’s monthly reports cover contributions for statewide candidates in July, August and September. Campaigns aren’t required to share their expenditures over that timeframe. Still, the reports offer a glimpse of a campaign’s finances during the months between the post-primary and pre-general reports.
Acton’s latest figures
During the month of September, Acton’s campaign raised slightly more than $6 million. In August, the campaign raised $4 million, and in July it brought in $5.8 million.
The campaign’s biggest donor in September was the Ohio Democratic party. The state candidate fund gave her $232,000 across three different donations. Aside from that, Acton collected several contributions organized labor, fellow candidates and interest groups.
Unions representing bricklayers, auto workers, teachers and firefighters all gave $10,000 or more. Emily’s List, which backs female candidates who support abortion access, and the PAC for America’s Future, which supports Democratic state candidates, both effectively maxed out for Acton.
Among others, she got big donations from the CEO of the major league soccer team FC Cincinnati, a vice president at Oracle, and a couple of nursing home executives.
More than $5.5 million of Acton’s September contributions came from individuals, and $3.5 million, or 63%, of that total came from Ohioans.
Ramaswamy’s contributions
In September, Ramaswamy’s campaign raised a little more than $3 million. Its August fundraising was just shy of $2.6 million and in July the campaign brought in nearly $4 million.
Where Acton’s donations from political action committees lean toward labor, Ramaswamy’s lean toward business.
Committees representing Ohio hospitals and contractors both maxed out for Ramaswamy. The Ohio Chamber of Commerce gave $16,000, and American Property Casualty Insurance gave $16,600. Two groups representing home builders gave a total of $10,000.
Ramaswamy also got significant backing from OHCANN, a trade group representing licensed cannabis companies in the state. In September, the group gave $15,000 between two donations.
The cannabis industry shows up in Ramaswamy’s big ticket individual donations as well.
The President and CEO of Illinois-based Green Thumb, which operates Rise Dispensaries, both maxed out in September.
Ohio Chamber executives Steve Stivers and Rick Carfagna, both former lawmakers, tapped funds leftover in their previous campaign accounts, giving Ramaswamy $5,000 and $2,000 respectively.
Ramaswamy also cashed big checks from the CEO of NetJets, a partner with the commerical real estate firm the Daimler Group, and leaders for the car dealerships Ricart Automotive and Kerry Automotive group.
Ramaswamy even got max donations from a father and son running an antiquarian book and photograph shop in New York.
A bit more than $1.6 million, or 57%, of the $2.8 million Ramaswamy raised from individuals in September came from Ohioans.
Ramaswamy’s loans
The campaign’s most substantial influx of cash, however, came in the form of Ramaswamy’s personal loans.
On the one hand, his largesse makes good on an early campaign promise. In July last year, he pledged to put at least $30 million behind his election effort.
Acton has outraised Ramaswamy on a regular basis, but the sum total of her donations since entering the race still fall about $5 million short of Ramaswamy’s personal contributions alone.
In addition to his $5 million loans in the two most recent monthly reports, Ramaswamy has made several highly specific loans ranging from $39,984.22 to $136,749.
The Ohio Capital Journal requested comment from Ramaswamy’s campaign but got no response.
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Nick Evans on X or on Bluesky.
