name: Utah News Dispatch
title: In a time of distrust, how do we know Utah’s elections are secure? Clerks show us
description: Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections. Ballots will start hitting Utahns’ mailboxes this week ahead of the contentious midterm elections, marking another year when a national spotlight has been cast on voting by mail — largely […]
text:
Davis County Clerk Brian McKenzie poses for a photo in a ballot processing center at the Davis County Administrative Building in Farmington on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections.
Ballots will start hitting Utahns’ mailboxes this week ahead of the contentious midterm elections, marking another year when a national spotlight has been cast on voting by mail — largely due to President Donald Trump’s ongoing rhetoric of widespread fraud without evidence. 
Utah clerks on both sides of the political aisle, frustrated by national discourse that’s not based in fact but has cast a shadow over voting by mail, are pushing back.
“The general rhetoric, I’m very tired of it because it continues,” Grand County Clerk/Auditor Gabe Woytek, who is unaffiliated, told KUER in an interview for the station’s State Street episode that aired Monday. “There continues to persist a rhetoric that threatens the idea that it’s safe and secure, when I know in practice that it is a very safe and secure system … and we continue to add in those safeguards. Yet the conspiracy and the discontent continues to persist.”

In Utah, voting by mail has a long history. Since 2018, when nearly all of Utah’s counties started running elections primarily by mail while also allowing in-person voting options, the system has been lauded by state leaders, Republicans and Democrats alike. But in recent years, as Trump has continued raising doubts about its security, Utah’s GOP-controlled Legislature has reacted. 
Lawmakers have enacted more ID requirements and slowly pulled back on universal, automatic voting by mail by requiring voters to opt in to continue receiving their ballots in the mail by 2029. 
Meanwhile, the federal debate rages on. 
Although Utah’s own top election official, Republican Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, has been ardently opposed to it, the state’s senior GOP Sen. Mike Lee continues to push the SAVE Act that would demand voters prove their citizenship in order to cast a ballot. And Trump, through an executive order, has tried to change how the U.S. Postal Services processes by-mail ballots. That rule would require states to send voter information to the federal government while also banning the Postal Service from delivering or collecting mail-in ballots from people who haven’t been confirmed as eligible voters. 
Had Trump’s Postal Service executive order not been blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court for this year’s election, Henderson, a Republican, has said it would have been an “unmitigated disaster,” since it would have been logistically impossible for clerks to adhere to it with such a short timeframe before the Nov. 3 election.
To highlight allegations of voter fraud and to make the case for Trump’s Postal Service rule, the Trump administration last month spotlighted federal charges against a former Utah letter carrier accused of throwing 300 primary ballots into a dumpster before they could be delivered to Eagle Mountain voters’ mailboxes. 
Utah’s top election chief says Trump admin’s ‘gamesmanship’ with voting keeps her up at night

In an interview with law enforcement, the ex-letter carrier indicated he did not have a political motive but said he threw away the mail, which also included advertisements, “because he wanted to ‘lighten his workload’ so he could presumably go home earlier,” prosecutors said in charging documents. 
The tossed ballots are unusual. Even so, 300 ballots make up a fraction of Utah’s more than 2 million registered voters, and the charges don’t indicate a concerted fraud effort. And multiple recent state audits, while they’ve found some areas of improvement, have concluded that Utah’s election system contains “no significant fraud.” 
All of this political debate over voting by mail has cast doubt and confusion over a longstanding voting system that Utah clerks of all political stripes — Republican, Democrat and unaffiliated — defend. 
‘When people have doubt, they disengage’
Davis County Clerk Brian McKenzie, a Republican, said in an interview with KUER one of his “biggest concerns” is that the rhetoric doesn’t match reality. 
“Even if our elections are run very well and are very efficient and are very accurate, we do have some criticism out there, recognizing that the system is not perfect; it never will be perfect,” he said. “But sometimes people take those small issues and amplify those and add to them when it’s not justified.”
McKenzie noted change is not a foreign concept to elections — in fact, in his more than two decades working in various election roles, he said the process has evolved “significantly.” But he gets concerned when big changes are proposed under a tight timeframe.
National scrutiny on mail ballots changed Utah’s elections system

“That creates disruption, that creates question, and when you have questions like that, that creates doubt. When people have doubt, they disengage,” McKenzie said. “That is a concern for me as an administrator. It’s a concern for me as a fellow voter as well.” 
From Wasatch County, Woytek shared a similar concern.
“Added rules, added regulations, more confusion for the voters, I can handle it,” he said. “You know, it’s my duty to follow the law, and I will do so, and I won’t complain about it. But what I will complain about is it causing discontent and confusion among voters, which either causes them to not participate at all, or develop their own uncertainty regarding the system that they wouldn’t have had otherwise.”
Henderson, another Republican and Utah’s top election official, has been a fierce defender of Utah’s vote-by-mail system, and she’s called out the Trump administration’s political “gamesmanship” with voting, which she said in a recent interview keeps her up at night. 
“I learned a long time ago that (the Trump administration doesn’t) want to know that we’re doing things OK,” Henderson said. “They don’t want to know that things are going well, because it goes against a narrative that is being pounded relentlessly of mass fraud or ineligible people voting. And the facts just don’t support that narrative.”
Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman, a Democrat, said Henderson’s willingness to speak out is “reassuring” in an interview with States Newsrooms’ CEO Chris Fitzsimon for a “Stories from the States” podcast episode that aired Friday. 


“It’s not just me. It’s not just me waking up in a panic at 3 a.m. The Republicans are too,” Chapman said. “This isn’t a partisan issue. This is (an) access issue. This is ensuring that voters who are eligible to participate in elections understand the methods that they can do so and make a plan ahead of time, as opposed to the chaos and confusion, frankly, that we’ve been inundated with over the last couple months.”
Chapman said since 2020, Utah lawmakers have passed more than 60 laws changing the state’s election administration — and clerks have been doing their best to keep up. She said for the most part, the changes have been good, increasing transparency and creating additional layers of security, but she’s critical of the shift away from automatic voting by mail. 
“It’s going to make it a lot more difficult for people to have that easy access to a ballot earlier on,” she said. “We’re going to notice more people waiting until closer to Election Day to participate in elections, causing maybe a little bit more congestion on Election Day, and a little bit more panic. … That’s not the Utah way.”
Janalyn Christensen feeds paper ballots through an “envelopener” machine at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
What happens to your ballot and how do you know it’s safe?
In an effort to combat distrust, Utah clerks welcome Utahns to come to their offices and see for themselves how ballots are processed. 
“I love to encourage people to come in and see how ballots are processed, and I’ve given hundreds of tours,” Chapman said. 
McKenzie did just that for KUER and PBS Utah last month. During a tour of the Davis County election center, he walked through how ballots are processed. As he did, he described layers of existing — and new — security measures. 
‘Not a widespread problem’: Lt. gov. releases early findings from voter citizenship review 

“There’s always going to be a minimum of two election workers that go and pick up those ballots, they have to log the date, the time, the location, and who it was that retrieved those ballots,” McKenzie said. “They’ll bring those ballots directly here to our election facility. The moment that they come into our building, they’re under 24/7 video surveillance.”
The election center, where ballots are stored and processed, is also armed with an alarm system. Only certain staff have access to it. When ballots are being processed, it has three observation areas where election watchers can keep an eye on everything. 
Each ballot envelope has a unique barcode that ensures no voter can vote twice, even if they request a second ballot, maybe because they lost it or if it was delivered to the wrong address.
“What’s important is any time that we issue a new ballot, the previous ballot has been canceled,” McKenzie said. “So that barcode has been canceled. It cannot be utilized again.”
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

When ballots are returned, election staff must follow chain of custody rules that ensure they’re always handled by two or more election workers. They log “where they came from, when they came in, and who received them,” McKenzie said. 
Ballots are then put through a machine to authenticate whether the envelope and the barcode are valid to ensure the voter hasn’t already voted, maybe through early voting or another method. It will also date stamp the ballot and take a picture that election workers can use to verify the signature. 
Ballots are then organized and stored into batches, while election workers verify votes one by one by looking at the image of the signature on the envelope and comparing that to the signatures the clerk’s office has on file. 
“We can have up to five different images of your signature,” McKenzie said, from voter registration records and driver’s license records. 
Under new state law, voters have the option to put the last four digits of their state ID, driver’s license or Social Security number on their envelope. Starting in 2029, those last four digits will be required. But currently, if voters include those digits, election workers must verify those numbers match as well. 
Utah Legislature approves bill to require voter ID, phase out automatic voting by mail by 2029

If signatures match and the ballot is validated, election workers then determine that it can be counted, and they’ll indicate that in the clerk’s system. If it can’t be validated and counted, they’ll indicate that and give a reason why, McKenzie said. 
“Maybe the signature doesn’t match, maybe the last four don’t match, or maybe the signature is missing, or any number of reasons,” McKenzie said. “Then those envelopes are going to be run through this machine again. It’s going to sort out the valid ones from the invalid ones. All of the invalid ones, we have to notify the voter and let them know that there’s a problem with their ballot and how they can correct it.” 
To count verified ballots, election workers then put them into machines that remove the ballots from their envelopes. An operator will watch to make sure the process goes smoothly, but the machines ensure votes are separated from their envelopes, “maintaining your constitutional right to a secret ballot,” McKenzie said. 
Ballots are then put through a scanner to capture an image and count the votes on each one. After ballots are scanned, their data is stored on machines, and whenever the data is transferred to the clerk’s election management software, it’s through a special encrypted device.
Ballots are scanned and sorted at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)
“These pieces of equipment really have multiple levels of encryption,” McKenzie said. “So you can’t just get a jump drive from Walmart, say, and plug it in here. … It has to be vendor specific. It has to be equipment specific. So that machine’s memory stick, I can’t take from there and plug it into this one. It won’t communicate.”
McKenzie said when it comes to data transfer, “nothing is wireless, nothing is web based. It’s all a physical manual process to transfer that data from one place to another.” 
“A lot of people ask, ‘How could our election results be manipulated or changed?’ You have to have physical access,” he said. “So nothing remote can connect into our facility here on any of our tabulation equipment.”
The only time that data is shared with a web accessible computer is when it’s shared with the state, he said. 
How to make sure your vote counts: By-mail ballots now have tighter deadlines

“Yes, we do transmit reports to the state, and sometimes people will say, ‘Well, that could be interrupted,’” McKenzie said. “In theory, yes, it could, but the official results will always be maintained here at the county. And so, if somebody was ever curious and (they) say, ‘Well, how do we know?’ Well, quite easy. You can look at the results that we’ve posted on our Davis County website and compare it to the results that are available on the state’s website.”
One of the best ways Utah voters can keep track of whether their ballot has made it safely back to the clerk’s office and been counted is by signing up for Track My Ballot notifications through the state’s website. If election workers run into a problem, they’ll automatically send a notification to voters urging them to contact the clerk’s office to resolve the issue. 
Clerks encourage voters not to wait until too close to the election to mail their ballots back, especially if they’re sending it through the mail. Under a new Utah law, ballots must be in clerks’ possession no later than 8 p.m. on election night, regardless of their postmark. 
Voters can also drop their ballots off at secure drop boxes (they can find locations on the state’s website) up until voting closes on election night. But for those sending them back through the mail, McKenzie recommended signing up for the Postal Service’s Informed Delivery notifications, a free service to track mail. 
“That empowers our citizens to be aware, to be to make sure that the process is transparent,” he said. “and that they can take responsibility on tracking and making sure that their ballots are being handled correctly.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: How Homeland Security infiltrated anti-ICE organizations during Operation Metro Surge
description: The Signal username “peanutbutterjelly” blended in among the silly monikers used by fellow members of Minneapolis chats dedicated to protesting immigration agents during the government’s aggressive winter deportation campaign. She attended an “upstander” training and anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement planning meetings and regularly messaged with other[...]
text:
(Photos and illustration by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The Signal username “peanutbutterjelly” blended in among the silly monikers used by fellow members of Minneapolis chats dedicated to protesting immigration agents during the government’s aggressive winter deportation campaign. She attended an “upstander” training and anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement planning meetings and regularly messaged with others doing the same. 
“…v interested in the financial organizing piece (I like numbers and data) & marrying that together with propaganda so would love to work on both sides of these groups!!” she messaged a group of activists in a chat called “art/money/comms club.”
But peanutbutterjelly wasn’t interested in advancing the group’s aims. She was actually undercover agent 9843, a Department of Homeland Security officer ingratiating herself into the world of anti-ICE activists, looking for evidence of crimes. 
Agent 9843 was just one arm of the broad surveillance campaign launched by the federal government during Operation Metro Surge, focused on “identifying and disrupting sophisticated, organized campaigns supporting and engaging in” violence, destruction of property, intimidation of federal officers and employees, and attempts to impede federal operations, according to a synopsis of the case in internal Department of Homeland Security documents, which are now part of court records in the case of 15 Minnesotans charged with conspiracy to harm or impede federal agents. 
The documents highlight the vast surveillance dragnet the federal government created alongside the immigration crackdown. Which means even as immigrants were being rounded up and deported and people of color routinely racially profiled, the thousands of Minnesotans who sought to help them face consequences of their own — they’ve been swept into a burgeoning surveillance state.
Whether any of the surveillance was illegal could determine the outcomes for dozens of Minnesotans facing criminal charges for their anti-ICE protests — the Minnesota 15 and the Cities Church protesters, all of whom have pleaded not guilty. 
“ICE is committed to protecting the public’s constitutional rights, including the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly, while carrying out its law enforcement mission,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in response to emailed questions from the Reformer. 
Federal agents on patrol in Minneapolis, Minnesota in January. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Undercover agents’ attendance at publicly-advertised meetings, or in large group chats, is legal — people in those settings have no expectation of privacy, said Jessica West, director of the First Amendment Activism clinic at the Mitchell Hamline School of Law. Private companies, including telecommunications firms and financial institutions, generally share users’ information with the government upon request, given that most terms and conditions agreements allow for such sharing, West said.
But, if agents were to search protesters’ phones without a warrant, using some of the spyware tools immigration agents have access to — that would be illegal, and the evidence not admissible in court. No evidence has emerged in court to suggest that agents used such tools to spy on defendants. They did use technology to record messages in Signal chats that agents joined on their undercover phones, according to court documents.
It’s lawful under certain circumstances for the police to make arrests, to use crowd control weapons, to charge people with crimes, to seek information, to go to people’s houses and knock on their doors and ask questions, said Kevin Riach, an attorney for one of the 15 Minnesotans charged with conspiracy to harm or impede federal agents. 
“But if the purpose is to chill someone’s First Amendment speech, to prevent them from exercising their First Amendment rights — then it becomes illegal,” Riach said. 
West, the First Amendment lawyer, said the extent of federal surveillance during Operation Metro Surge is indicative of the failure of privacy laws to keep up with new technologies.
“It just hasn’t developed in a way that reflects and is responsive to true needs for protection around surveillance,” West said. 
ICE used customs law to request personal data
Federal law grants ICE the power to issue summonses for the purposes of “ascertaining the correctness of any entry” and determining what customs fees, taxes or fines may be due upon entry to the country — for example, the summons can be used to investigate whether an importer paid the appropriate fees on their merchandise.
During Operation Metro Surge, however, Homeland Security used this customs law to gather vast amounts of information on unions, left-wing organizations and journalists. 
ICE agents used the customs law to send summonses to FedWire, a money transfer service run by the Federal Reserve, for financial records of Service Employees International Union, Communication Workers of America, Sunrise Movement, the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers. 
They sent similar summonses to PayPal and Venmo to get the addresses, phone numbers and transactions for the people associated with Voices for Racial Justice, whose website — as described in agents’ reports — “boasts several articles on ‘ICE OUT’ and or ‘Truth, Freedom and ICE out of MN.’”
In the case of the 39 people charged with disrupting a January service at Cities Church, where a senior ICE official serves as a pastor, Homeland Security issued 92 such summonses. Three journalists were among the people charged. 
The government sought and received call and text records for defendants, including independent journalist Georgia Fort. They sent summonses for flight and rental car records and information associated with social media accounts, according to court documents. 
Journalist Georgia Fort leaves the federal courthouse in downtown St. Paul on Feb. 17, 2026 after pleading not guilty to felony charges stemming from her coverage of a protest at a church. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)
And, on March 5, agents sent a customs summons to REI, the outdoor brand, seeking transaction information for everyone who purchased a particular beanie in the Twin Cities area since January 2024, according to a motion filed by defense attorneys in the Cities Church case, which in its title calls the use of the customs summons “outrageous.”
Attorneys in both the Minnesota 15 and Cities Church cases are arguing that the federal law does not grant the feds the power to use its summonses to investigate crimes unrelated to customs enforcement.
The government argued in court filings that there is “nothing unusual about the summonses.”

“It is a tool in the (Homelands Security Investigations) investigatory toolbox that is regularly used to obtain third-party information in which defendants do not have a Fourth Amendment privacy interest,” prosecutors wrote in a filing in the Cities Church case.
The validity of such summons to investigate crimes unrelated to customs duties has come under question before. 
In 2017, during the first Trump administration, U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a summons to Twitter for the personal information of the user behind @ALT_USCIS, an anonymous account criticizing the president’s immigration policy. Twitter refused to provide the information and sued the federal government, but before the case could be decided by a judge, CBP rescinded its request and Twitter dropped the lawsuit. 
An internal Homeland Security watchdog investigated the incident and found that the agency improperly used the summons and repeatedly violated department policy. Homeland Security leadership agreed with the findings, and promised to take corrective action. 
But a 2023 Wired investigation found that the Department of Homeland Security issued more than 170,000 summonses from 2016 through mid-August 2022 — including to an abortion provider, an elementary school and journalists. 
Three cars filled with federal agents stop in front of Elle Neubauer and another observer, surrounding the car and threatening arrest during an early morning watch observing ICE in South Minneapolis Monday, Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Tracking cars
During Operation Metro Surge, neighbors coordinated with one another to track ICE activity in their neighborhoods. Some patrolled in cars, following suspected ICE vehicles through cities and suburbs, reporting their locations and distracting the agents from their mission. 
Patrollers noted that the federal agents seemed to be photographing their license plates, and in some cases, their faces. In January, one patroller told the Reformer, “if my plate wasn’t in their database, it is now,” after agents boxed in her car and warned her to stop following them. 
Court documents provide some clues as to how that information may have been used. 
Agent 9843 — peanutbutterjelly — participated in a February meeting of anti-ICE activists at Prince of Peace Lutheran Church in Roseville, while other agents scanned the license plates in the parking lot outside to add to their database. 
Agents then used the license plate photos to obtain the names of the attendees, search social media for pictures, and compile an “intel workup” that included addresses, family and employment information and vehicle registration information, according to a filing by Riach in the Minnesota 15 case. 
Agents also ran photographs of protesters through Clearview AI — a facial recognition software — to compile photo dossiers of activists and protesters, including many who were not charged. In at least one case, the software misidentified the person in the photograph, linking him to an unrelated person. 
“Our use of Clearview AI and other facial recognition technology is governed by applicable DHS and ICE policy, privacy compliance documentation, rules of behavior, and required training,” the Department of Homeland Security said in its emailed statement.
The Star Tribune reported in July that around 30 state, county and federal agencies across the country searched Flock camera data in at least eight Twin Cities suburbs for immigration enforcement between November and March, including the Mille Lacs County Sheriff’s Office, which collaborates with ICE. 
The Department of Homeland Security told the Star Tribune that it doesn’t have a contract with Flock, and did not answer a follow-up question about whether it relied on local law enforcement agencies to access the data on their behalf. 
Tens of thousands of Minnesotans gathered at the State Capitol for No Kings, a protest against the Trump administration. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
The surveilled
On Feb. 2, Drew Harmon arrived at the Augsburg Park Library in Richfield to lead the monthly gathering of members of Minnesota 50501, the state chapter of the anti-Trump group that organized the massive “Hands Off” and “No Kings” protests nationwide. 
The meeting and those like it, Harmon told the Reformer in a recent interview, are “for anyone in the public who’s interested in what we’re doing and who wants to get involved, or for anyone who’s already involved who has questions for the leadership of the organization.” 
During the February meeting, he gave an overview of 50501 and the Minnesota chapter, which in those days was focused on getting ICE out of Minnesota. Then, Nick Benson, who tracks deportation flights out of the Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport, provided an update on his work and urged attendees to pressure Delta for more information on its facilitation of deportations. 
Later in the meeting, participants discussed the possibility of ICE agents infiltrating their organization. 
An attorney warned attendees not to put anything in writing that they wouldn’t want to be seen in court. 
“We may be thinking we want all ICE agents to die, but don’t put those statements in writing,” the attorney said, according to notes from an undercover agent who was sitting in the audience. 
“People would say stuff like that, and I’d roll my eyes and be like, you know, they’re listening to everything we do,” Harmon said. “There was already some evidence at this point that we were being infiltrated, because we saw their cars everywhere.”
And, on Jan. 17, the day right-wing provocateur Jake Lang held a sparsely-attended anti-Islam rally in downtown Minneapolis, video emerged that appeared to show federal agents picking up a man off the street, who many viewers assumed was an undercover agent. (The Reformer has been unable to verify who the man was and whether he was a government agent.)
The assumption that undercover agents were in meetings and group chats was ubiquitous among participants, leading to extensive debate over the “operational security” or “op-sec” measures necessary to protect the groups’ activities. One measure that most agreed on was using nicknames in Signal chats.
Harmon, like many members of the Minnesota 15, pointed out that the use of government resources to surveil left-wing groups coincided with the Department of Justice’s refusal to investigate the killings of two Americans and other abuses by federal agents. 
Gabriel Van De Water, an artist and community organizer who is among the Minnesota 15, said at an August press conference that the killers of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, “have been hidden away and protected, while DHS turns its attention towards spying on union members, civil rights organizations, churches and individuals who stood up for their community in whatever ways they were able.” 
Riach, the defense attorney, is trying to force the government to turn over more records related to spying — even on organizations and individuals who are not implicated in the case. 
If he’s successful in convincing the judge that those records are relevant to the defense of his client, the public may soon learn more about the surveillance campaign.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘Quiet loud nature’: New Mexico opponents of Roadless Rule repeal describe fear of lost solitude
description: All but five of 594 comments from New Mexico residents oppose the repeal of the Roadless Rule, which protects 1.6 million acres of New Mexico national forests from road construction and logging.
text:
More than 99% of New Mexico residents who submitted comments to the United States Forest Service oppose repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule. Dozens of them used the federal government’s comment portal to reflect on solitude in nature. (Photo of Gila National Forest courtesy USDA) Most of the roughly 600 New Mexico residents who weighed in on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s proposal to end the 2001 Roadless Rule said it should remain in place to protect watersheds and wildlife, as well as spare roughly 1.6 million acres of the state’s forestland from extractive industries. 
But beyond the policy itself, dozens of them, via a public comment portal on Regulations.gov, offered personal reflections about profound experiences in untamed nature, which they see as at risk if the USDA moves forward with the rule’s repeal.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We never saw nor heard another person, vehicle or anything else manmade,” one person wrote about a backpacking trip in the Gila National Forest, of which roughly one quarter is protected under the Roadless Rule. “Instead we saw skies so lit up with stars we almost didn’t need headlamps to cook. We were woken up at night by a large herd of elk thundering past.”
“Nature is actually quite loud when it’s not drowned out by humans and our trucks, cars, heavy machinery, utility infrastructure constantly buzzing,” the commenter continued. “I dream of the Gila and hope I have the privilege to trek through its quiet loud nature again.”
Another commenter, who described himself as elderly man, said his New Mexico wilderness experiences were the most meaningful of his life. He wrote that he hopes his sons have the same chances to “explore, love, and be restored by these wild places in the same way I have been.”
“Opportunities for solitude are a rare commodity in the modern world,” he said. “We must protect them like the precious treasures that they are.”
The department last week closed its public comment period soliciting feedback for its proposal to repeal the rule, which protects roughly 58 million acres of national forests nationwide from logging, road construction or other development. 
The department received more than 370,000 comments from members of the public between Aug. 18 and Oct. 6 on its proposed repeal of the rule. A recent analysis from the Center for Western Priorities, an environmental advocacy group, used an AI large language model to analyze the comments and concluded that more than 99% of them urged the department to keep the rule in place.
USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins first announced her intention to repeal the rule while in Santa Fe in June 2025. The administration has justified repealing the rule as a way to return control to local administrators, reduce wildfires and support the logging industry. 
Source NM reviewed comments submitted to Regulations.gov from those who say they’re New Mexico residents or who mention one of five national forests in the state. All but five of the 594 comments from New Mexico residents oppose the repeal. All 120 comments from those who mention the state’s national forests hope the rule stays in place. 
Among those in opposition to the repeal were those who identified themselves as ranchers, hikers, hunters, fishermen, and business owners in communities surrounding the Gila National Forest. 
USDA says repealing ‘roadless’ protections will prevent wildfires. A new study disagrees

Twenty-four comments mention “solitude”; 20 describe the protected areas as “sacred.” One comment came from a 6-year-old child who described enjoying climbing trees and rocks, as well as skiing in the Cibola National Forest. 
“I think you should keep the Roadless Rule,” the child wrote. 
In addition to those from individuals, several of the comments submitted by New Mexico environmental groups were on behalf of thousands of state residents. 
New Mexico Wild, for example, submitted letters opposing the repeal signed by approximately 3,300 state residents. The organization held a series of “people’s public hearings” mobilizing opposition to the repeal after the USDA refused to hold its own public hearings on the matter. 
Of the five people who supported repealing the rule, all but one did not provide their names, which was voluntary. Those commenters mentioned concern about wildfires and said the rule gets in the way of commonsense forest management in New Mexico. 
Studies have shown that wildfires are less common in areas the Roadless Rule protects. Introducing roads to protected areas increases the risk of human-caused wildfires, advocacy groups contend. 
The one signed letter from a Roadless Rule opponent came from John Paul Bradley, the general manager of the Sipapu Ski Resort in the Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. He said that a roadless area sits adjacent to the ski resort, and he’s concerned the rule means the area  “cannot be managed to improve forest health.”
“We believe in returning decisions to the local level and giving the Forest Service all the tools and support they need to actively manage these beautiful national forests across the West,” he wrote.
Bradley did not respond to Source NM’s requests for further comment last week.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington among 4 states with highest rate of whale entanglements, report shows
description: Across the Pacific coast, reports of large whales tangled in buoys, gillnets and other fishing equipment are increasing.  In 2025, Washington was among four states where nearly 80% of reported whale entanglements occurred, according to a recent report by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.  Of the Pacific coastal states with the most reports[...]
text:
Washington state is home to the only team federally authorized to lead a full response to whale entanglement in the Pacific Northwest. (Photo courtesy of NOAA Fisheries/Marine Mammal Health and Stranding Response Program) Across the Pacific coast, reports of large whales tangled in buoys, gillnets and other fishing equipment are increasing. 
In 2025, Washington was among four states where nearly 80% of reported whale entanglements occurred, according to a recent report by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 
Of the Pacific coastal states with the most reports, California had the highest at 27.6%; Alaska had 23.7%; Hawaii, 15.8%; and Washington, 11.8%. 
Disentanglement is a dangerous and highly skilled job. There are very few responders federally authorized to lead an entanglement response. Jenn Tackaberry is one of them. 
“The whales never know that we’re helping,” said Tackaberry, co-director of the entanglement response team at the small nonprofit Cascadia Research Collective. “If you think about it, the whales are having one of the worst days of their life.”
The organization, based out of Olympia, is home to the only team in the Pacific Northwest federally authorized to lead a full response. 
Sometimes, it’s too dangerous for the team to respond, Tackaberry said. Whales can become aggravated and slap the surface of the water, make rumbling noises and thrash. When whale behavior is deemed unsafe, the team will leave and try again another day.
During an entanglement response, whales can become aggravated and thrash or make loud rumbling noises. When it becomes too dangerous, responders leave the whale with a plan to return. (Photo courtesy of NOAA Fisheries/Marine Mammal Health and Stranding Response Program)
Washington had nine of the 76 confirmed reports. Responders fully freed two whales and partially disentangled one. Four whales, including a killer whale, broke free on their own. One gray whale died, and responders could not reach another whale that was last reported still entangled. 
Reports in 2025 were up over 50% from 2024. Officials point to warming oceans as one reason for the increase.
Most fishing occurs in coastal ecosystems where biodiversity is abundant. When marine heat waves push colder water against the coast, it leads anchovies, and as a result whales, into fishing territory, said Michael Milstein, NOAA spokesperson. 
The crew at the Cascadia Research Collective has five highly trained responders, including Doug Sandilands and John Calambokidis, who are also trained to lead a whale disentanglement.  The nonprofit collaborates with other lower-level responders across the region and is a leader in whale necropsy expertise.
During a response, staff members do not get in the water but work from small research boats using poles with hook knives and other gear to cut the lines. 
Many entanglement responders are seeing more reports than usual this year, which historically occur during El Niño conditions, Tackaberry said. The higher number of 2026 responses has already taken up their budget, she added. 
On top of that, the nonprofit will face a gap in federal funding beginning in January due to the cancellation of a federal grant in 2025, Tackaberry said. 
“2027 is shaping up to be a tough year,” she said. Funding is needed to “respond to animals in need, and ensure proper data is collected to prevent future human-caused injury and mortality in the future.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri auditor candidates split over how office should confront state budget problems
description: Missouri is headed toward a potentially painful budget reckoning as state spending continues to outpace revenue growth. The two candidates for state auditor agree that should be a major concern for the office. They disagree over what the auditor can — and should — do about it. Republican incumbent Scott Fitzpatrick argues the auditor’s responsibility […]
text:
Republican State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, left, and Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson (photos submitted).Missouri is headed toward a potentially painful budget reckoning as state spending continues to outpace revenue growth.
The two candidates for state auditor agree that should be a major concern for the office. They disagree over what the auditor can — and should — do about it.
Republican incumbent Scott Fitzpatrick argues the auditor’s responsibility is to independently assess the state’s finances, warn policymakers about looming problems and root out waste, fraud and abuse.
Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson, who has held leadership positions in several state agencies over two decades, wants the office to take a more active role in finding ways for state government to save money and improve its performance.
The divide has become a central issue in their race for an office that has no power to write the state budget but broad authority to examine how taxpayer money is spent.
Fitzpatrick issued a report in January warning legislators about the difficult budget decisions ahead. Before becoming state treasurer in 2019, Fitzpatrick served two years as chairman of the Missouri House Budget Committee.
“I do not see any prospects of a federal bailout coming to soften the blow of what’s about to happen this time,” he told The Independent. “I think what we’re getting ready to encounter is unprecedented. It’s certainly going to be much worse than anything I dealt with when I was the House budget chairman.”
Fitzpatrick said his job is to start the conversation and “bring a level of seriousness to this to the issue that I think has not existed.”
Wilson believes the auditor’s job should go beyond that.
“You may have heard the current auditor say that his job is basically to tell people when they’re going to run out of money, so they can start planning,” Wilson said. “That’s not an auditor. That’s a doomsday clock.” 
Wilson said his experience leading state agencies convinced him the auditor should take a more proactive approach, evaluating not only whether public money was properly spent but whether government programs are working as efficiently as possible.
Fitzpatrick notes that the auditor cannot appropriate money, veto spending or force agencies to adopt its recommendations.
“That’s between the legislature and the governor,” he said, “and I’m neither one of those.”
 Expanding the watchdog role

Fitzpatrick points to his office’s investigations of waste, fraud and abuse, particularly in local governments, as evidence that he has strengthened the auditor’s traditional watchdog role.
In 2024, Fitzpatrick pushed for legislation to give his office greater discretion to audit municipalities when wrongdoing is uncovered through a whistleblower complaint.
Previously under state law, the auditor’s office had the ability to investigate whistleblower complaints. Previously, the auditor generally needed a petition from residents or an invitation from a local governing body before launching an audit. The new law allows the office under certain circumstances to move directly from an investigation to an audit and use subpoena power during the investigative stage. It passed unanimously in both chambers.
“Our first audit that we conducted under that expanded authority was the city of Arnold,” Fitzpatrick said, “which was kind of a banger of an audit in my view.”
It exposed, he said, the city’s practice of creating transportation development districts as a way “to basically tax the citizens of the city without a vote of the people.” 
“The city of Arnold had basically turned this into like a forever tax or a forever district,” he said, “where they just kind of wanted to have an open-ended list of projects that they could use this money on.”
That was the first time the office used its subpoena power, he said, “and I think that was a good use of that authority.”
Fitzpatrick also points to his office’s work on Jackson County’s 2023 property assessments. The auditor found problems with the county’s assessment and appeals process, and separate litigation brought by the state ultimately resulted in a settlement worth up to $250 million for affected property owners. 
When he first became auditor, he thought most of his time would be spent on auditing state agencies. However, because Missouri has the second largest number of political subdivisions of any state in the country, with over 4,000 of them, his office has spent much of its time investigating local governments. That’s where they’ve found most of the fraud cases. 
“There’s always going to be more things that need our attention than we have capacity to manage at any given time,” he said, “and so you really are in a situation where you have to kind of figure out what’s the most pressing thing and what’s the thing that could be most impactful for for the taxpayers.”
 A broader role for the auditor

The fact that Missouri has so many political subdivisions is why Wilson believes prevention should be the office’s central focus.
“Traditional audits look backward at whether the books balance,” he said. “That’s important, but it’s not enough.”
He wants to restructure the state auditor’s office more like the federal Government Accountability Office, to look ahead at ways to save money and improve outcomes, as well as offer more training for local officials. By doing this, he believes he can save up to $1 billion a year “while actually improving outcomes.”
“Training and developing your human resources is going to accomplish as much as any of our audits,” Wilson said. “When I’m the auditor, it’s going to be a real bang for the buck and satisfaction for people.”
Wilson said the approach reflects practices he used during two decades in state government.
When Wilson first became the director of revenue in 1998, the first thing he did was walk through every step a tax return went through before it got back to the taxpayer. He realized the reason it was taking about 37 days for residents to see their returns was because there were too many unnecessary steps. 
“It isn’t rocket science,” he said. “We reengineered it and went from 37 days to four days to get a refund.”
An unexpected cost savings came when the call centers’ workload decreased because people were calling less to check on a refund status. 
After his time as revenue director, he went on to become cabinet director under Gov. Bob Holden in 2001. He was tasked with using that streamlining model on various projects, including transportation and worker safety, environmental permitting, correctional reform and mental health. 
He touts leading a team of four people to generate about millions in state cost savings. Among them was a $6 million savings of simply changing the motor vehicle registration requirements from every year to every two years.  
Streamlining the process of compliance alone can save the state a lot of money, he said.
As the revenue director, his team made the instructions on complying with tax laws easier to understand and less open to interpretation.
“We had much lower volume of appeals,” he said, “so it was voluntary compliance and I think the same thing applies to auditing.”
Wilson has criticized some of Fitzpatrick’s audits for taking too long, arguing that reports can arrive after the underlying problems have changed or the officials responsible have left office.
Wilson has also questioned Fitzpatrick’s independence from fellow Republicans, pointing to allegations in a wrongful termination lawsuit filed by a former employee of the Secretary of State’s Office. The lawsuit alleges Fitzpatrick’s chief of staff participated in a conversation about how concerns over voter registration data could be submitted through the auditor’s whistleblower process.
“With one party controlling state government, Missouri needs an auditor with the independence and management experience to ask tough questions, follow the money and demand results,” Quentin said in a statement.
Fitzpatrick disputed the lawsuit’s characterization, saying his chief of staff only explained the office’s normal procedures for submitting a whistleblower complaint and protecting anonymous complainants. No complaint was ultimately submitted, he said. Fitzpatrick said his audits of other statewide officials demonstrate that he holds officeholders accountable regardless of party.
Wilson argues Missouri’s fiscal outlook makes a more proactive approach increasingly important.
“It is the auditor’s job to help people streamline and improve,” he said. “That’s what GAO does. That’s not what many state auditors do, but I’m going to, and I think it has to be done.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Andrew Bailey is back in Missouri and talking like a candidate
description: Andrew Bailey has been back in Missouri for about two weeks, and he already has a message. Speaking to a recent gathering of Boone County Republicans, the former attorney general said there’s “a real disconnect right now between where the people are and where some of our leadership is.” He said lobbyists and political consultants […]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey answers questions from reporters about Gov. Mike Kehoe's executive orders in January 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Andrew Bailey has been back in Missouri for about two weeks, and he already has a message.
Speaking to a recent gathering of Boone County Republicans, the former attorney general said there’s “a real disconnect right now between where the people are and where some of our leadership is.” He said lobbyists and political consultants are interfering at the Capitol. He said it’s time to take power from “the moneyed interests” and return it to voters.
It’s the easiest pitch in modern politics. The people in charge are the problem, and I’m not one of them.
But it’s a strange pitch coming from Bailey.
He didn’t reach statewide office by beating Jefferson City. He was appointed by it.
Former Gov. Mike Parson, a man who spent decades in elected office and whose comfort in the Capitol’s culture became a common knock against him, picked Bailey for attorney general in 2023.
His 2024 political operation was built with substantial help from Steve Tilley, the former House speaker turned lobbyist and consultant who helped Bailey raise money and whose network of PACs poured cash into his campaign and allied committee. And as attorney general, that money caused Bailey headaches and inspired accusations about whether it shaped his office’s actions.
Judge orders Missouri AG Andrew Bailey to sit for deposition over possible ethics breach

None of this is a new observation. It was the entire case against him in the 2024 Republican primary. Will Scharf spent the campaign arguing Bailey was a creature of Jefferson City. Voters disagreed. But the man who ran as the establishment’s choice two years ago is now running against it.
Or not running. Bailey keeps saying he isn’t running for anything.
The speech in Columbia sounded otherwise. He talked about gas prices, data centers, transmission lines and the county jail. He said he was “energized” and planned to travel the state. Several people in the room left convinced he is eyeing a comeback. His allied PAC still has more than half a million dollars in the bank.
Then there is the question of why he came back.
Bailey told the crowd he “stepped down on my own” from the FBI, that his wife told him to come home and that it was good to be back. Everyone close to Bailey will tell you how big a part of his life his family is. There’s no reason to doubt it played a role.
But it was not a triumphant year in D.C.
National outlets reported tension with FBI Director Kash Patel. People close to Bailey describe him to me as miserable in the job, iced out and unable to get much done. His one high-profile moment came in Fulton County, Georgia, where he was on hand as agents seized 2020 election records.
That fits. In Columbia, Bailey was still warning that blue states are “lying, cheating and stealing elections.” He offered no evidence. There isn’t any. Georgia’s 2020 presidential ballots were counted three times, including once by hand, with each count confirming the result. Courts likewise rejected efforts to overturn the outcome.
Which leaves the bigger question.
In November 2024, voters gave Bailey a four-year term as attorney general. He left after eight months. He lasted about a year at the FBI. If at some point he asks for four more years, somebody should ask him what the over-under is.
Friendly voices in Jefferson City political circles have been floating him as a future statewide candidate for months. The Missouri Times, a website owned by longtime Bailey booster Scott Faughn, covered his return like a homecoming. Its editor, posting from the Columbia event, referred to Bailey as “the war hero from Hermann.”
The Jefferson City insiders who helped build Bailey’s political career are clearly glad to have him back. Bailey would probably prefer you didn’t notice.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: George Ayoub: Letting them read ‘The Vanities of October’
description: Lost in the din of a presidential visit to Nebraska, the ongoing glut of political campaign ads, a slew of prediction market come-ons and the sports world’s busiest month was Banned Books Week, which readers from bibliophiles to the casual celebrate annually. While I do not play the prediction markets but am an avid sports […]
text:
George Orwell's novel "1984" is displayed at The Last Bookstore on Jan. 25, 2017, in Los Angeles. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Lost in the din of a presidential visit to Nebraska, the ongoing glut of political campaign ads, a slew of prediction market come-ons and the sports world’s busiest month was Banned Books Week, which readers from bibliophiles to the casual celebrate annually.
While I do not play the prediction markets but am an avid sports fan and a voter, it was the president’s stopover that caught my attention. For the wrong reason. That’s because he suggested — to cheers — that the price to pay for our current war was letting Iran “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. Aides and apologists later argued that the broadside was misinterpreted. 
Like millions of others, I’m a hard pass of such backwalking because for some of us, the insult was not only disgusting, it was personal. He said it in my hometown, Grand Island. I lived in Los Angeles for 10 years and still have scores of friends there. San Diego is home to members of my extended family, some of whom served our country in the military. 
Let’s move on to another effluvium: book banning, which remains a thing … and getting worse. According to literacy advocate, PEN America, nearly 12,000 books were banned in American schools during the last school year. Over 7,000 of those were unique titles. That’s nearly twice the number of bans from the previous school year.
We’re doing quite well in Nebraska. PEN lists Nebraska as one of 28 states with no book bans last school year. A new law, LB 390, which we discussed in the space last spring, should further keep the banners at bay, heading off all but the most overt attempts to limit titles for students. It requires schools to have a catalog of books that is easily accessible for parents (which school libraries already had) and a system for parents to be notified when their child checks out a book.
One improvement to LB 390 would have required those requesting a book be banned from a school library or a classroom to prove they have read the book and understand it. Perhaps we could also add the same codicil for anyone who has gone as far as attempting to remove titles from public libraries. 
Meanwhile, events took place in Nebraska bookstores and libraries and on college campuses to celebrate Banned Books Week, a time when we champion the freedom to read what you want. Some of the festivities included public readings of notably banned books, which could have included Toni Morrison’s “Beloved,” Roald Dahl’s “Matilda” and any of J.K. Rowling’s Harry Potter books, what with the witchcraft, the Ministry of Magic and that whole Horcrux thing.  
Some banning comes from deep left field. Consider those who want to put the kibosh on “The Wonderful World of Oz” (gender roles and “godless” values), “Charlotte’s Web” (talking critters apparently a no-no) and “Hansel and Gretel” (more witchcraft). Even Dr. Seuss’ “The Lorax” was pulled in a California town because some there believe the story to be anti-logging.
Throw in the significant jump in challenges across the country and celebrating Banned Books Week carried even more weight this year. Plus, while book banning remains a scourge in a society that once valued enlightenment, scholarship and plain old smarts — even the kind you get from books — the practice is part of an inexplicable but growing disdain for education. 
When that happens, we pull books from school classrooms, thereby stifling curiosity. We mitigate the horrors of slavery by conditioning schools’ curricula in what can only be called a rewriting of history. We question science and the scientific methods leading to dangerous policies and deregulation concerning vaccinations, product efficacy and food safety. The consequences? Measles has returned to the public square and the worst cyclospora food poisoning event in history occurred. Nearly 13,000 people in 21 states were affected including 570 hospitalizations, and 2 deaths.
Perhaps some day a history book will be published about this time (working title “The Vanities of October”), detailing a nasty, expensive election season filled with lies, innuendoes and threats to two great American cities; how Americans bet on everything down to which color of Gatorade bath would be poured on the winning Super Bowl coach; or the lengths consumers went to make ends meet during what was the period’s “Affordability Crisis.” 
Such a volume would be critical reading for students to learn how, at a certain point in our history, we chose our leaders, talked about and treated our neighbors with whom we disagreed, entertained ourselves and with what regard we held education. 
Of course, we’d have to let them read it first.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Ballot proposal would impact Oklahoma judicial selection panel
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Voters on Nov. 3 will be asked to make changes to a panel that vets judicial candidates and sends their top picks to the governor for possible appointment. Critics say the proposed changes in State Question 845 could result in one political party having too much influence.  Supporters say reforming the Judicial […]
text:
The Oklahoma Judicial Center is the headquarters of the Oklahoma Supreme Court and Court of Criminal Appeals. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Voters on Nov. 3 will be asked to make changes to a panel that vets judicial candidates and sends their top picks to the governor for possible appointment.
Critics say the proposed changes in State Question 845 could result in one political party having too much influence. 
Supporters say reforming the Judicial Nominating Commission is needed to better reflect the Republican super majority in the Legislature and GOP control of all statewide elective offices.
The state question seeks to reshape a constitutional provision that defines who can serve on the 15-member Judicial Nominating Commission that plays an influential role in selecting the state’s judges. 
The state question seeks to remove party affiliation restrictions and the prohibition that certain members not be attorneys or have family members who practice law, the length of time commissioners can serve and realign the district boundaries where they can reside.
The current construction of the Judicial Nominating Commission favors Democrats, said Sen. Todd Gollihare, R-Sapulpa, during debate earlier this year. 
He is the Senate author of the state question, which lawmakers voted to put on the November ballot. Gollihare did not return messages seeking comment.
“The majority party is running behind the minority party because of the structure of the Judicial Nominating Commission,” he said.
He said it was not equitable for the majority party to have five members when the minority party has 10.
The 15-member Judicial Nominating Commission was approved by voters in 1967 by a constitutional amendment following a judicial scandal in which Supreme Court justices took bribes. The Commission was created when Democrats controlled the Legislature.
Prior to the creation of the body, appellate court judges ran as politicians and accepted campaign donations.
Under the existing structure, the Commission selects three nominees to fill judicial vacancies that the governor then chooses from.  
The Oklahoma Bar Association picks six members who serve staggered six-year terms.
The governor chooses six to serve staggered six-year terms.
No more than three of the governor’s six appointees can come from one political party. The Senate Pro Tem and House Speaker each have an appointee. The 14 members of the Nominating Commission then elect the final member. 
Of the latter three, no more than two can be from the same political party. They serve 2-year terms.
If approved by voters, the measure would limit members to serve 12 years in total, removing language that prohibited members from back-to-back terms.
“Because we do believe that institutional knowledge is important, especially with a function as critical as providing names to a governor from which he or she must choose a justice, that we should allow the member of the commission to serve a second term,” said Senate Majority Floor Leader Julie Daniels, R-Bartlesville.
But Andy Fugate, D-Del City, said the existing structure is designed to ensure the Commission is not overly partisan.
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Oklahoma City, speaks during a special legislative session on Jan. 31, 2024, in the House chamber of the Oklahoma State Capitol. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)
“The process is intended to bring multiple parties to the table, not focus on a single party,” he said. Fugate voted for the measure, but said he only supported it at the time in exchange for action on another bill. 
Fugate said he opposes the changes.
“The party in power wants a judiciary that will play ball and what the people of Oklahoma deserve is a judiciary that will follow the law and the Constitution,” Fugate said.
Rep. Anthony Moore, R-Clinton, the House author, did not return phone calls seeking comment.
The Judicial Nominating Commission and the Oklahoma Supreme Court have been targets of the Republican-controlled Legislature after numerous GOP-backed bills were deemed unconstitutional.
In 2010, voters approved State Question 752 that added two members to the panel to be appointed by the Senate Pro Tem and House Speaker. That constitutional amendment was put on the ballot by lawmakers. The measure passed by nearly 63%, according to the Oklahoma State Election Board.
Last year, a bill that proposed asking voters to abolish the Judicial Nominating Commission failed to secure the support needed to advance out of the Legislature.
In 2024, a bill that would require appellate and district court judges to retire at 75 also failed to garner enough support. Daniels, the author, said the bill was needed because justices had invalidated Republican bills.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma judges are behaving badly with no real consequences. Why are they getting away with it?
description: Imagine being a defendant in a courtroom when suddenly the judge exits the bench, fists raised as if wanting to fight you. Or you have the misfortune to appear before that judge who also apparently ignores sentencing guidelines and has yelled at a public defender. Or you’re in a courtroom with a judge, who has […]
text:
From left, Oklahoma Supreme Court justices Noma Gurich, M. John Kane IV and Travis Jett stand for the governor's State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)Imagine being a defendant in a courtroom when suddenly the judge exits the bench, fists raised as if wanting to fight you.
Or you have the misfortune to appear before that judge who also apparently ignores sentencing guidelines and has yelled at a public defender.
Or you’re in a courtroom with a judge, who has demonstrated substantiated biases toward some attorneys and a “poor demeanor” toward lawyers and courthouse employees, yet justifies the bad behavior because they’re not a “morning person.”
Or you’re involved in a paternity case where the judge apparently used artificial intelligence to generate a court order that contained two made up court cases. And, that same judge has faced allegations of possibly eavesdropping on jury deliberations, according to The Oklahoman.
These have all rocked Oklahoma’s judiciary since 2025, yet the Oklahoma Supreme Court, which is one of the bodies tasked with policing judges, has allowed these officials to continue presiding.
In two of those cases, the Supreme Court chose to publicly reprimand the judges with the equivalent of a slap on the wrist. They don’t appear to have acted on the allegations facing the third judge yet.
As an outsider this judicial conduct is egregious, and allowing these folks to remain on the bench risks undermining Oklahomans’ faith in our entire judiciary system.
It also risks tarnishing the reputation of the many judges who are doing it right, following the laws that our Legislature has put into place, even if they don’t like them, and treating all people that appear before them with respect and dignity.
The lack of substantive action against these three judges also raises some very serious questions: 

What sort of conduct does it take for a judge to recommend removing another judge? 
Is our system that relies on judges to police each other working? 
And what sort of message does it send about how we want our courts to function if our top judges, who have initially been selected by our governors to serve on the Supreme Court, continue to excuse this type of behavior?

Something feels wrong with our discipline system, but I’m not quite sure why.
Oklahoma has a state agency tasked with investigating judicial complaints. The Council on Judicial Complaints is designed to function separately from the judicial branch, but when needed sends its findings to the Oklahoma Supreme Court’s chief justice. The Council can recommend action, but does not have the authority to enforce it.
In the case of Tulsa County Judge Sharon Holmes the Council recommended her removal after substantiating accusations that she had improper communications with jurors and a defendant, ignored sentencing guidelines, yelled at a public defender and even “left the bench and approached an agitated defendant with her fists raised as if she was going to fight him.”
The Oklahoma Supreme Court decided that Holmes should only receive a reprimand for conduct that they themselves called “indefensible.” They said it reflected a lack of judgment, but while serious, did not represent an excessive use of judicial authority.
The Oklahoma Supreme Court did acknowledge that some of Holmes’ conduct “created the appearance of impropriety, undermining the public’s confidence in the independence, integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.”
 You know what really “undermines the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary”? A high court that inexplicably refuses to follow the recommendations of an independent investigatory state agency to can a judge.
And because they didn’t, Holmes will serve another judicial term after she ran for reelection unopposed. The court didn’t issue its reprimand until September, after the primary election cycle was complete.
In August 2025, Special Judge Emily Mueller also received a reprimand by the Oklahoma Supreme Court after substantiated accusations of “poor demeanor toward certain attorneys and courthouse staff and bias against certain attorneys.” She was also accused of having discussed issues without another party’s attorney being present, which the high court found violates the Judicial Code of Conduct.
Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe wrote that Mueller, whose judicial district encompasses Pottawatomie and Lincoln counties, “admitted that her attitude has fallen short in interactions with attorneys and even her co-workers, but ultimately attributed her poor interactions to not being a ‘morning person.’”
Lots of us are not a “morning person,” but we drink our caffeinated beverages and push through. If we acted like that, we’d be fired.
Mueller’s conduct “reflects a serious departure from the standards required of a judicial officer and erodes the public’s confidence in the Judiciary,” Rowe wrote.
He hit the nail on the head, yet the court didn’t recommend her removal. 
And then there’s Stephens County Associate District Judge Lawrence Wheeler, who is accused of using AI to prepare a court order that cited two imaginary cases, and who also has faced accusations that he “eavesdropped on jury deliberations,” according to The Oklahoman.
The Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation was called in to investigate by the Oklahoma Council on Judicial Complaints.
The Attorney General’s Office declined to file criminal charges, but told The Oklahoman that the Oklahoma Supreme Court and the Court on the Judiciary hold ultimate power over Wheeler’s future on the bench.
That’s because we’ve empowered the Oklahoma Court on the Judiciary to remove judges from their positions. This body, whose current membership is not clearly listed anywhere I can easily find, is composed of 18 judges: nine that serve in an appellate role, and nine that oversee trials. Surprisingly, no citizens are permitted to serve on this policing body.
The Oklahoman reported the last time a judge has been removed by the body was 2020.
Removing judges should only be a last resort, but if we’ve got ones who are behaving badly on the bench, even if it’s not criminal, someone needs to be holding them accountable.
And if the Oklahoma Supreme Court isn’t willing to do that or refer cases to this Court on the Judiciary, are these justices willing to do one the hard parts of their job? And should we feel confident in retaining them when their retention is next on the ballot?
I don’t know. I do know that Oklahoma courtrooms are supposed to be dignified places where justice is blind and AI isn’t presiding. 
And if our judges can’t find the willpower to hold each other accountable, particularly when an independent board recommends removal, then maybe it’s time for Oklahoma lawmakers to take a closer look at creating a system that will.

title: Idaho state controller’s race: Former state evaluator challenges GOP incumbent in general election
description: A longtime state performance evaluator is running against Idaho’s longest currently serving statewide elected official in the 2026 general election for Idaho state controller. Democratic candidate Rakesh Mohan is challenging incumbent Republican State Controller Brandon Woolf, who has served as state controller since being appointed in 2012.  The state contr[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballot for the primary election on May 19, 2026, at Club Apple in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A longtime state performance evaluator is running against Idaho’s longest currently serving statewide elected official in the 2026 general election for Idaho state controller.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Democratic candidate Rakesh Mohan is challenging incumbent Republican State Controller Brandon Woolf, who has served as state controller since being appointed in 2012. 
The state controller is a constitutional officer that serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and serves on the Idaho State Board of Land Commissioners, which is commonly referred to as the Land Board. The position is for a four-year term and comes with an annual salary of $128,690.
 Meet Democratic challenger Rakesh Mohan 

Mohan worked as a government auditor and evaluator for 31 years, working for state legislatures in Idaho, Washington, Louisiana and Kansas. He spent the last 21 years of his evaluation career as director of the nonpartisan Idaho Office of Performance Evaluations until he retired in June 2024. After that, Mohan served as a visiting professor at the School of Public Policy at Boise State University. 
Mohan is not an accountant or IT professional, but he said his 30-plus years of experience evaluating and auditing government policy and programs has prepared him to serve as controller. He said he is running because he believes in accountability and transparency and did not want to see Woolf run unopposed, like Woolf did in the 2014 and 2018 general elections. 
“Since I decided to run and I started talking to people, the very first questions I get asked are, ‘Do we have a controller? Who is the controller? What does the controller do?’” Mohan said. “So my very first thought was, boy, the controller and the state talk about transparency in government. But if people don’t even know we exist, then what kind of transparency do we have here?”
Rakesh Mohan
Mohan said he views the controller’s job as looking over taxpayer dollars that go to the state. The job also includes overseeing payroll for all state employees and making sure the right amount of money goes to the right place at the right time. Mohan said the office is responsible for statewide accounting and the state’s large data systems.
“It may sound boring to most people, but it is an extremely important job,” Mohan said. “And the controller is also responsible for paying all the bills. That includes multi-million dollar contracts.”
Mohan has two adult children and three grandchildren. He was married to his wife, Carolyn, for 44 years until she died in 2024.
 Meet incumbent Republican State Controller Brandon Woolf

Woolf first started at the Idaho State Controller’s Office as an intern in 1997 after graduating from Utah State University. 
He worked his way up to become payroll division administrator and, eventually, chief of staff for former Idaho State Controller Donna Jones. 
After Jones was seriously injured in a car accident in 2012, former Gov. Butch Otter appointed Woolf to finish Jones’ term while she focused on her recovery. Woolf ran for the position himself and won in 2014. He is finishing his third term of his own as state controller. 
Woolf said he thinks of the controller’s office as the “checkbook side” of the state government. The office is responsible for state payments, the largest of which is payroll to more than 37,000 state and university employees. 
Brandon Woolf
Beginning with his first day as state controller in 2012, Woolf said he focused on increasing transparency around state government, contracting and payroll. In 2013, the state launched the Transparent Idaho website, which Woolf says makes all state financial and organizational data accessible to the public. 
“It was always my vision that it’s not my money, it’s not the state’s money,” Woolf said. “We’ve been entrusted with those sacred tax dollars. And so where there is a lot of money that is being spent and being appropriated, it’s only right and correct that the citizens have a right to see where that money is spent. And so it’s truly opening the books and shining a light.”
Woolf is about to celebrate his 32nd wedding anniversary to his childhood sweetheart, Janalee. Together, Woolf and Janalee have three adult children and three grandchildren. 
 Idaho state controller candidates disagree over rollout of Luma statewide business system

One of the largest and most public projects under Woolf and the Idaho State Controller’s Office in recent years has been the 2023 launch of Luma, the massive statewide business system that is designed to centralize all of the state’s business, budget, payroll, human resources, procurement and financial management systems in one spot. State officials refer to Luma as a cloud-based enterprise resource planning system that more than 80 state agencies are tied into. 
Luma replaced a pair of 1980s-era business systems that had exceeded their lifecycle and were vulnerable to security threats and disruptions. Woolf said that many of the people who knew how to operate the old systems have retired, and the state was no longer able to update or receive any technical support for the old systems.
However, the rollout of Luma was dogged by data entry and reporting errors, some late or inaccurate state payments, uneven employee training and delays, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Even last year, some state budget analysts told state legislators there have been delays in required financial reports and state adults that were attributed to Luma. 
Citing an Idaho Office of Performance Evaluations report on Luma released after he retired, Mohan said he attributes many of Luma’s challenges to leadership challenges in the Idaho State Controller’s Office. 
Mohan alleged there has not been state accountability with Luma because Woolf is running for a new term and because one of the former top deputies in the controller’s office who worked with Luma now works with Infor, one of the companies that got the state contract for Luma.
“If I was the controller (when Luma rolled out), I would have resigned in disgrace,” Mohan said. “Maybe that’s a different way to perceive these things. His perception might be different than mine, but I would not have stayed in that position. And so that’s one accountability thing.”
Woolf said Luma works and is a safer, more modern system that does not have the same security vulnerabilities the legacy systems had.
“This was a massive, generational change,” Woolf said. 
“There were probably 50 or 60 different accounting systems in all these state agencies that are now merged into one and so, again, that was a massive lift,” Woolf said. “We did it within budget, and we felt that our procurement process was the right process and now we are being able to share lessons learned. Was it easy? No. Did we have our hiccups? Yeah, I won’t shy away from that. … Luma is working well, and it is doing what it is intended to do.”
Woolf said he would make the move to Luma again if he had to make the decision over again.

Republican incumbent State Controller Brandon Woolf: www.brandonwoolf.com
