name: WyoFile
title: State urges households to apply for underused low-income energy assistance ahead of winter heating season
description:
Only about 16% of eligible households take advantage of the federally funded Low Income Energy Assistance Program. Applications are now open.
The post State urges households to apply for underused low-income energy assistance ahead of winter heating season appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Too many qualifying Wyoming households go without federally funded dollars dedicated to help with winter heating bills, state officials say.
The Low Income Energy Assistance Program has about $11 million available for the upcoming winter heating season, which is comparable to past years and based on detailed data estimating the need in the state, LIEAP Program Manager Kristina Packard said. Yet, typically, only about 16% of eligible households actually apply for the help.


“I know there are families who are eligible for this that have not applied,” Packard told WyoFile. “It doesn’t hurt to apply. The assistance is there, and we just encourage everyone to complete the application.”
Even fewer than the annual average 16% of qualifying households applied to the program last winter, likely due to the fact that it was unusually mild, Packard said. Still, you never know what Wyoming might hold in store for any winter season. The LIEAP program is designed to help those households that pay a disproportionate amount of monthly income on essential services such as heat in the winter, she added.
The qualifying benchmark for Wyoming households — whether homeowners, renters or residents of permanently parked RVs and campers — is a gross annual income at or below 60% of the state’s median income. That translates to about $2,988 a month for an individual, $3,908 for a couple or $5,747 for a family of four.


How to applyTo find out if your household qualifies for winter heating assistance, apply online at mylieapwyo.org, or call (800) 246-4221, and the LIEAP team can help with your application over the phone. You can also reach out to Energy Share of Wyoming, which also provides energy assistance for households with special circumstances.


The assistance is for heating-related bills for electricity, natural gas, propane, wood pellets and other sources. The program pays for a portion of heating bills, Packard said, not necessarily a household’s total bills for the season. For example, the maximum benefit for a household’s electric bill is about $1,280 for the winter season. The benefit is recalculated each year to account for rising rates, she added. This season, the maximum benefit for electric heating bills is about 4% more than last season.

Wyoming Low Income Energy Assistance Program profile for the 2024-25 winter heating season. (Wyoming LIEAP)

Americans are projected to spend 8.7% more on home heating costs this winter compared to last season, primarily driven by higher electricity rates and heating oil costs, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. “More than 275 electric and natural gas utilities have either increased rates, received approval for rate increases or proposed increases since 2025,” the group said in a September report. “These increases could raise electricity and natural gas customers’ bills by more than $101 billion through 2028.”
Whether this year’s 4% benefit increase in Wyoming keeps pace with the rising cost of utilities may depend on who is serving up the energy.
Wyoming’s largest electric utility Rocky Mountain Power is seeking a 8.8% electrical rate increase, while Black Hills Energy has whittled a rate increase request of about 32% to below 29%, limited to about 2,600 customers in the northeast corner of the state. Torrington and the surrounding area tied to the city’s utility could see an 18% increase for summer electricity rates and 22% increase for wintertime rates, due to a change in how the cost of electrical transmission is calculated, which would increase monthly bills by about $11.
Another good reason to apply for LIEAP assistance, Packard said, is that if a household qualifies, it speeds up an assessment to potentially qualify for a replacement heating system — another part of the program that is vastly under-utilized.
“Not enough people know about that,” Packard said. “A $10,000 furnace replacement — that would impact anyone.”
Though LIEAP applications were especially anemic during the past mild winter, program staff received a flood of inquiries this summer, Packard said, when air-conditioning units worked overtime and Wyoming residents scrambled to find swamp coolers to combat a historically blistering, prolonged heat wave.
Wyoming Low Income Energy Assistance Program disbursements for the 2024-25 winter heating season. (Wyoming LIEAP)
Wyoming LIEAP couldn’t help, she said. The state’s annual application for the federal funds has exclusively been limited to winter heating because Wyoming is considered a “cold weather state” in terms of the federal program. There have been discussions about whether the state might one day apply to extend the federal assistance to summer cooling bills.
“It’s something that we are always looking at,” Packard said.
Last year, the Trump administration fired staff and threatened to defund the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, resulting in a 45-day delay before resuming disbursements to states in December.

name: WyoFile
title: Conservationists beware
description:
Don’t fall for the siren song of billionaire-backed ecotourism dressed up as conservation in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, writes guest columnist Lisi Krall.
The post Conservationists beware appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
My good friend Wes Jackson, who started the nonprofit organization The Land Institute, has an adage that I love. It’s simple: Money finds trouble. 

Opinion

When it comes to conservation, I believe Jackson’s adage is mostly true. It’s something to consider more critically for those of us who reside in or care about the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. From my home and vantage point along the Upper Hoback River, money is finding trouble — not conservation, as one nearby landowner claims — unless we stretch the definition of “conservation” to the point  it is meaningless. 
The narrative du jour is  that conservation is best done as a joint private/public effort.  I won’t argue that there isn’t a place for private conservation — people and organizations engage in setting up land trusts, conservation easements and other mechanisms of conservation on private land all the time. They even buy land and give it back to the state; the strategy of Tompkins Conservation. But the overarching notion that private/public efforts are the best way to effectively conserve land and habitat seems mostly snake oil. Public sector conservation has been a resounding success as attested to by national parks, national forests, wildlife refuges, national monuments, public lands and the myriad ways the government conserves the more-than-human world. 
The reality of private sector conservation is that it depends entirely on what the landowner is inclined to do. It becomes most dangerous, most compromising of conservation, when it is bolstered by the foundational belief that business and conservation can weave together the tapestry of the future relationship of humans and earth.  
The facts on the ground in the southern reaches of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem speak to a different reality of private conservation. This reality is that there are few opportunities of the economic variety that mesh with the mission of conservation. Here the snake oil of private/public conservation is more often than not a losing proposition for conservation. Yet it appears that somehow much of the conservation community has bought into the snake oil being promulgated. A narrative has been sold that there is a magical alchemy taking place where money is not finding trouble and conservation is moving ahead full speed under the watchful eyes of the billionaires. Look again. 
Perhaps conservationists have been thrown off their game by the allure of banded birds, biodiversity research, herds of domestic buffalo and “private landowner engagement.” The sales pitch is that these disparate efforts at conservation fold neatly into one big effective package for conservation. They don’t. In the southern reaches of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, private/public conservation partnerships have mostly meant figuring out a way to develop the private part.  
When I zoom in on a more detailed look of the private/public partnerships, what I find is an old story. Just look at the development along Granite Creek in Teton County. Thus far, this private initiative is a matter of heavy trucks and heavy machines moving lots of earth to build an elaborate ecotourism center called “The Hawken” that will cater to the very wealthy and make them feel like mountain men. It has meant massive noise and disruption to all creatures who normally take up any residence in the Granite Creek drainage in the summer, and it will mean cordoning off an area for the very wealthy that could have been brought into the national forest preserve. The U.S. Forest Service would not have engaged this initiative, and I suspect conservation and the general public would have been better served for it.  
Then there’s the Upper Hoback River which has been plagued for years by the threat of large-scale ecotourism enterprises catering to the wealthy. Keeping this ilk of private development at bay has been a full-time battle for many conservationists and concerned citizens of the Upper Hoback region. The battle goes on as another ecotourism initiative, “The Confluence” was proposed and problematically given a green light. Thankfully, the Sublette County Board of County Commissioners abided by the zoning laws that govern Sublette County and rescinded the green light, reverting the land back to agricultural zoning.    
So I am doling out some advice based on years of experience in the conservation trenches: Conservationists need to think carefully about the snake oil they buy. Understand that there is a massive public relations campaign to sell as conservation these cases of money finding trouble. The truth is there is only one way for conservation and certainly conservation of the wild — migratory paths, breeding grounds, winter range, open space — to take place. Let the words of the essayist and poet Gary Snyder speak to conservation: “Wilderness is a place where the wild potential is fully expressed, a diversity of living and non-living beings flourishing according to their own sorts of order.” My emphasis. Massive ecotourism lodges pretty much eliminate “their own sorts of order” for everything else. Expansive ecotourism sites for the wealthy, up small river valleys, smack dab in the middle of migratory paths don’t qualify as conservation. This is not rocket science.
Private conservation is not a bad thing if it’s really conservation; that is, if it’s conservation given over to the preservation of the wild where we humans and our economic enterprises actually step back, but what I see happening is not conservation — it’s just money finding trouble masked as some sort of cockamamie conservation alchemy that we would all be well served to think twice about.

title: In north Alabama congressional race, a Democrat pitches affordability and political reform
description: Throughout all of the 20th Century, Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, anchored in north Alabama, was represented by a Democrat. But in 2010, after the two parties had evolved and ideologically solidified into what they are today, voters sent Republican Mo Brooks to Congress, upending that longstanding electoral stasis. For nearly two decades now, the Rep[...]
text:
Andrew Sneed, the Democratic nominee for Alabama's 5th Congressional District, introduces Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones at a rally at Mars Music Hall in Huntsville, Alabama on Oct. 11, 2026. (Ben Sessoms for Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

In Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, incumbent U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, faces Democratic challenger Andrew Sneed, a businessman.
The district is rated R+15 by the Cook Political Report, but through June Sneed had managed to hold his own in fundraising.
Sneed’s campaign is focused on improving affordability, coupled with reform of the federal government and has accused Strong of not being available to constituents.
Strong cites his efforts to bring jobs and federal funding to the district and cites several tele-town halls he has held during his time in Congress.




Throughout all of the 20th Century, Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, anchored in north Alabama, was represented by a Democrat. But in 2010, after the two parties had evolved and ideologically solidified into what they are today, voters sent Republican Mo Brooks to Congress, upending that longstanding electoral stasis.
For nearly two decades now, the Republican Party has dominated the region. Brooks held the seat for 12 years, and incumbent Republican Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, has been in office since 2023 — with both winning with 60% or more of the vote each election cycle. In 2020 and 2024, Brooks and Strong won uncontested.
Enter Andrew Sneed, a Huntsville native whose professional career has taken him from the restaurant industry and the trades to starting his own contracting business in 2019. Now the Democratic candidate for the 5th Congressional District, an ostensibly deep red region, Sneed is daring to give politics a try.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Even with the seemingly long odds — the Cook Political Report rates the district solidly Republican — Sneed, 46, believes he has what it takes to pull off the upset, amid Donald Trump’s unpopularity and Republicans like Strong, according to Sneed, who are failing to hold the president accountable and deliver for ordinary people.
“We’re going to win because we’re actually addressing the needs and listening to folks. That’s exactly what he’s not doing,” Sneed said, referring to Strong. “I have 25 years in service. That’s all I’ve ever done. I’ve worked with my hands for 25 years — 10 years in restaurants, 15 years in the trades — as opposed to a career politician.”
When it comes to raising funds, Sneed has been competitive with Strong. While the incumbent retained an overall advantage in spending, fundraising and cash on hand through the end of June, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission, Sneed outraised Strong $162,000 to $125,600 between April and June. (Campaign finance reports for the race only run through June 30; filings covering July to September are due on Oct. 15.) 
Strong, a Huntsville area native, did not agree to an interview, but in emailed responses to questions, the incumbent said he believes his record warrants another term in office.
“In the last year I have brought home millions of dollars for new roads, secured a new veteran’s clinic and funding for the first Veteran’s cemetery in our community,” Strong said in an email. “I am also proud of my record on new jobs by bringing the Space Command Headquarters to Alabama plus more funding for Redstone Arsenal missile and aviation programs and the Marshall Space Flight Center.”

Affordability, political reform

Since Trump has returned to office, the Democratic Party’s primary electoral strategy in special and off-year elections, especially with high gas prices due to the president’s war in Iran, has been to focus on making the economy more affordable for the average American.
Mirroring this approach, Sneed’s platform centers on reducing housing, healthcare and energy costs. He has campaigned in particular against Republican cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act as well as Trump’s tariff policy, which the Yale Budget Lab has estimated to increase annual costs for the average American household by $1,100.
Voters in midterm elections identify a culprit for rising cost of living: Trump’s tariffs

For Sneed, though, the unaffordable economy doesn’t solely come from Trump’s agenda, nor is it a one-party issue; it is a problem with the current political system more broadly.
“What’s different about this campaign from truly most other campaigns in the country is that we immediately draw the connection to also what is deeply broken and how we got to this place,” Sneed said. “We’ve had a Democratic House, Senate, White House — the same with Republicans. But it seems like so often nothing changes, and we just find ourselves in this position.”
“We desperately as a district, but also as a nation,” he continued, “need Congress to be Congress again and do their damn jobs.”
Donald Trump tells Mobile rally to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’

As a remedy, Sneed has proposed a set of reforms through a coalition he founded called Balance Accountability Candidates, a slate of Democrats nationwide running for office who want to restructure the political and campaign finance system.
It boils down to five proposals: term-limiting members of Congress; overturning the flood of money into politics allowed by the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision Citizens United; prohibiting members of Congress from trading stocks; imposing a five-year moratorium on lobbying for former members of Congress; and establishing an enforceable code of ethics for the Supreme Court.
“Democrats around the country can talk about affordability all they want, but if people aren’t willing to vote for a Democrat because they don’t trust Democrats, then we’re just whistling Dixie,” Sneed said.
“I have heard all the time, and what I’ve even allowed to sort of feel within myself, is this idea that all politicians are the same,” he continued. “It’s a lack of trust. When you have Democrats getting rich in Congress and Republicans getting rich in Congress, why should they believe anything anyone says?”
Using tariffs as an example, Sneed said Congress should be exerting its authority to curb Trump’s overreach. But on any issue, Sneed sees a legislative body, one meant to derive its power from the people, unresponsive to its constituents.
“The job description for a representative is in the title; that’s represent,” Sneed said. “You can’t represent folks you don’t listen to.”
U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, arrives at the Hyatt Regency on November 13, 2022 in Washington, DC. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
Sneed has held numerous town halls throughout north Alabama during the campaign. He’s criticized Strong for turning down his invites to public speaking events and failing to hold town halls himself — “Dale Strong has refused to hold a real public town since he’s been in office, literally,” Sneed said. At a ribbon-cutting in August, Strong, referring to Sneed, told reporters that he doesn’t “know who the other guy is.”
In an email, responding to Sneed’s criticism, Strong said, “I have held several tele-town halls over the last two years reaching thousands of participants and giving them the opportunity to ask their questions to me directly.”
When it comes to fuel costs, Strong said in an email that the war has shown the United States to be too reliant on foreign oil. “Bad actors like Iran have too much control over our gas prices,” he said. “We need to become more energy independent by producing more oil in the US and building more refining capacity here at home.”
And when it comes to Trump, Strong said he is “running my own race.” 
“But I am confident that when voters compare the agenda that Democrats in Congress are pushing to what our Republican majority has achieved such as tax cuts for families, closing our border and increasing funding for our national defense, they will vote to continue our leadership,” he said.

The educational divide

Perhaps the greatest indicator of who chooses a Democrat in the Trump era, according to many political scientists, is educational attainment.
Per a Pew Research Center survey, 55% of respondents with a college degree were Democrats or leaned left. Conversely, 39% aligned themselves with the GOP or are inclined to.
This is a relevant statistic for Huntsville and Alabama’s 5th Congressional District. As reported by Forbes, the city, home to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, has the highest number of engineers per capita in the country.
According to the most recent data from the U.S. Census Bureau, 46.4% of residents in Madison County, of which Huntsville is the seat, have attained a bachelor’s degree — higher than the statewide rate of 28.4% and an increase from that a decade ago at 38.6%.
The other counties completely within the district — Limestone, Lawrence, Morgan and Jackson (only the eastern part of Lauderdale is in district) — have all seen the proportion of their populations with bachelor’s degrees grow in that time.

Seth McKee, a professor at Oklahoma State University whose research centers on politics in the South, said this link between greater educational attainment and Democratic Party affiliation wasn’t always the case; it was the opposite during the political era under President Ronald Reagan.
But starting in the early 2000s, he said, the trend started to reverse, and Trump accelerated it into the wide educational divide seen now.
“Trump’s been a catalyst just because of the way he presents himself,” McKee said. “That populist appeal, that doesn’t really grab on to people with more education. I think more educated people kind of know that this guy’s a clown and a grifter.”
Still, a majority of the 5th Congressional District does not have a bachelor’s degree — but Trump’s command over that base, given his performance in office over his second term, may be beginning to wane, at least in the immediate future.
“If you can’t perform, you’re going to disenchant people who otherwise would support you,” McKee said. “But longer term, I don’t know how much of an effect it will have.”

An urbanizing region

Big Spring International Park in Huntsville is seen on Oct. 11, 2026. The city surpassed Birmingham as Alabama’s most populous in 2021. (Ben Sessoms for Alabama Reflector)
That educational divide reinforces the ongoing rural-urban divide in American politics, McKee said. There is an incentive for those with higher education degrees to leave rural areas for economic opportunity in cities.
“The higher educated are going to be more likely to be in thriving metropolitan centers, a new economy, if you will,” McKee said. “So when you look at rural areas that are not growing, they tend to have lower education.”
This correlation between educational attainment and urbanization has borne out in Huntsville, which in 2021 overtook Birmingham to become Alabama’s largest city.  The surrounding counties in the district have seen a population increase as well.


David Damore, a political scientist at UNLV and co-author of “Blue Metros, Red States: The Shifting Urban/Rural Divide in America’s Swing States,” said that with urbanization, as that seen in the Huntsville area, there is generally a more Democratic-leaning electorate that forms, what he calls the presence of density and diversity.
“You’re exposed to lots of different viewpoints compared to a rural space that’s much more homogeneous. You tend not to have one dominant group who controls all the politics,” Damore said. “There’s coalition building, a lot more willingness to work with others who aren’t like you.”
The dynamic of urbanization in the South creating a more Democratic electorate has already happened in other parts of the region, such as in Georgia and North Carolina, though Florida is certainly, at the moment, an outlier.
But as of now, north Alabama, at least in Congress, is still red. But Democrats remain hopeful in the Huntsville area. Democratic Rep. Marilyn Lands flipped House District 10 blue in 2024, giving Alabama Democrats their first net seat gain in the Alabama Legislature in decades.
“We have so much growth here, so many people moving in from other states and even other countries,” Lands said. “It is changing very, very rapidly here.”
Whether it’s changing fast enough to turn the 5th Congressional District blue in November is an open question. For Sneed, the answer is a confident yes.
“We’re going to win,” Sneed said. “That change is coming, if we’ll just go out and fight for it and grab the reins.”

title: While Nashville’s downtown bar owners seek bailout from new tourism board, Haslam voices concerns
description: ​A board designed to oversee the distribution of excess tax revenue in downtown Nashville met for the first time earlier this month, with the state’s former governor voicing concerns about giving money directly to businesses. ​The board was partially tasked with finding a way to provide a government bailout after several bar owners in downntown […]
text:
Former Gov. Bill Haslam Former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam, left, a member of the Joint Capitol Tourism Board, expressed concerns about giving direct grants to businesses downtown. Haslam is pictured with sportscaster and Nashville resident Jim Nantz at the May 19 announcement the Super Bowl will be held in Nashville in 2030. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)​A board designed to oversee the distribution of excess tax revenue in downtown Nashville met for the first time earlier this month, with the state’s former governor voicing concerns about giving money directly to businesses.
​The board was partially tasked with finding a way to provide a government bailout after several bar owners in downntown Nashville on Broadway complained that large property valuation increases were driving up their tax bills.
​Former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam, a board member, said during the meeting that instead of giving money directly to companies, he would “encourage” the board to look into spending the money on projects for the “greater good.”
​“I think when we get into this with individual businesses it’s going to be a nightmare,” Haslam said. “You’re going to have companies, one across the street that is eligible, and one that is not.” 
Top Republicans push creation of a new state board to oversee Nashville tourism tax revenues

​Tennessee lawmakers created the nine-member Joint Capital Tourism Board earlier this year to distribute excess tax revenue created by downtown Nashville’s tourism development zone, TDZ.
​As part of the legislation, lawmakers wanted a way to move money from the TDZ to a different tourism zone on the city’s east bank to help fund road improvements, such as a connection between Oracle’s new campus and the East Nashville neighborhood.
​Tennessee Comptroller Jason Mumpower told board members that the excess revenue could be in the “tens of millions of dollars,” with an exact figure likely to be determined by the end of the year.
Officials estimated that there are nearly 2,600 businesses in the TDZ that could be eligible for the money. Haslam is majority owner of the National Hockey League’s Nashville Predators, who play in Bridgestone Arenaon Broadway.
​The new board is part of state Republicans’ continued attempts to assert more authority over the Democratic-run Nashville. 
Republican leaders in the legislature have advocated for property tax relief for Nashville’s downtown bar owners, who have complained about their tax bills after a recent property reassessment quadrupled valuations in some cases.



Quotation







I think when we get into this with individual businesses it’s going to be a nightmare.


– Former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam


​Nashville didn’t raise its property tax rate in 2025 but saw property values rise 45% across the city. Instead of lowering the tax rate to offset the higher valuation, the mayor and Metro Council kept rates at a level that resulted in a net increase in tax bills for many in the county.
​The downtown tax issue is further complicated because many bar owners are locked into a “triple-net lease,” which means they don’t own the property but are responsible for the higher tax bills.
​The millions in excess revenue, overseen by the new capital board, explicitly allows for property tax relief grants, payments to cover events such as the 2030 Super Bowl held at the new Tennessee Titans stadium, and public safety grants.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Northwest Arkansas candidates consider Iran war, immigration in US House race
description: Whoever is elected in November to represent Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District will have plenty of issues to address in Washington, including the Iran war, immigration and the nation’s budget.  Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack is vying for a ninth term in Congress and said he still has the energy, passion and drive to continue serving […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack, Democrat Robb Ryerse and Libertarian Bobby Wilson are seeking to represent Arkansas' 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. (Photos courtesy of the Arkansas secretary of state's office and Bobby Wilson)Whoever is elected in November to represent Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District will have plenty of issues to address in Washington, including the Iran war, immigration and the nation’s budget. 
Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack is vying for a ninth term in Congress and said he still has the energy, passion and drive to continue serving the district. The 69-year-old incumbent from Rogers faces challenges from Springdale Democrat Robb Ryerse and Bentonville Libertarian Bobby Wilson. 
Womack defeated Wilson in the 2024 general election and Ryerse in the 2018 Republican primary.
Diesel prices shoot upward as top farm-state GOP senator begs Trump for export embargo

All three candidates agreed it’s time to end the war in Iran, which has increased gas prices, an additional strain for Arkansans struggling with the rising cost of groceries. 
Womack said he believes the United States has achieved its objectives in the conflict, including taking out Iran’s ballistic missile capability and degrading the country’s capacity to develop a nuclear weapon.
“It’s time for that conflict to end, that we can get oil flowing through that Strait of Hormuz, give relief to the rest of the world and move on to the bigger threats out there,” he said. “And I think the pacing threat really right now is China and what’s happening in the Pacific.”
Wilson, chief operations officer of a trim and door company, said he is against the war and “being the world’s police force.” 
“Even if Iran is one of the worst governments, which I think they are, I just think it’s not our job,” he said. 
Ryerse, a 51-year-old pastor of a nondenominational church and director of development for a nonprofit working to end chronic homelessness, said to lower the costs of everything, the U.S. needs to end the Iran war and address tariffs President Donald Trump has levied since returning to office in 2025.
“If there’s anything economists hate, it’s uncertainty, so Congress needs to take back its tariff authority from the president so that we could have some predictability in our economy again,” Ryerse said. 
A resolution to curb the president’s military action in Iran that the U.S. House approved last month failed in the Senate.
Womack did not vote on the resolution, which was debated the week of his mother’s death. The Republican joined Arkansas’ Congressional delegation in voting against previous versions of the resolution earlier this year. 
Springdale Mayor Doug Sprouse (right) speaks with U.S. Rep. Steve Womack during the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale’s Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Immigration
A crackdown on immigration has been a hallmark of Trump’s second term. Womack agrees with “deporting criminal aliens,” but said there have been “unfortunate” outcomes in places like Minnesota.
A surge of immigration enforcement in January in Minneapolis led to community protests where federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens.
Arkansas grassroots initiatives that formed following Trump’s election have been critical of immigration enforcement in the state, which is often precipitated through partnerships between municipalities and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
An Arkansas community founded by Italian immigrants becomes a flashpoint over ICE

Womack said he supports going after the “worst of the worst,” but he wouldn’t have been as hard on immigrants who were “collateral” arrests, meaning they weren’t the original target of law enforcement operations. 
There are immigrants who come to the U.S. legally and overstay their visa, but that’s a different set of circumstances that requires a different solution, Womack said. 
“You can’t just put a mask on a Homeland Security officer, an ICE officer, and deal with them all in exactly the same way,” he said. “I think there are different levels of illegal behavior.”
Wilson said he has mixed opinions about immigration enforcement. Wilson supports restricting immigrants’ access to some federal programs, such as U.S. Small Business Association loans, and offering money to people who self-deport, but said he opposes “the cruelty” of how policies have been implemented. 
“If I do have one critique, it’s that I think that people actually and generally support a lot of these deportations, but don’t support the methods,” he said. 
Wilson said he supports border security because “the world’s a scary place with bioterrorism,” and is “agnostic” to Trump’s efforts to build a wall along the southern border.
Ryerse said he wants to abolish ICE. The agency is only two decades old, and customs and border patrol can enforce immigration laws as they did prior to its creation, he said. 
Trump directed billions of dollars to ICE in a 2025 tax and spending cut bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Ryerse said he’d use that money to make the nation’s “atrocious” immigration system more efficient by hiring asylum judges and staff to clear a backlog of cases.
“We have made this system so complicated and so convoluted that it’s actually easier to cross the desert than it is to navigate the American immigration system, and I just think that’s a tragedy,” he said.  
Democrat Robb Ryerse speaks to a group gathered for a Vote Common Good event in Rogers on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Ryerse said he also supports amnesty, something Republican President Ronald Reagan provided 40 years ago through legislation he signed that offered legalization to undocumented migrants who entered the country prior to 1982.
Details would need to be determined, but Ryerse said he would support a path to legalization for some of the nation’s undocumented immigrants who live in our communities, pay taxes and are “stuck in a system that moves very, very slowly.”
Federal budget
With the nation’s debt surpassing a record $40 trillion in August, the federal budget continues to be a concern for Congress. 
In June, Womack introduced a bipartisan bill to reform Congress’ budgeting process. The legislation calls for the creation of an 18-member bipartisan commission — appointed by the president and Congressional leaders — to develop policies to reduce the federal deficit.
Womack said there’s a challenge with safety net programs like Social Security, which will cut recipients’ benefits in 2032 without a plan to address insufficient funding. 
There are several options on the table, including raising the retirement age or looking at the threshold at which people stop paying taxes into the program, he said.
They’re tough decisions that elected officials concerned with losing elections don’t want to make, but Congress has to have a resolve to fix the problem, Womack said. 
“And the fix is probably going to hurt a lot of people, maybe everybody, but if the program’s going to survive, we’re going to have to do this,” he said. 
Wilson agreed no one is willing to address the cost of federal safety net programs.
US Senate candidates in 9 key races quiet about Social Security benefits cliff

“You’re really not going to touch the deficit until people are honest about Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid,” he said. “Everything else is just window dressing because the debt is massive.”
Wilson said he’d like to see more options for people under 35 to opt out of Social Security because the program likely won’t be there when they retire. If there were more retirement options for people paying into the program, that would lead to better outcomes, he said. 
Wilson is supportive of tax-advantaged “Trump Accounts” that receive $1,000 from the government for certain babies born in the U.S. between 2025 and 2028. Families and friends can contribute up to a combined $5,000 annually into the investment accounts that will gain interest. 
“Forty years in they’re going to have really good retirements, and I just think that the second and third and fourth order effects of this is just going to be so good for the country,” Wilson said.  
Ryerse said the people making decisions about how the country spends its money recently care more about priorities other than things that matter to the American public. 
“I think that budgets are moral documents that ought to reflect our values,” he said. 
It would be a better use of the country’s money to spend it “on things that are going to make a difference in people’s lives,” Ryerse said. That could look like addressing the affordable housing crisis with a program that provides down payment assistance for people like teachers and first responders so they can afford to live in the communities they serve, he said. 
Wilson said energy production could also help address affordability issues and bring down the cost of other goods and services.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Debates have changed the course of U.S. history. They could change Tennessee’s.
description: One of my hills to die on is that candidates for office should be willing to stand up before a public audience and state their cases. If a person believes they are the best person to serve in elected office, it should be a simple matter to state their qualifications, what they intend to do […]
text:
The last time U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn participated in a public forum, unconstricted by partisan politics, was furiThe last time U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn participated in a public forum, unconstricted by partisan politics, was during the 2018 U.S. Senate race with former Gov. Phil Bredesen. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)One of my hills to die on is that candidates for office should be willing to stand up before a public audience and state their cases.
If a person believes they are the best person to serve in elected office, it should be a simple matter to state their qualifications, what they intend to do in office, to at least have an idea about how they might accomplish it and to advocate for why they are the best choice.
And yet, over the last decade, it has become increasingly difficult to hold candidates accountable through forums.
This isn’t for a lack of effort: the Tennessee Press Association, TPA, which represents more than 135 news outlets across the state, invited the four major candidates — Republican nominee U.S. Sen Marsha Blackburn, Democratic nominee and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green and independent candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston — to an Oct. 27 gubernatorial forum at Middle Tennessee State University. 
In full transparency, I am a member of the TPA board.



				At this point in the process of trying to organize a forum, I’m considering setting up a “CSI”- style string-and-thumbtack chart in my office to keep track of who will debate whom and under what conditions.  


For ease of participation, TPA offered the candidates three dates from which to choose. Closed studio setting — no big public audience with which to contend, no security risks — live-streamed statewide, content distributed to organization members, held at Tennessee’s second-largest institute of higher education. 
But it’s been no easy thing to get candidates to confirm.
We got no response from Blackburn’s campaign despite multiple efforts: this wasn’t a surprise as Blackburn has agreed to no forums or debates throughout the campaign, including in the Republican primary. 
Blackburn, who has nearly 30 years of electoral experience in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to statewide office in 20 years, is the likely frontrunner. It’s no surprise every other gubernatorial candidate wants to get on a stage with her.
Several weeks ago, Hatley offered $1 million to three charities if Blackburn would debate him. 
Green, who has repeatedly challenged Blackburn to a showdown, confirmed her attendance after initially sending a news release saying she would only agree to participate if Blackburn did and blasting TPA for including the two independents, questioning TPA’s “criteria” for their inclusion.
Pinkston said she would debate anyone.
At this point, I’m considering setting up a “CSI”- style string-and-thumbtack chart in my office to keep track of who will debate whom and under what conditions. 
Gubernatorial candidates, clockwise from top, Lauren Pinkston, Democratic nominee Jerri Green and David Hatley will participate in an Oct. 27 sponsored by the Tennessee Press Association. (Photos: Pinkston and Hatley, John Partipilo; Green, Karen Pulfer-Focht)
In the not-so-distant past, debates, or public forums at least, were common in most Tennessee races. Traditionally, news outlets have hosted nonpartisan forums. Gannett, the parent company of the Tennessean in Nashville, the Memphis Commercial Appeal, and the Knoxville News Sentinel, among other outlets, has hosted many such events. 
They hosted a series of three in 2018 when Blackburn and Democratic nominee and former Gov. Phil Bredesen were vying for the U.S. Senate — the last time Blackburn participated in a fully open, nonpartisan public event. 
In 2022, The Tennessean held six candidate events statewide in the primary alone. 
But over the last decade, Republicans in Tennessee’s supermajority have become loath to debate, and GOP candidates rarely agree to do so. When Gov. Bill Lee ran for reelection in 2022, he said he couldn’t participate in a debate with Democratic nominee Dr. Jason Martin because of his wife’s health: First Lady Maria Lee was battling a rare lymphoma. 
No one will fault a guy prioritizing his wife’s health. But at the same time, Lee did find time to sit down solo with Tennessean Editor Michael Anastasi for a one-on-one at the University of Tennessee, and when questioned by Lookout Senior Reporter Sam Stockard in October 2022 on debate plans with Martin, Lee shied from answering.
I’m glad Tennessee voters will have the chance to see at least three of the gubernatorial candidates in action at the TPA forum, but there won’t be a public forum in the hotly contested 9th Congressional District, a race that has drawn national interest, between Rep. Justin J. Pearson, the Democratic nominee, and Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor.. 
Fifth District Republican nominee Charlie Hatcher has said he will debate his Democratic opponent, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, in an event sponsored by the Nashville Scene, but the election is less than a month away, and there’s nothing scheduled. 
I may be screaming into a void, but I firmly believe debates, or forums, are one of America’s noble political traditions. Without the 1858 Illinois U.S. Senate debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, would Lincoln have won the Senate seat and ultimately become president? 
Political scholars still cite the 1960 presidential debate between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon as a triumph of television, then a new medium: radio listeners thought Nixon the clear winner while TV viewers, taking note of Nixon’s pallor and sweat as he recovered from a knee infection, viewed the tanned Kennedy as the winner.
Public interaction between candidates has, literally, changed the course of U.S. history. 
And, with or without Republican participation, it’s likely to change Tennessee’s, too.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Digital system will help some WV Medicaid recipients navigate coming work requirements
description: With work requirements going into effect for many Medicaid recipients next year, one of West Virginia’s four managed care organizations is offering a new digital platform designed to make it easier for them to keep up with paperwork.
text:
Starting in January, work requirements will go into effect for many Medicaid recipients. (Photo via Getty Images)With work requirements going into effect for many Medicaid recipients next year, one of West Virginia’s four managed care organizations is offering a new digital platform designed to make it easier for them to keep up with paperwork. 
Highmark Health Options West Virginia is partnering with Fortuna Health, a program described as “Turbotax for Medicaid,” that’s designed to help them navigate the new rules. The platform will be available to the 20,000 state Medicaid recipients that have HHO as their managed care organization.
Jason Landers, president and CEO of Highmark Health Options West Virginia, said that “without question,” people who are eligible for Medicaid will lose their health coverage, at least temporarily, after the work requirements go into effect. 
“We are very concerned, and we know that people will lose coverage that are eligible,” Landers told West Virginia Watch. “And probably a lot of people that are even engaged in care management programs around diabetes management, or hypertension, or any number of things — they will lose coverage. They’ll regain it eventually, but they will lose coverage. 
“That’s not a provocative statement. That’s a statement of fact,” Landers said. 
With some exceptions, people 19 through 64 on expanded Medicaid will be required to work, train or volunteer at least 80 hours per month in order to keep their health coverage. Expanded Medicaid — available to low-income residents who earn up to $45,540 for a four-member family — covered 156,000 state residents as of earlier this year.
More information about the work requirements is available through the state’s website, wvmedicaidhelp.org. 
Medicaid will also increase the number of times it redetermines a person’s eligibility for the program from once to twice per year. 
An analysis by the state Department of Human Services earlier this year found that about 33,000 West Virginia residents would be affected by the changes. Policy analysts say eligible people will lose their health coverage because of the increased paperwork requirements.
The Medicaid changes are part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or H.R. 1, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance. President Donald Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025. 
Landers said the majority of Medicaid recipients who use Highmark have jobs, though they’re not traditional ones with employer-sponsored health coverage. An estimated 20% of HHO’s low-income Medicaid recipients will lose coverage, he said. 
“These are 20% of people that are deemed eligible,” he said. “They are eligible. They meet the requirements, but they will lose their coverage through an administrative decision because they likely won’t all redetermine.”
Landers said redetermining for Medicaid can be a “daunting” and “scary” task, much like filing taxes. He compared the Fortuna platform to what TurboTax does for filing taxes. Users answer a series of questions and the program guides them based on their answers. 
“They’ve implemented a lot of really smart AI that makes it feel conversational, almost,” he said. “Something as daunting sounding as ‘I’ve got to redetermine for my Medicaid’ becomes a very streamlined, simple sitting-in-your-living-room process, which is really nice.”
A spokesman for Fortuna Health said the platform will be a “digital Medicaid navigator” for Highmark Health Options members. The company will support members in three ways:

Targeted renewal outreach and reminders through email, SMS and Voice AI
Guided navigation through the redetermination process and 
Multi-lingual live agent support from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time during the week. Members can get answers about renewal status, deadlines, required documents, income calculations, and related questions, he said. 

The Fortuna program will steer people to PATH, West Virginia’s online management program.
Medicaid recipients don’t need to do anything immediately in order to stay on Medicaid, Landers said. Fortuna will reach out to them about redeterminations. 
“We know the dates that they’re required to do redetermination, so we’ll obviously focus our efforts around the dates for those specific members,” Landers said. “We’re not going to annoy members that don’t need a redetermination… We’re going to focus our efforts around the time that they actually need to do this interaction.”

title: North Dakota on pace to lose out on $66M from permanent oil tax break questioned by lawmakers
description: This is the first in a two-part series supported by a grant from the Fund for Investigative Journalism. Coming Tuesday, how North Dakota compares to other major oil-producing states. An obscure tax incentive to keep older oil wells afloat is potentially costing North Dakota hundreds of millions of dollars in tax revenue, even as many […]
text:
This oil well operated by XTO Energy in Williams County, pictured Sept. 2, 2026, is certified as a stripper well. It produced 280 barrels of oil per day in May, eight times the threshold for the tax exemption, state data shows. (By Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)This is the first in a two-part series supported by a grant from the Fund for Investigative Journalism. Coming Tuesday, how North Dakota compares to other major oil-producing states.
An obscure tax incentive to keep older oil wells afloat is potentially costing North Dakota hundreds of millions of dollars in tax revenue, even as many of those wells no longer meet the program’s criteria.
The state is on pace to lose $66 million in tax revenue this year from the more than 700 oil wells that no longer qualify for the tax break but continue reaping the benefits, a North Dakota Monitor investigation found. 
Unlike other top oil-producing states, North Dakota’s tax exemption is permanent even when a well begins producing more oil. 
“I just don’t think this is good policy,” said Rep. Jon Nelson, R-Rugby. “I’m disappointed that we’ve let this go this long without taking some action.”
More than half of the 20,000 active oil wells in North Dakota have been certified as stripper wells, or low-producing wells, and pay a 5% gross production tax. But they are exempt from paying a 5% oil extraction tax. 
The program as a whole is on pace to cost the state an estimated $260 million in tax revenue this year, the investigation found. The North Dakota tax department has told lawmakers the tax break cost more than $200 million annually since the start of the 2023-2025 biennium. 
“I don’t think anybody can deny that that is substantial,” said Sen. Mark Enget, R-Powers Lake. “That’s considerable. It’s material. No doubt about it.”
Thousands of oil wells were drilled during the Bakken oil boom, which saw a peak drilling rig count in 2012. But new drilling has slowed significantly, and many of the wells drilled during the boom are aging and less productive. Stripper wells accounted for 16% of the state’s total oil production in 2025, Department of Mineral Resources data shows. 
(Source: Department of Mineral Resources. Graphic by Kayden Schmitcke/For the North Dakota Monitor)
The stripper well tax exemption was established in 1980, according to Legislative Council research. But it was in 2025 when lawmakers learned the tax break was being used so much it effectively reduced the state’s tax on oil by a full percentage point. 
Rep. Don Vigesaa, R-Cooperstown, said it was an “eye-opener.” 
Bakken and Three Forks wells, which account for most of North Dakota’s production, can be certified as stripper wells when their oil production falls below 35 barrels per day for 12 consecutive months. 
But a well’s production can be restored to peak levels and still retain the reduced tax rate. 
“A producer can just pump up the volume through technology and whatever, and we’re missing out on a lot of tax revenue,” said Vigesaa, one of the Legislature’s top budget writers. 
One example is an XTO Energy oil well drilled in Williams County in 2009 and certified as a stripper well in 2017. Its production skyrocketed in 2024, according to Department of Mineral Resources data. The well has produced 228,000 barrels of oil, averaging around 300 barrels per day, in the last two years. But it was still taxed as a stripper well at half the rate.
The oil from those two years likely generated an estimated $14.9 million in revenue, according to calculations using Energy Information Administration pricing data. XTO Energy is a subsidiary of ExxonMobil, the largest American oil company. 
North Dakota law does not contain any provision for revoking a stripper well’s tax exemption if its production swells. More than 700 stripper wells produced in excess of 35 barrels per day while still benefiting from the reduced tax in the first five months of 2026, state data shows. 
Ron Ness, president of the North Dakota Petroleum Council, said the tax incentive helps encourage companies to keep older, less profitable wells online. Those wells pay local taxes, employ local workers and have already paid their fair share at the full tax rate, he said. 
“They paid their taxes. They paid their dues. So it’s like taxing the elderly or taxing people that are at the end of their careers,” Ness said. 
An ExxonMobil spokesperson said the company invests $500 million in the Bakken annually, supports around 1,000 jobs and is investing in enhanced oil recovery technologies that could benefit North Dakota. 
“Increasing the cost of those projects by changing regulations to increase taxes will make it less likely for investments to come to North Dakota versus other assets that can also benefit from that technology,” the spokesperson said in an email. 
Rep. Craig Headland, from left, Sen. Mark Enget and Sen. Brad Bekkedahl participate in a lawmaker panel Sept. 17, 2025, during the North Dakota Petroleum Council annual meeting in Watford City. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Many state officials consider the development of enhanced oil recovery technology, including the use of carbon dioxide injections to restore the productivity of older wells, the key to extending North Dakota’s oil production. Rep. Craig Headland, R-Montpelier, said modifying the stripper well tax policy is premature until that technology breakthrough occurs.  
“We’ve become an energy powerhouse in oil production, and we’re hoping that we can remain that way,” Headland said. “It’s going to take some incenting. How are we going to get the oil industry to invest in enhanced oil recovery, just so we can tax the hell out of them?”
Yet some lawmakers said the tax break warrants discussion when the Legislature convenes in 2027 because new revenue could help address more immediate challenges facing North Dakotans. 
“Every dollar could be used for something for our citizens,” said Rep. Karla Rose Hanson, D-Fargo. 
If a ballot measure to provide free school meals passes in November, lawmakers will be tasked with finding a way to pay an estimated $67 million per year for the program.
No recertification
North Dakota is unusual among major oil-producing states because its stripper well tax designation is permanent. There is no process in state law that allows an agency to revoke that status after it is granted. 
“That’s fairly unique. I haven’t heard of that before,” said Dewey Bartlett, a board member with the National Stripper Well Association.
Bartlett, the owner of an oil company in Oklahoma that focuses on stripper wells, said it’s typical to have to reapply for stripper well tax breaks annually and self-certify that a well meets eligibility requirements, just like someone doing their income taxes. He said it should be easy for regulators to determine which wells are overproducing and correct the tax status.
“The rule is the rule, and if they do exceed that status, then I think that it needs to revert back,” Bartlett said. “I think it’s only fair.”
North Dakota sees uptick in oil wells that qualify for tax exemption

Enget said he was surprised to learn North Dakota doesn’t already have a review process in place. The lawmaker retired after working in the oil industry in other states for decades. 
“I don’t know why there aren’t any laws in place that can cause a redesignation of the well and take the stripper status away from it,” Enget said.
North Dakota is the only one of the top eight oil-producing states to grant a permanent tax status for stripper wells. Alaska and California do not have an equivalent program. Oklahoma, Wyoming and Colorado handle eligibility through an annual tax filing process. Texas and New Mexico offer tax reductions during periods of low oil prices that only apply to qualifying wells.
The idea of an annual review process was briefly suggested during a committee meeting at the end of the 2013 legislative session but never added to state law. Lynn Helms, then the chief oil and gas regulator for the state, said at the time “it would be somewhat burdensome” depending on the details, “but it would be doable,” according to legislative audio records. 
Lost revenue
The most productive stripper well in North Dakota in May was another well owned by XTO Energy in Williams County that began producing oil along the north shore of Lake Sakakawea in 2009. 
In May, it produced an average of 529 barrels of oil per day, or nearly 15 times more than a stripper well should, and more than the well had ever produced before.
It was certified as a stripper well in 2021. The most productive months of the well’s life have come in April through July of this year, according to state production data. 
XTO Energy’s well was one of eight stripper wells in North Dakota that produced more than 345 barrels of oil per day in May, around 10 times the threshold for stripper well status. There were at least 719 stripper wells that produced above the 35-barrel threshold in May, according to state data. 
“They should lose that stripper well status at that point,” Nelson said. “That just seems to be elementary to me.”
Rep. Jon Nelson, R-Rugby, speaks during a legislative committee meeting on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The 700-plus wells in that category have been exempt from paying an estimated nearly $28 million in taxes in the first five months of this year, according to state production data and average oil prices from the Energy Information Administration. That puts them on pace for around $66 million in all of 2026.
Wells less than 10,000 feet deep, or from formations other than the Bakken, have lower production thresholds for the tax break. The Department of Mineral Resources told lawmakers last winter the total number for all formations was 892.
The exemption applies to more than 12,000 stripper wells. This year, the tax break has cost the state an estimated $109 million as of May 31, according to state data and Energy Information Administration pricing. That is on pace to be around $260 million by the end of 2026.
Oil taxes are the single largest source of tax revenue for North Dakota state government and account for around half of the state’s general fund budget, said Joe Morrissette, director of the Office of Management and Budget. 
“The truth is that over the last like 15 years, we have had significant tax relief,” Morrissette said, citing income, corporate and property tax cuts. “Those things are made possible because of the revenues that the state collects from oil activity. So we should all care about that.”
Large companies, small communities benefit
Stripper wells can be an important source of employment, economic activity and tax revenue for local communities. Enget said big companies will often sell older oil wells to smaller companies that are often locally owned, who continue paying taxes on the oil production. 
“It’s good for the state. Good for the local economy. I would say it’s good all the way around,” Enget said. 
He said many smaller companies operate stripper wells in Burke County, where he lives. But that isn’t always the case in North Dakota as thousands of Bakken wells become eligible for the tax break. 
A Continental Resources well pad south of Ray, North Dakota, photographed from a drone on Sept. 2, 2026. One of the wells is a stripper well that produced 158 barrels of oil per day in May. (By Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)
The largest oil company in North Dakota, Chord Energy, operates nearly one-quarter of the state’s stripper wells. The five largest oil companies in the state operated slightly more than half of the 12,872 stripper wells that were active in 2025, according to state data. 
Those stripper wells remain important for North Dakota communities, regardless of how big the company that owns them is. The tax break for stripper wells reduces the revenue collected by the state. But those stripper wells continue paying a 5% gross production tax that is primarily distributed among counties, cities, school districts and townships.
State officials worry companies could choose to shut down stripper wells if changes to the tax incentive make those wells unprofitable. Morrissette said that possibility, which is difficult to project, throws a wrench into any attempt to estimate how much additional tax revenue a change could generate. 
“You’re still getting 5%,” Morrissette said. “You might be getting zero if those wells were shut in.”
Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston, pointed out that if the state is losing out on millions of dollars of revenue, then local governments continue to collect an equal amount from the same wells. 
“The tradeoff is, do you compromise that funding stream by further burdening the economics of these wells so they are no longer producing any tax revenue?” Bekkedahl said during a legislative meeting last month. 
Return on investment
A Bakken oil well is most productive in its first months of oil production. Charles Gorecki, CEO of the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota, said an average Bakken well produces about 75% of its oil in the first seven years of production before being certified as a stripper well. The remaining 25% of the oil could take decades to produce and would be at the reduced tax rate. 
But sometimes a well can be returned to near-peak production — for a variety of reasons. Production from one of the XTO Energy wells surged in 2024 when the company hydraulically fractured the Bakken rock formation in the area for a new group of wells nearby. 
Companies can achieve similar results through other restimulation methods, like refractures. Many Bakken wells drilled prior to 2013 used less effective fracking techniques. If an oil company invests to refracture the underground rock using modern technology, that well’s production can surge. 
(Graphic by Kayden Schmitcke/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Gorecki said a successful refracture could restart the clock on how much of a well’s potential oil has been pumped to the surface. But this time the well retains the 50% tax cut of a stripper well. 
Lawmakers interviewed for this article said they are concerned companies are incentivized to wait until a well reaches stripper well status before investing in any process that may increase oil production — but with half the tax. 
“From a business standpoint, it makes perfect sense to do it,” Nelson said.
Nathan Anderson, director of the North Dakota Department of Mineral Resources, said it is unlikely publicly traded oil companies would plan decades ahead in order to let an oil well receive stripper well status before restoring production levels. 
“Wall Street’s greedy, and they’re not waiting for 25 years from now to get their return. They want their returns today because the people that are investing in them want that,” Anderson said.
A refracture is one of the most expensive methods of increasing production at between $2 million and $3 million, and is not always successful, Ness said. He warned that trying to “squeeze every penny out of these wells” could discourage that investment into older oil wells. 
State data shows there have been 216 refractures since 2022. Companies’ expense and profit data on refractures is not reported to the state. 
Ness said he does not support making any changes to the stripper well tax incentive at this time.
Possible change in 2027
The prospect of additional state revenue is a big issue for some lawmakers, who see a list of needs in the state that could benefit from funding. 
“This is a significant source of revenue that we need to look at. There are significant needs across our state,” Hanson said. “Even $40 million, while it might not be a big percentage of a $20 billion budget, still could make a significant difference in a program that changes a family’s life.”
Other lawmakers, like Headland, said they believe the potential of new revenue is not enough to justify making changes that could prompt oil companies to plug less productive wells and deprive local governments of even more in tax revenue. 
Lawmakers said they expect stripper wells to be discussed during the 2027 legislative session. 
“I think we need to keep this on the front burner. I really do,” Nelson said. “There’s a happy medium here that we could try.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Roll the tape: A look back at memorable Arkansas debates
description: It’s debate week in Arkansas. Candidates for the state’s top races on the ballot this year are squaring off over the next four days in Conway as Arkansas TV hosts a series of debates. Debates may not necessarily win an election, but they can provide memorable exchanges and fodder for political attacks.  To prepare for […]
text:
Republican incumbent French Hill and Democratic challenger Marcus Jones (at right) participate in a televised debate Oct. 7, 2024. (Screenshot from Arkansas PBS)It’s debate week in Arkansas.
Candidates for the state’s top races on the ballot this year are squaring off over the next four days in Conway as Arkansas TV hosts a series of debates.
Debates may not necessarily win an election, but they can provide memorable exchanges and fodder for political attacks. 
To prepare for this week’s debates, here’s a look at some recent debates in Arkansas politics.
2022: Sanders’ debate debut
Sarah Huckabee Sanders had experience fielding questions from her time as White House press secretary, but 2022 was her first experience debating as a candidate.
Sanders faced Democrat Chris Jones and Libertarian Ricky Dale Harrington in the debate on Arkansas public television. 
Sanders will debate Democratic nominee Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby Tuesday.



 
2020: Another Cotton-less debate
The Senate debate this week won’t include Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who’s being challenged by Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin.
Cotton, who is seeking a third term, has so far only agreed to a debate with Shoffner on a conservative Christian media outlet.
Cotton opted out of the Arkansas public television debate six years ago. That year, the only Democrat who was running dropped out after the filing period ended. 
Without Cotton, the debate only featured Harrington, who was the Libertarian nominee.



 
2014: A bruiser of a Senate debate
Cotton participated in two debates in 2014 when he successfully challenged then-Democratic Sen. Mark Pryor. 
More than $50 million was spent by both sides in the nationally watched race for Senate that year, and the debates reflected just how intense the campaign had begun.
One of the most memorable exchanges came when Pryor was asked to define the middle class.



 
2018: Another time Democrats eyed Hill’s seat
U.S. Rep. French Hill is in a familiar position this year as national Democrats are investing resources to flip his central Arkansas district.
Hill, who debates Democratic challenger Chris Jones this week, has attracted similar attention before. In 2018, Democratic Sen. Clarke Tucker ran against Hill for the 2nd District seat.
Tucker repeatedly criticized Hill for his efforts to repeal the Affordable Care Act, though questions about healthcare didn’t come up  when they faced off for a debate.



 
2026: Sanders’ rivals set their sights on her and each other
Sanders wasn’t on stage when Love and Shelby debated at the Arkansas Press Association’s convention earlier this year. But the Republican governor’s policies were the main topic.
Love and Shelby exchanged criticism of each other, but mostly focused on distinguishing themselves from Sanders during the debate. Notably, Love vowed to sign an executive order ending the school voucher program created under Sanders’ signature education law.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina Muslims have spent decades building political power. What has it produced?
description: On a blistering Friday morning at a Durham mosque, Nigel Edwards sets up a table with voter registration materials that include buttons, signs, posters and flyers.  “Are you registered to vote?” he asks those filing past as sweat drips down his chin. Some are already registered, others are noncitizens, and a few say voting doesn’t […]
text:
Nigel Edwards speaks with attendees at a voter registration table after Friday prayers at a Durham mosque. 
(Photo: Ahmed Jallow/NC Newsline)
On a blistering Friday morning at a Durham mosque, Nigel Edwards sets up a table with voter registration materials that include buttons, signs, posters and flyers. 
“Are you registered to vote?” he asks those filing past as sweat drips down his chin. Some are already registered, others are noncitizens, and a few say voting doesn’t matter. 
“We want candidates to motivate us to vote, but unless we show up as a community, those candidates will never appear in the first place,” said Edwards, an immigration attorney and president of the North Carolina-based Muslim American Public Affairs Council. 
In recent years, Muslim organizers in North Carolina have been working to build a political infrastructure to register voters, engage candidates and give the state’s growing Muslim population a more organized voice in government. 
Several of those organizations now meet monthly to discuss their current initiatives and how they can support one another.
“We meet once a month, and we say who’s doing what, what’s their initiatives right now, and how can we assist each other on those initiatives,” said Al Rieder, regional community engagement manager for the Council on American-Islamic Relations. 
CAIR, a Muslim civil rights and advocacy group, expanded into North Carolina in 2023 to serve the state’s growing Muslim population. North Carolina now has 130,000 Muslim residents, the 11th-largest population in the country.
Building political power
When Muslim Women For was founded in 2016, Lela Ali was a college student trying to figure out how to build safety and political power in her community. 
Three young Muslims had been killed in Chapel Hill the year before, as the country headed into a presidential campaign marked by anti-Muslim rhetoric. The violence, Ali said, felt painfully close to home. 
“It was a moment where we were very shook to our core that this sort of violence would just hit our community and our backyard in this way,” said Ali. 
Ali and the other founders wanted to build something in response. But she said young Muslims had a few places to organize outside traditional religious institutions. 
“There was very little organizing happening,” said Lela Ali, a co-founder of the group. “There were very little spaces that created that sense of a political home for young people, especially young Muslims.” 
A decade later, Muslim organizers have built some of the infrastructure Ali said was missing. The Charlotte Muslim Caucus maps early voting sites near mosques, organizes “Prayers to the Polls” events, and interviews candidates before deciding whether to endorse them, said Nasif Majeed, the group’s president and co-founder.
“We wanted to give our masjids a way to engage the community in civic politics and grassroots engagement,” Majeed said. The organization was founded in 2023. 
Last year, the group endorsed newcomer JD Mazuera Arias, who defeated incumbent Marjorie Molina by 34 votes to win a seat on the Charlotte City Council. 
“The Muslim caucus endorsement is meaningful because it does reflect a community that is increasingly organized and engaged in our local democracy,” said Mazuera Arias.
The relationship has continued beyond the election, Mazuera Arias said. Since taking office, he has consulted the caucus on issues affecting Muslim residents and businesses, including restrictions involving halal food trucks. 
Durham County Commissioner Nida Allam speaks to the media. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
That kind of organizing was harder to find when Nida Allam first ran for office in Durham in 2019.
“It was very eye-opening,” Allam said. “Even in the most progressive county of North Carolina, like the bluest county, I was faced with a lot of Islamophobia and xenophobia that I didn’t expect.”
The experience led Allam to look for another elected Muslim woman in North Carolina who could advise her on dealing with the hostility she faced. She found none. 
In 2020, Allam became the first Muslim woman elected to office in North Carolina. Since then, she said, groups like Muslim Women For have developed resources that did not exist when she first ran.
“Now they have established themselves, and they have paid canvassers, they have paid phone bankers, folks that they can send to the polls to do voter protection, and that didn’t exist when I first ran,” Allam said.
Muslim political organizing in North Carolina has been around for decades. 
North Carolina Muslim groups push voter registration ahead of November election

At 14, Fleming El-Amin went with a barber to hear a Nation of Islam preacher speak about Black history and pride. It was his first visit to a Nation of Islam temple and the beginning of a decades-long connection to Muslim civic and political organizing. 
He later served as president of the American Coalition for Good Government, founded in Charlotte in 1997 to encourage Muslims to engage in politics and run for office. He also served on the Forsyth County Board of Commissioners from 2016 to 2022. 
“When I first got involved, it was almost like a new thing, a new idea of religion,” said El-Amin, who is now 74. Muslims, he said, were “not very much engaged in community prayers outside of their own mission. But over time, you know, the community has grown substantially.” 
That growth has changed how Muslim organizers interact with elected officials, El-Amin said. He pointed to his work with former state Senator Larry Shaw to establish the right for Muslim elected officials in North Carolina to take their oaths of office on the Quran. He also pointed to the governor’s Ramadan dinners, which began in 2018, as an example of how the relationship between Muslim leaders and state government has changed.
“It was unimaginable 30 years ago that the governor of North Carolina would invite us to the mansion to have a dinner sponsored by him, for the most part, for all the Muslim leaders in the state of North Carolina,” he said. “That’s been a good example of how the community’s progressed over the years.”
How much influence?
The growth of that infrastructure does not necessarily mean Muslim organizers have developed a consistent political force across the state. 
Chris Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University, said he looks for three things when assessing whether a community has developed meaningful political capacity: size, organization and stability. 
Prof. Chris Cooper (Photo: wcu.edu)
Size matters because “politics is ultimately a game of numbers,” Cooper said. But having people with similar interests is different from having an organization capable of mobilizing them. Stability, he said, means being able to remain part of the political conversation election after election. 
By those measures, Cooper sees Muslim political organizing taking hold in parts of North Carolina, but not statewide yet. 
“I think there are pockets of that, some localized pockets, which is a good thing for influence,” Cooper said, “but it doesn’t appear to be repeated consistently across the state.” 
Cooper said he also could not identify a single statewide Muslim organization comparable to groups such as the AARP or NRA. Building that kind of influence takes time, he said. 
“I think that’s what the Muslim community should be aspiring to: the ability to play the long game,” Cooper said.
Edwards has seen that evolution from inside MAPAC. 
He was initially only loosely involved with the organization after being introduced to it through someone who rented office space where he worked. His involvement grew around an effort to reopen the mosque at Shaw University. 
MAPAC formed after the Sept. 11 attacks, when organizers saw a need for greater political engagement amid backlash against Muslims. Edwards said the organization was built around establishing relationships with elected officials before the community needs their help. 
Those relationships have sometimes paid off, he said. Edwards pointed to the effort to reopen the mosque at Shaw University, where MAPAC members used their relationships with Raleigh City Council members to bring attention to the issue while the university was pursuing a rezoning. 
But Edwards said the harder challenge is getting people to participate consistently. 
MAPAC has held candidate forums, produced voter guides and registered voters, but turnout at some events remains low, he said, and politicians do not always respond to invitations. 
“It’s hard to tell people to show up when the candidates don’t come,” Edwards said. “So it’s a chicken-and-egg problem.”
